thirtyDayPlan.title: Lock in the fundamentals
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Spend the first week on networking and OS basics: TCP/IP, DNS, common ports, Windows/Linux command line. Use Professor Messer's free Network+ and Security+ videos as your spine.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Build a home lab
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Install VirtualBox, spin up a Kali Linux and a Windows VM, and stand up a free SIEM (Elastic or Splunk free tier). Generate and ingest some logs so you can see real telemetry.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Learn the attacker's playbook
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Work through the MITRE ATT&CK framework and map 10 common techniques (phishing, credential dumping, lateral movement) to what they look like in logs.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Practice real triage
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Do the LetsDefend or TryHackMe 'SOC Analyst' path for at least 15 alerts, writing a short investigation note for each as if handing it off to a teammate.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Mini project: build a phishing-alert triage runbook
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Take a real phishing email sample, analyze its headers, URLs, and attachment hash in VirtualBox/VirusTotal, and write a one-page step-by-step runbook plus a verdict. This is a portfolio piece.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Start Security+ prep
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Schedule the CompTIA Security+ exam ~8-10 weeks out and begin structured study; it is the credential most entry-level SOC job postings actually ask for.

automates: First-pass alert triage and enrichment (auto-pulling IP reputation, hashes, and user context into one summary).
Summarizing long log timelines and writing first-draft incident notes.
Correlating events across tools and flagging which alerts statistically resemble known attack patterns.
Auto-closing high-confidence false positives and deduplicating repetitive alerts.
Drafting and suggesting detection rules and regex from natural-language descriptions.
humanValue: Final judgment on whether a genuinely ambiguous alert is a real incident, weighing business context the AI cannot see.
Out-of-band verification with real people (calling the user, confirming with HR) before taking disruptive action.
Incident command and communication under pressure - coordinating teams, briefing executives, making containment trade-offs.
Ethical and legal judgment on disclosure, evidence handling, and proportional response.
Adversarial creativity: anticipating novel attacker behavior that no model has seen in training data.
aiImpact.riskNote: AI is automating the high-volume Tier-1 triage that used to be the entry-level on-ramp, so the easiest junior roles are shrinking and getting harder to land. But demand is still projected to grow ~33% through 2033, and the core of the job - judgment under uncertainty, incident response, and adversarial thinking against humans who actively evade automation - resists full automation. Net effect: the floor rises, the bar for entry goes up, but the profession itself is not disappearing.

shift.intro: It's 10:58 PM, you've just badged into the SOC for a night shift, and the overnight SIEM queue already glows with 312 unread alerts stacked on the wall monitor.
shift.closer: You spent eight hours proving that 311 alerts were nothing so that you could catch the one that was everything, and the hardest part wasn't the hacker, it was staying sharp through the noise and standing your ground when everyone wanted you to just close the ticket.

beats.title: The Overnight Queue
beats.situation: The handoff note from the swing-shift analyst reads only: 'Quiet night, queue's a mess, good luck.' You have 312 open alerts from the last eight hours. Most are noise: a credentialed vuln scanner lit up every host, an HR app keeps throwing malformed-cert warnings, and a sales rep is bouncing between VPN exit nodes. Somewhere in here might be something real, and you have one set of eyes until 7 AM.
beats.decision: How do you attack the queue at the start of your shift?

options.text: Sort by severity, then bulk-suppress the known scanner's host range after confirming the scan window in the change calendar, so the real signals surface.
options.consequence: You clear 180 scanner alerts in twelve minutes with a justification tied to ticket CHG-4471. By midnight you're working a clean queue and have the bandwidth to notice the one alert that actually matters at 2:40 AM.

options.text: Work strictly top-to-bottom in timestamp order so nothing gets skipped, reading every single alert in full.
options.consequence: You're thorough but slow. By 2 AM you're only 40% through, fatigued, and giving a low-value cert warning the same attention as a real threat. You technically touched everything but burned your sharpest hours on noise.

options.text: Select-all the yellow alerts and mass-close them as 'routine noise' to crush the count, then start fresh on the reds.
options.consequence: Two days later an audit sampling pulls three of your bulk-closed alerts and finds one was a real lateral-movement probe you never read. Your name is on the closure with no justification, and now you're explaining it to the SOC lead and a compliance officer.

beats.title: The Phishing Report
beats.situation: An employee in Finance forwards a suspicious email to the phishing inbox: an invoice from a 'vendor' with a link to a OneDrive-looking login page. The user swears they didn't enter credentials but 'clicked to see what it was.' The sender domain is three days old. Six other people in Finance were on the To: line.
beats.decision: What's your move on this user-reported phish?

options.text: Detonate the link in a sandbox to confirm it's a credential harvester, then search mail logs for all recipients and pull the message from every inbox, and check auth logs for any of the six who may have entered creds.
options.consequence: The sandbox confirms a Microsoft 365 credential-harvesting kit. You purge the email from all seven mailboxes before the morning rush, find one recipient who did submit a password, and force-reset them. You quietly stopped a breach before it started.

options.text: Confirm it's malicious, block the sender domain at the gateway, and reply to the reporter thanking them, but don't hunt for the other recipients.
options.consequence: You stopped this domain, but the attacker rotates to a new lookalike domain by morning and the other five Finance recipients never got warned. One of them clicks the new link at 9:15 AM. Now it's an active incident on day shift instead of a closed ticket on yours.

options.text: Tag it 'user education needed,' send the reporter a phishing-awareness PDF, and close the ticket since they say they didn't enter credentials.
options.consequence: You trusted the user's self-report. The one recipient who actually entered their password gets their mailbox rules hijacked, and an attacker uses it to send a wire-fraud request to the controller four days later. The post-incident review traces it straight back to this closed ticket.

beats.title: Impossible Travel on the CFO
beats.situation: Your SIEM fires a high-severity 'impossible travel' alert. The CFO's account had a successful VPN login from an IP geolocated in another country, only 25 minutes after a normal login from headquarters. The session shows MFA was satisfied via a single push approval, and there are zero failed login attempts. The CFO is asleep and not answering email. The night is dead quiet otherwise.
beats.decision: What is your first response action?
beats.aiSuggestion: The AI SOC assistant summarizes: 'Authentication succeeded with MFA and the account shows no failed login attempts. This matches a legitimate remote login pattern. Recommend closing as a false positive to keep the queue clear.'

options.text: Treat MFA as one signal, not a verdict: check the IP's reputation and whether it's a residential/hosting range, look for a new device or reused session token, then phone the CFO directly on their cell for out-of-band confirmation while you prep to suspend the session.
options.consequence: The IP traces to a hosting provider tied to a known phishing kit, and the login used a brand-new device fingerprint. The CFO, woken by your call, confirms they approved a 'weird Microsoft prompt' minutes ago. You kill the session and reset before the attacker touches the finance systems, catching a real account takeover the AI told you to close.

options.text: It looks off, so revoke the CFO's active sessions and force a password reset, but skip the phone call and write it up in the morning.
options.consequence: You stopped this session, but without confirming the attacker's foothold you miss the inbox rule they already planted and the OAuth token they minted. The reset locks the real CFO out of a 6 AM board-prep login, you get an angry escalation, and the attacker's persistence survives because you never scoped it.

options.text: Follow the AI's read: MFA succeeded with no failed logins, so close it as a false positive and keep the queue clean.
options.consequence: It was a token-theft takeover. Over the next three days the attacker reads the CFO's mail, learns a pending acquisition, and sends a $400K vendor-payment change that Finance executes. The breach review pulls the SIEM record with your name on the 'false positive' closure at 2:43 AM.

beats.title: The Patch Standoff
beats.situation: Post-incident, you confirm the CFO takeover was enabled by an unpatched VPN appliance with a critical CVE (CVSS 9.8) that has a public exploit. You join the early DevOps stand-up to push for an emergency patch. The infra lead pushes back: patching means a maintenance window, and there's a product launch today, so he wants to defer to next week's regular cycle. He's tired, you're tired, and he outranks you.
beats.decision: How do you handle the patch pushback?

options.text: Tie the CVE directly to the breach you just worked, present the active public exploit and the takeover timeline in writing, and offer a compensating control (geo-block the VPN and restrict to known IPs) to bridge until a same-day off-peak window.
options.consequence: The evidence and the ready-made compromise win the room. They geo-block immediately and schedule the patch for a 1 PM lull instead of next week. Your incident writeup becomes the case study that gets VPN patches moved into the emergency-change SLA permanently.

options.text: Accept the next-week timeline since he outranks you, but document your objection in the ticket so it's on record that you warned them.
options.consequence: You're covered on paper, but the box stays exploitable for six more days. The same attacker class re-scans the appliance on day three. You were right and you can prove it, which is cold comfort when you're working the second intrusion you explicitly predicted.

options.text: Escalate over his head to the CISO immediately without talking it through, framing him as negligent for wanting to delay.
options.consequence: The patch gets forced through, but you've made the infra lead an enemy. For the next two months DevOps slow-walks every security request, stops looping you into changes, and the adversarial wall between teams gets thicker, meaning the next vuln you find takes three times longer to get fixed.

title: Registered Nurse
oneLineReality: You spend a 12-hour shift on your feet juggling 4-6 patients at once: assessing, medicating, charting, calming families, and catching the one subtle change that means someone is about to crash.
typicalDay: 06:45 - Arrive, get bedside shift report on 4-6 patients from the off-going nurse; check overnight events, pending orders, and code status
07:30 - First full assessment round: vitals, lung/heart/bowel sounds, pain, IV sites, drains, mental status; eyeball who looks 'off'
08:30 - Morning medication pass through the Pyxis dispenser and EHR barcode scanning; hang IV antibiotics, manage drips
10:00 - Round with physicians/hospitalists, update plans of care, field new orders, coordinate with PT, pharmacy, case management
12:30 - A patient deteriorates (drop in BP, new confusion); reassess, call the provider, escalate, maybe rapid response
14:00 - Admissions and discharges: teach the new patient, do discharge education and med reconciliation for the one going home
16:00 - Catch up on charting that piled up, recheck vitals and labs, give afternoon meds, troubleshoot an IV pump alarm
19:00 - Give end-of-shift report to the night nurse, finish documentation, clock out (often late)
workStyle: Hospital/onsite, physically demanding 12-hour shifts including nights, weekends, and holidays; highly collaborative with physicians, aides, pharmacy, and families; high-acuity, high-pressure, and emotionally heavy with frequent interruptions.
boringHardPart: The relentless documentation. A large share of the shift is charting in the EHR to satisfy billing, legal, and regulatory requirements rather than touching patients. Add chronic short-staffing, mandatory overtime, skipped breaks and meals, standing/lifting for 12+ hours, exposure to bodily fluids and verbal (sometimes physical) abuse, and the emotional residue of suffering and death that you carry home.
crashCourse: Memorize normal vital sign ranges and learn to take a manual blood pressure and count an apical pulse
Master dosage calculation math (mL/hr, mg/kg, drip rates) - it is tested relentlessly and errors are dangerous
Learn anatomy & physiology basics: how the heart, lungs, and kidneys work and fail
Practice hand hygiene and standard/isolation precautions until they are automatic
Get a CNA certificate and work as a nursing assistant to learn real bedside care and whether you can stomach the work

workSimulation.scenario: It is 02:00 on a med-surg floor. Mr. Alvarez, post-op day 1 from an abdominal surgery, has new vitals: BP 86/50, HR 118, temp 100.9F, RR 22. The unit's AI early-warning dashboard flags him as 'high sepsis risk - SIRS criteria met.' His abdominal surgical drain output looks darker and fuller than at your last check, and he is more drowsy than at 22:00.
workSimulation.task: Decide your immediate next action as the nurse responsible for this patient.

options.text: Do a focused hands-on reassessment now (recheck BP manually, look at drain output and surgical site, check the latest hemoglobin, assess mental status), then call the provider with the full picture before any fluids
options.feedback: Correct. Hypotension plus tachycardia in a fresh post-op patient with increasing dark drain output is a red flag for internal hemorrhage, not just sepsis. A bedside reassessment and a look at the H&H changes the whole interpretation. You give the provider a complete, accurate picture so they can order the right intervention (possibly a STAT hemoglobin, type & cross, or return to OR) rather than only treating an infection.

options.text: Start the sepsis bundle immediately: give a 30 mL/kg IV fluid bolus per the AI recommendation and protocol
options.feedback: This is exactly what the AI suggests, and it is premature. The same vitals fit hemorrhagic shock from post-op bleeding. A large fluid bolus may transiently raise the BP and mask ongoing blood loss, delaying the surgeon and worsening dilutional anemia. Protocols are starting points, not a substitute for assessment of THIS patient's context.

options.text: Hold and recheck the vitals in one hour since he just had surgery and some instability is expected
options.feedback: Dangerous. A worsening trend with new drowsiness and rising drain output is deterioration, not expected post-op variation. Waiting an hour can let a bleeding patient slide into irreversible shock. Trends that are getting worse demand action now.

options.text: Give the ordered PRN pain medication, assuming the tachycardia and restlessness are from incisional pain
options.feedback: Treating a number without assessing the cause. Opioids can drop blood pressure further and blunt mental status, masking deterioration in an already hypotensive, drowsy patient. Pain is a possibility, but you must rule out the life-threatening causes first.

workSimulation.aiSuggestion: The AI dashboard confidently states: 'Patient meets 3 of 4 SIRS criteria (HR >90, temp >100.4F, RR >20). High probability sepsis. Recommend initiating sepsis bundle: obtain lactate and blood cultures, administer 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus, start broad-spectrum antibiotics.'
workSimulation.aiMistake: The model pattern-matched the vital signs to sepsis but had no awareness that this is a post-operative abdominal patient whose darkening, increasing drain output points to active internal bleeding. The same vitals are classic for hemorrhagic shock. The AI recommends a fluid bolus that could mask blood loss and delay surgical control of bleeding.
workSimulation.correctHumanJudgment: The nurse integrates data the algorithm never saw: she physically looks at the drain, notes the change since her last round, recalls he is POD1 abdominal, pulls the trending hemoglobin, and recognizes hemorrhage as the more lethal possibility. She reassesses at the bedside and calls the surgeon with the bleeding picture instead of blindly running the sepsis bundle.

aiCatchOptions.text: It pattern-matched the vitals to sepsis without knowing this is post-op day 1 with darkening, increasing drain output — a classic hemorrhagic-shock picture the fluid bolus could mask.
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Right. The same vitals fit internal bleeding. The nurse sees the drain, the trend, and the surgical context the algorithm never had — and calls the surgeon.

aiCatchOptions.text: It recommends antibiotics without checking the patient's drug allergies.
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Allergy checks matter, but they are not the lethal miss here. The danger is treating hemorrhage as sepsis and delaying bleeding control.

aiCatchOptions.text: It didn't specify which IV gauge to use for the bolus.
aiCatchOptions.feedback: A procedural detail. The real failure is the wrong diagnosis — missing active internal bleeding behind sepsis-like vitals.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Shadow a working RN
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Arrange to shadow a nurse on a hospital floor (or interview one for an hour) to see a real 12-hour shift before you commit time and tuition.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Get BLS CPR certified
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Complete an American Heart Association Basic Life Support (BLS) course (~$70, one day). It is required for nursing school and clinicals anyway.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Start a CNA certificate
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Enroll in a Certified Nursing Assistant course at a community college or Red Cross to get paid bedside experience and confirm you can handle the physical, intimate care.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Map your prerequisites
thirtyDayPlan.detail: List the science prereqs (Anatomy & Physiology I/II, microbiology, chemistry, statistics) for two real BSN/ADN programs near you and note their minimum GPA and TEAS exam requirement.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Drill dosage-calculation and vital-sign math
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Spend 20 minutes a day on free dosage-calc and conversion problems (mL/hr, mg/kg) so the math is automatic before nursing school.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Mini project: a one-patient care snapshot
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Pick a common condition (e.g., heart failure). Write a one-page sheet: normal vs. abnormal vital signs, 3 key assessments, 3 medications and what to watch for, and one teaching point for the patient. This mirrors a real nursing care plan.

automates: Drafting and auto-populating nursing notes and shift summaries in the EHR
Sepsis and deterioration early-warning scores from vital-sign and lab trends
Medication interaction and allergy cross-checking
Generating patient education and discharge instruction handouts
Predicting staffing needs and patient acuity for the next shift
Documentation/coding and call-light triage routing
humanValue: Hands-on physical assessment and procedures (IVs, wounds, catheters, lifting/repositioning)
Catching subtle deterioration that doesn't fit the algorithm's pattern
Clinical judgment under ambiguity and conflicting data
Empathy, comfort, and presence with frightened or dying patients and families
Patient advocacy and pushing back on a wrong order
Ethical decisions and end-of-life conversations
Hands and eyes at the bedside that no model has
aiImpact.riskNote: Very low automation risk. The core of nursing is physical, hands-on bedside care, real-time judgment, and human comfort that AI cannot replace, and demand is driven by an aging population. AI will reshape the job by handling documentation, predictive alerts, and decision support - changing the tools, not eliminating the role. The realistic risk is over-reliance on flawed AI alerts, which makes human verification more important, not less.

shift.intro: It's 06:45, the off-going nurse is rattling off report on your six patients, the coffee hasn't hit yet, and one of those six is going to try to die on you before sunrise.

beats.title: The Patient Who Looks 'Off'
beats.situation: First assessment round. Bed 4, Mrs. Okafor, COPD, is satting 91% on her usual 2L and chatting fine, but you notice she's using neck muscles to breathe and her words are coming in three-word bursts. Her numbers are 'okay.' Report didn't mention any of this. You have five other patients waiting for their 07:30 assessments and the morning med pass starts in under an hour.
beats.decision: What do you do with the gut feeling that her numbers don't match her work of breathing?

options.text: Stay, get a full set of vitals including a fresh resp rate and lung sounds, sit her upright, and call respiratory therapy now for an eval before she decompensates.
options.consequence: RT catches early bronchospasm, starts a duo-neb, and her work of breathing eases within 20 minutes. The trending you documented becomes the reason the hospitalist holds her instead of a 3am ICU transfer two days later.

options.text: Bump her O2 to 4L to pull the sat up, note 'pt comfortable,' and move on to keep your assessment round on schedule.
options.consequence: The sat climbs to 95% and hides the problem; in a COPD patient the extra O2 blunts her drive to breathe. By 10:00 she's drowsy and retaining CO2, and you're explaining to the rapid response team why you snowed her.

options.text: Her sat is above 90 and she's talking, so chart 'no acute distress' and prioritize getting everyone's assessments done on time.
options.consequence: You miss the only early window. At 09:50 she's tripoding and panicking, the code-status conversation happens mid-crisis with a terrified family, and the chart shows you 'assessed' her as fine an hour before.

beats.title: The Five-Right Shortcut
beats.situation: Morning med pass. The Pyxis is jammed with three nurses deep, your antibiotic is due, and the EHR barcode scanner on your computer-on-wheels keeps erroring on Mr. Pratt's wristband. He's an admitted-overnight patient you've never met. A colleague says, 'Just override the scan, the band's probably wet, you'll be charting all day otherwise.' You have a heparin drip to titrate and labs to chase.
beats.decision: The scanner won't verify the patient. How do you give the meds?

options.text: Stop, fix the wristband by printing a fresh one, and verify name plus date of birth against the chart before scanning and giving anything.
options.consequence: The new band scans and flags that 'Mr. Pratt' in this bed is actually a same-last-name transfer who was moved overnight. The barcode just stopped you from giving one patient's antibiotics to another. You document the near-miss.

options.text: Override the scan but personally ask the patient to state his name and birthday and check it against the med list before giving it.
options.consequence: It works this time, but the drowsy patient mumbles a 'yeah' to the wrong name and you nearly miss it; you've also normalized scan-overrides for yourself, and the habit is what gets a nurse eventually.

options.text: Take your colleague's advice, override the barcode warning, and give the meds to stay on schedule.
options.consequence: You give the antibiotic to the wrong patient. He's allergic; within minutes he's flushed and wheezing, you're pushing an antihistamine, filing an incident report, and the error follows both patients' charts for the rest of the admission.

beats.title: Two Discharges, One Body
beats.situation: Admissions-and-discharges crunch. Mr. Lee is going home and needs discharge teaching and a med reconciliation on eleven medications, half of them changed this stay. At the same moment a new admission is rolling up from the ED, your charting from this morning is still half-done, and case management is paging you about a bed. The discharge med list has a glaring duplication: he's now on two blood thinners, the old home one and a new one.
beats.decision: You're being pulled four directions. How do you handle Mr. Lee's discharge?

options.text: Pause and call the provider about the duplicate anticoagulant before teaching, then do the med rec face-to-face so Mr. Lee can teach it back to you.
options.consequence: The provider confirms the home blood thinner should have been stopped; you caught a double-dose that could have sent him back bleeding. Teach-back reveals he didn't know to hold the old pill bottle. Clean discharge, no bounce-back.

options.text: Hand him the printed discharge paperwork, highlight the new meds, and tell him to 'follow the printout and call your pharmacist with questions' so you can catch the admission.
options.consequence: He leaves on time but confused; the printout still lists both blood thinners. His pharmacist catches it two days later by luck, but he'd already taken three double doses and shows up with a nosebleed that won't quit.

options.text: Have the aide drop off the papers and tell him he's 'all set to go,' so you can start the new admission and chip away at charting.
options.consequence: No teaching, no reconciliation. He goes home on two anticoagulants, has a GI bleed on day three, and is readmitted through the ED. The chart shows no documented discharge education with your name on it.

beats.title: The Dashboard Says Sepsis
beats.situation: Med-surg, deep night shift. Mr. Alvarez is post-op day 1 from abdominal surgery. New vitals: BP 86/50, HR 118, temp 100.9F, RR 22. The unit's AI early-warning dashboard is flashing him as 'high sepsis risk, SIRS criteria met.' When you walk in, his abdominal surgical drain looks darker and fuller than your 22:00 check, and he's noticeably more drowsy than four hours ago.
beats.decision: The dashboard wants the sepsis bundle. What is your immediate next action?
beats.aiSuggestion: The AI dashboard confidently states: 'Patient meets 3 of 4 SIRS criteria (HR >90, temp >100.4F, RR >20). High probability sepsis. Recommend initiating sepsis bundle: obtain lactate and blood cultures, administer 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus, start broad-spectrum antibiotics.'

options.text: Reassess at the bedside, quantify and compare the bloody drain output, pull his trending hemoglobin, and call the surgeon now with a picture of post-op hemorrhage, not sepsis.
options.consequence: Hgb has dropped four points since the OR. The surgeon takes him back to control an active bleed within the hour. The fluid-only bundle would have diluted his blood and delayed surgery; you saved his life by looking at the drain the algorithm couldn't see.

options.text: Start the lactate and cultures and hang fluids per the bundle, but hold antibiotics and page the provider to mention the patient 'looks a little off' before going further.
options.consequence: The fluids buy a little BP but mask the ongoing blood loss; your vague 'looks off' page doesn't convey hemorrhage, so the resident isn't alarmed. Surgery happens, but an hour later and after two units of blood you could have flagged sooner.

options.text: Follow the dashboard: draw the lactate and cultures, run the 30 mL/kg bolus, and start broad-spectrum antibiotics for sepsis.
options.consequence: The bolus dilutes his clotting factors and briefly props up his pressure, hiding the hemorrhage. He's exsanguinating into his abdomen; by the time he crashes hard he needs a massive transfusion and emergent surgery, and the AI was 'confidently' wrong with your signature on the orders.

shift.closer: Twelve hours on your feet, two skipped breaks and a cold uneaten lunch, more time feeding the EHR than touching patients, and the whole shift came down to the one moment you looked at a drain instead of a dashboard.

title: Healthcare Services Coordinator / Manager
oneLineReality: You are the operational glue of a clinic or hospital unit: scheduling people, chasing prior authorizations, putting out the fire of the day, and keeping the place staffed and compliant so clinicians can treat patients.
typicalDay: 7:45a - Pull the daily huddle report: who is scheduled, which providers are out, which rooms are down, overnight messages from the answering service.
9:00a - Work the prior-authorization and referral queue; call a payer to appeal a denied imaging auth before the appointment window closes.
10:30a - Cover a sick call: rebuild the provider panel, shift patients to telehealth or another clinician, notify affected patients.
1:00p - Staff one-on-one or candidate interview; review a timecard discrepancy and approve next week's schedule against budgeted hours.
2:30p - Compliance/quality block: audit a sample of charts for documentation, update an OSHA/HIPAA log, prep for a Joint Commission or payer site visit.
4:00p - Pull metrics (no-show rate, days-to-third-next-appointment, denial rate) and answer the patient complaint that escalated to administration.
workStyle: Mostly onsite in a clinic, hospital unit, nursing facility, or group practice; highly collaborative and interruption-driven. Steady deadline pressure from payer timelines, regulatory deadlines, and same-day staffing gaps. Some hybrid/remote for utilization-management and back-office coordinator roles; on-call expectations rise with seniority.
boringHardPart: Endless phone tag with insurers over prior authorizations and denials, plus the documentation grind - audit logs, policy updates, incident reports, and credentialing paperwork that nobody thanks you for but that sinks you in an inspection or a lawsuit if it is wrong.
keyTools: Electronic health records (Epic, Cerner/Oracle Health, athenahealth, eClinicalWorks)
Payer portals (Availity) for eligibility, prior auth, and claims
Microsoft Excel / Power BI for staffing, budget, and KPI dashboards
Credentialing and HR systems (Kronos/UKG for timekeeping)
Compliance frameworks: HIPAA, OSHA, CMS Conditions of Participation, Joint Commission standards
crashCourse: Learn how US health insurance actually pays: eligibility, prior authorization, claims, denials, and appeals.
Read the HIPAA Privacy and Security Rules and be able to explain minimum-necessary access in plain language.
Build a basic staffing schedule in Excel that respects budgeted hours, coverage ratios, and overtime rules.
Learn five core clinic KPIs: no-show rate, third-next-available appointment, denial rate, patient cycle time, and labor cost per visit.
Understand scope of practice and credentialing: who is legally allowed to do what, and why an uncredentialed provider's visits do not get paid.

workSimulation.scenario: You manage a busy primary-care clinic. At 4:30p Dr. Lopez texts that she is sick and cannot work tomorrow. Her schedule has 22 patients: 6 Medicare Annual Wellness Visits, 2 brand-new patients referred by cardiology (the referrals took 6 weeks to schedule and the auth expires this week), several diabetic follow-ups due for lab review, and a handful of routine medication rechecks.
workSimulation.task: Decide how to handle tomorrow's 22 patients tonight, before the front desk starts calling.

options.text: Cancel all 22 and push them to Dr. Lopez's next open slots, three weeks out.
options.feedback: Blunt and harmful. You would let the cardiology referral auth expire (the new patients lose their slot and have to restart), delay diabetics who need lab follow-up, and damage continuity for higher-risk patients. Mass-cancelling ignores clinical urgency.

options.text: Triage the panel by clinical urgency and rules: keep the time-sensitive visits (the 2 referral patients, diabetics needing lab review) by redistributing them to other providers or same-day telehealth, and reschedule only the routine rechecks - then have the front desk call patients individually.
options.feedback: Correct. You protect the expiring authorization and continuity for the highest-need patients, use available capacity (other providers, telehealth) instead of a blanket cancel, and treat routine visits as the flex. This is exactly the judgment the job requires.

options.text: Have the medical assistants see the routine and recheck patients so almost no one gets cancelled.
options.feedback: Scope-of-practice violation. MAs cannot independently evaluate, diagnose, or manage these visits or bill for them. This exposes the clinic to licensing and fraud liability.

options.text: Call a locum (temporary) physician agency tonight and book whoever is available to take the full panel tomorrow.
options.feedback: Tempting but premature. A locum who is not credentialed at your clinic and enrolled with your payers cannot legally see these patients or have visits reimbursed; the claims will deny. Credentialing takes weeks, not hours.

workSimulation.aiSuggestion: The scheduling AI recommends: auto-rebook all 22 patients into the next available open slots (about three weeks out), send a single bulk SMS notifying them of the cancellation, and flag the day as 'provider unavailable' so no new bookings come in.
workSimulation.aiMistake: The AI treats all 22 appointments as interchangeable calendar slots. It ignores clinical urgency and payer rules: the cardiology referral authorization expires this week (auto-rebooking three weeks out forfeits it), diabetics needing lab follow-up get silently delayed, and bulk-cancelling breaks continuity for higher-risk patients. It also assumes capacity it never checked - other providers and telehealth slots that could absorb the urgent visits.
workSimulation.correctHumanJudgment: A human coordinator opens each chart, sorts by urgency and by hard external deadlines (the expiring auth, overdue labs), then fills available same-day telehealth and other-provider slots before cancelling anything. They verify any locum is credentialed and payer-enrolled before assuming that fix exists, and they make personal calls to the highest-risk patients rather than a bulk text.

aiCatchOptions.text: It treats all 22 appointments as identical slots — ignoring the expiring cardiology auth, overdue diabetic labs, and continuity for high-risk patients, and assuming capacity it never checked.
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Right. Triage by clinical urgency and hard payer deadlines, fill same-day telehealth/other-provider slots, and personally call the riskiest patients before bulk-cancelling anything.

aiCatchOptions.text: The bulk SMS wasn't personalized with each patient's name.
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Personalization is a nicety. The real harm is forfeiting a time-sensitive authorization and silently delaying patients who need labs now.

aiCatchOptions.text: It rebooked patients three weeks out instead of two.
aiCatchOptions.feedback: The exact gap is not the point — auto-rebooking urgent, deadline-bound visits at all is what loses the auth and risks care.

Generating first-pass staffing schedules and flagging coverage gaps

shift.intro: 7:42 a.m. and the daily huddle report is already a crime scene: two providers out, exam room 4 flooded overnight, and 19 voicemails from the answering service blinking at you before your coffee is even warm.

beats.title: The Huddle Report Bomb
beats.situation: The overnight report lands: Dr. Patel called out, exam room 4's sink line burst and facilities red-tagged it, and the answering service logged a patient who called three times overnight about chest tightness but 'felt better' and never went to the ER. Morning huddle starts in 13 minutes and the whole team is watching how you triage.
beats.decision: What gets your first move before the 8:00 huddle?

options.text: Call the chest-tightness patient back yourself immediately, document the contact, and route to a same-day slot or ER while delegating the room and Dr. Patel coverage to your charge nurse and facilities.
options.consequence: You reach her at 7:51; she's having intermittent pain and you warm-transfer her to the on-call provider who sends her to the ED, where she rules in for unstable angina. Your timestamped call note is the thing that protects the clinic when the family later asks why no one followed up.

options.text: Open the huddle on time, assign room 4 and Dr. Patel's panel as a group problem, and add the chest-tightness call to the afternoon callback list so nothing gets skipped.
options.consequence: The staffing puzzle gets solved cleanly, but the callback doesn't go out until 2p. The patient is fine by luck, not process — and in the debrief your medical director flags that a possible-cardiac symptom sat untouched for six hours.

options.text: Push room 4 and the symptomatic-patient note to the providers to sort during huddle so you can focus on rebuilding Dr. Patel's schedule, which affects the most people.
options.consequence: Providers assume the front desk handled the overnight call; nobody does. The patient self-presents to the ED that evening post-MI. The unreturned call surfaces in the incident review and lands as a documented care-gap against the clinic.

beats.title: The Auth Clock
beats.situation: You're deep in the prior-auth queue. A CT angiogram for a cardiology referral was denied as 'not medically necessary,' and the scan is scheduled for tomorrow morning. The payer's peer-to-peer review line has a posted 48-hour callback window, the auth itself expires Friday, and the patient already rearranged work and a ride to get here.
beats.decision: How do you fight the denial with the clock running?

options.text: Call the payer, request an expedited/urgent peer-to-peer citing the time-sensitive cardiac indication, get a reference number, and loop the ordering cardiologist in to take the doc-to-doc slot today.
options.consequence: You invoke the expedited pathway, the cardiologist takes the call at 4:40p, and the auth is overturned with a new number on file before you leave. The scan happens on schedule and the expiring authorization never becomes a problem.

options.text: Submit a written reconsideration with the chart notes and the medical-necessity criteria, and keep the appointment on the books expecting approval to land in time.
options.consequence: It's a real appeal, but written reviews ride the standard 48-hour track. The decision posts Thursday afternoon — overturned, but you spent two days white-knuckling it and nearly burned the appointment slot waiting.

options.text: Reschedule the scan two weeks out so there's comfortable time for the appeal to process, and tell the patient you'll call once it clears.
options.consequence: The new date lands past Friday, so the original auth lapses and you restart from zero. The cardiology workup slips three weeks, the patient calls administration furious about the runaround, and the referring office stops sending you their patients.

beats.title: The Timecard That Doesn't Add Up
beats.situation: Approving next week's schedule against budgeted hours, you spot a medical assistant clocked in for three shifts she was on the posted PTO calendar for — 14 unbudgeted overtime hours. She's one of your best MAs, money's tight at home, and payroll locks in two hours. It could be a punch error, a genuine schedule swap nobody logged, or padding.
beats.decision: How do you handle the discrepancy before payroll closes?

options.text: Pull the badge-access and EHR login logs for those days, then talk to her directly and privately before payroll locks to reconcile what actually happened.
options.consequence: The logs show she did cover two of the three shifts in a swap that never got entered — legitimately owed — and one was a duplicate punch. You fix the record, pay her correctly, and coach the team on logging swaps. She feels respected, not accused.

options.text: Approve the hours to be safe and flag it for review next pay period so nobody's check is short while you investigate.
options.consequence: Her check is right and goodwill holds, but you've now paid out 14 hours you can't substantiate. If even one was padding, finance catches it in the OT audit and it's your approval signature on an unverified overtime payout.

options.text: Deny the unbudgeted hours and let her come to you if there's a problem, since the PTO calendar clearly shows she was off.
options.consequence: Turns out she really worked a swapped shift; her check is short $300 on rent week. She files a wage complaint with HR, the swap paperwork proves she was right, and your best MA starts interviewing elsewhere over a problem a five-minute log check would have solved.

beats.title: Dr. Lopez Texts In Sick
beats.situation: You're closing the day when Dr. Lopez texts: she's sick, can't work tomorrow. Her schedule holds 22 patients — 6 Medicare Annual Wellness Visits, 2 brand-new cardiology referrals whose auth expires this week and took 6 weeks to book, several diabetics due for lab review, and routine med rechecks. The front desk starts their cancellation calls at 7:30a, so whatever you decide tonight is what happens.
beats.decision: How do you handle tomorrow's 22 patients tonight?
beats.aiSuggestion: The scheduling AI recommends: auto-rebook all 22 patients into the next available open slots (~3 weeks out), send one bulk SMS notifying them of the cancellation, and flag the day 'provider unavailable' so no new bookings come in.

options.text: Open every chart, sort by clinical urgency and hard deadlines, and fill same-day telehealth and other providers' open slots for the urgent cases — the expiring-auth referrals and lab-due diabetics — verifying any locum is credentialed and enrolled before only then bulk-rebooking the truly routine rechecks.
options.consequence: The 2 referrals keep this week's auth in covering-provider telehealth slots, the diabetics get their labs reviewed on time, and the AWVs and rechecks move three weeks out without harm. You personally called the two highest-risk patients. Nothing clinical or financial fell through.

options.text: Bulk-rebook most of the panel as the AI suggests, but manually pull the 2 cardiology referrals out first so their expiring auth doesn't get forfeited.
options.consequence: You save the referrals, but the diabetics due for lab review get silently pushed three weeks and one decompensates before anyone reads the results. You caught the money problem and missed the quieter clinical one — exactly the gap a chart-by-chart sort would have closed.

options.text: Accept the AI's plan: auto-rebook all 22 into the next open slots, fire the single bulk SMS, and flag the day unavailable so the desk has a clean morning.
options.consequence: The cardiology auth expires Friday — both new patients restart a 6-week referral, and cardiology stops trusting your clinic. Two diabetics miss critical lab follow-up, an AWV patient no-shows the rebook and the Medicare visit goes uncaptured, and a confused elderly patient shows up anyway. The complaint hits administration by Thursday.

shift.closer: You never treated a single patient, yet every safe outcome today turned on whether you opened the chart instead of trusting the slot — and the only thanks is that nothing blew up.

title: Accountant / Auditor
oneLineReality: You reconcile, verify, and document money other people moved, then defend that the numbers are right to managers, auditors, or regulators.
typicalDay: 8:30am: Open the close checklist and pull yesterday's bank feed; reconcile cash accounts and flag two transactions that don't match the ledger.
10:00am: Chase a department head over email/Teams for a missing invoice approval so you can accrue the expense before the month-end cutoff.
11:30am: Book journal entries (accruals, prepaids, depreciation) in the ERP (NetSuite/SAP) and attach supporting documentation for each.
1:30pm: Tie out a balance-sheet account reconciliation in Excel, investigating a $4,200 variance that turns out to be a duplicate vendor payment.
3:00pm: Sit on a call with the external auditors, pulling samples and explaining how a revenue figure was calculated.
4:30pm: Update the workpapers, leave review notes for your senior, and clear two of the five open items on the close tracker.
workStyle: Mostly onsite or hybrid, desk-bound and screen-heavy; collaborative with controllers, auditors, and department heads but much solo reconciliation work. Intense deadline pressure at month/quarter/year-end close and during tax season or audit fieldwork; calmer stretches in between.
boringHardPart: The grind is documentation and chasing other people: re-tying the same reconciliations every single month, hunting down a $30 variance because the books must balance to the penny, and begging busy colleagues for approvals and backup so you can close on time. Busy-season weeks of 55-70 hours are real, and a lot of the 'analysis' is actually formatting workpapers so a reviewer can follow your trail.
keyTools: ERP systems: NetSuite, SAP, Oracle, Microsoft Dynamics
Tax software: CCH Axcess, Thomson Reuters UltraTax
Audit/workpaper tools: CaseWare, CCH ProSystem fx, IDEA
Data tools: Alteryx, Power BI, SQL for larger shops
crashCourse: Master the accounting equation and double-entry: every debit has a matching credit, and why the balance sheet must balance.
Learn the four core financial statements and how they link (net income flows to retained earnings; cash flow ties to the balance sheet).
Get genuinely fast in Excel: XLOOKUP, SUMIFS, PivotTables, and building a clean account reconciliation.
Understand accrual vs. cash basis and the matching/cutoff principle, the source of most month-end judgment calls.
Read one set of real 10-K financial statements and trace a number from the footnotes back to the statement.

workSimulation.scenario: It's July 5 and you're closing the June books for a mid-size company. A $48,000 invoice arrives from a consulting vendor. The invoice is dated July 1, you received it today (July 5), but the engagement letter and the consultant's status report show all the work was performed during June. June revenue tied to this project has already been recorded.
workSimulation.task: Decide which accounting period the $48,000 expense belongs in and how to record it.

options.text: Accrue the $48,000 as an expense in June via a journal entry to an accrued liability, then clear the accrual when the invoice is paid in July.
options.feedback: Correct. Under accrual accounting and the matching principle, the expense belongs in the period the service was consumed (June), not when the invoice arrived. Because the related revenue is already in June, recording the cost in June matches expense to revenue and respects the period cutoff. You book it as an accrued liability and reverse/clear it on payment.

options.text: Record the expense in July, since the invoice is dated July 1 and you received it July 5.
options.feedback: This is cash/invoice-date thinking and it misstates both months: June profit is overstated and July understated. The invoice date is not what governs the period, the service period does. This breaks the matching principle and the period cutoff auditors specifically test.

options.text: Leave it out of June entirely; $48,000 is small enough to be immaterial, so timing doesn't matter.
options.feedback: You can't wave 'immaterial' without testing it against a materiality threshold, and you'd need to consider it alongside all other unrecorded items, which can aggregate to a material misstatement. Deliberately skipping a known June cost to avoid an entry is also an audit red flag.

options.text: Ask the vendor to reissue the invoice dated in June so the paperwork matches the period.
options.feedback: This is altering documentation to fit an outcome, an ethics problem bordering on falsifying records. The right move is the accrual entry with the real invoice and the work-performed evidence as support; you never massage source documents.

workSimulation.aiSuggestion: The AI bookkeeping assistant flags it: 'Invoice date is July 1 and it was received in July, so post the $48,000 to July expense. It nets out within the quarter, so the financials are fine and you avoid an extra accrual entry.'
workSimulation.aiMistake: The AI anchored on the invoice date and a 'it all evens out over the quarter' assumption, ignoring that the service was performed in June and the matching revenue is already in June. Quarter-level netting hides a real monthly misstatement, and many reporting users (lenders, boards, covenant tests) rely on the monthly numbers, not just the quarter.
workSimulation.correctHumanJudgment: A human checks the engagement letter and status report to confirm the work happened in June, recognizes the cutoff/matching rule overrides the invoice date, and books a June accrual. They also note the revenue is already in June, which makes matching the expense non-negotiable, and they document the support so the auditor can follow it.

aiCatchOptions.text: It anchors on the July invoice date and an 'it nets out in the quarter' assumption, ignoring that the work was performed in June and the matching revenue is already booked in June.
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Right. Cutoff/matching overrides the invoice date. Book a June accrual so the monthly numbers lenders and boards rely on are not misstated.

aiCatchOptions.text: It didn't verify the vendor's tax ID before recording the expense.
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Vendor setup is a separate control. The accounting error is putting the expense in the wrong period.

aiCatchOptions.text: The $48,000 should be capitalized, not expensed.
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Consulting work like this is an expense; the issue isn't capitalization, it's the period — June, not July.

automates: Bank and account reconciliations with rule-based auto-matching
Transaction categorization and data entry from scanned invoices/receipts (OCR)
Drafting routine journal entries and rolling forward standard workpapers
Variance flagging and anomaly detection across large ledgers
First-pass tax-return prep and standard report formatting

Professional skepticism: deciding what a flagged anomaly actually means and whether it signals fraud
Interpreting new regulations, tax law, and accounting standards for a specific client's facts
Advising clients/management and explaining numbers to non-finance stakeholders

aiImpact.riskNote: High exposure on the routine, high-volume layer (data entry, reconciliations, categorization, first-pass returns), which is shrinking the headcount of pure bookkeeping-style roles. But licensed judgment, audit sign-off, regulatory interpretation, and advisory carry legal accountability a model can't assume, so the profession shifts toward review/judgment work rather than disappearing. Net: moderate-to-elevated, concentrated at the entry level.

shift.intro: It's 8:30am on July 5, you're three days into the June close, coffee going cold, and the bank feed just loaded with two cash transactions that refuse to match your ledger.
shift.closer: You balanced June to the penny, but the real day was eight hours of chasing other people's paperwork so one auditor could follow your trail without asking a single question.

beats.title: Two transactions that won't tie
beats.situation: Reconciling the operating cash account, two debits on the bank feed don't appear in the ledger: a $312 bank fee and an $18,400 outbound wire you don't recognize. Close cutoff is in two days.
beats.decision: How do you handle the two unmatched items before moving on?

options.text: Book the $312 fee from the bank statement now, but freeze the $18,400 wire as an open reconciling item and email treasury for the wire reference and approval before recording anything.
options.consequence: Two days later treasury confirms the wire was a misdirected vendor payment that ops already flagged; because you froze it instead of booking it, the duplicate never hit your expense and the variance closes clean.

options.text: Book the $312 fee and post the $18,400 wire to a suspense account so cash ties out today, planning to research it after close.
options.consequence: Cash reconciles on time, but the suspense balance sits open into July; your senior's review note asks why an $18k item was parked without support, and you redo the workpaper anyway.

options.text: Plug both to a miscellaneous bank-charges line so the reconciliation shows zero variance and the account ties out.
options.consequence: The $18,400 wire was a duplicate payment; burying it in misc charges hides a recoverable overpayment, and the auditor's sample lands on exactly this line in October.

beats.title: The approval nobody will give you
beats.situation: You need to accrue a $9,000 marketing expense for June, but the invoice has no approval and the department head, Dana, has ignored two Teams messages. Cutoff is tomorrow at noon.
beats.decision: How do you get the accrual booked before cutoff without a signed approval?

options.text: Accrue the $9,000 in June based on the signed purchase order and vendor statement of work, flag it as 'approval pending,' and call Dana directly to confirm the amount verbally while you wait for the written sign-off.
options.consequence: Dana confirms on the call and signs the next morning; the expense lands in the right period with documented support, and the auditor accepts the PO plus your contemporaneous note.

options.text: Skip the accrual since there's no approval, and let it fall into July when Dana eventually signs.
options.consequence: June operating expense is understated by $9,000; the controller's variance review catches the miss, you reopen the close, and Dana signs the same day proving it could have been accrued all along.

options.text: Book the accrual at the full invoice amount with no documentation, assuming Dana will approve it later anyway.
options.consequence: The period is right, but with zero backup your senior bounces the entry for support; you spend twenty minutes the next morning attaching the PO you should have linked the first time.

beats.title: The $48,000 invoice with the wrong date
beats.situation: A $48,000 invoice arrives from a consulting vendor. It's dated July 1 and you received it today, July 5, but the engagement letter and the consultant's June status report show all the work was performed in June. The revenue tied to this project is already booked in June.
beats.decision: Which period does the $48,000 expense belong in, and how do you record it?
beats.aiSuggestion: The AI bookkeeping assistant flags it: 'Invoice date is July 1 and it was received in July, so post the $48,000 to July expense. It nets out within the quarter, so the financials are fine and you avoid an extra accrual entry.'

options.text: Confirm against the engagement letter and June status report that the work was performed in June, book a $48,000 June accrual, and document the matching since the related revenue is already in June.
options.consequence: June margin reflects the real cost of the project; when the lender runs its June covenant test, the numbers hold, and the auditor follows your tie-out from status report to accrual without a single follow-up.

options.text: Follow the AI: post the $48,000 to July expense because the invoice is dated July 1 and it all nets out within the quarter.
options.consequence: June revenue carries no matching cost, overstating June profit by $48,000; the board sees an inflated June margin, the year-end auditor proposes a passed adjustment, and you write a memo explaining the cutoff miss.

options.text: Notice the timing feels off and split the cost, accruing half to June and leaving half in July to be safe.
options.consequence: Half-matching still understates June cost by $24,000; your senior asks what basis supports the 50/50 split, and there isn't one, so you reverse it and book the full June accrual anyway.

beats.title: The auditor pulls your sample live
beats.situation: On the call, the external auditor selects the consulting project from the revenue sample and asks you to walk through how the June revenue figure and its matching cost were calculated, in real time, while your controller listens.
beats.decision: How do you respond when the auditor asks for the support on the spot?

options.text: Share your screen and walk them from the engagement letter to the June status report to the revenue recognition and the matching $48,000 accrual you just booked, then send the workpaper link so they have the trail.
options.consequence: The auditor closes the sample with no exception and notes your documentation as strong; the project never resurfaces in fieldwork, clearing one of your five open close items.

options.text: Explain the numbers verbally from memory and promise to send the supporting documents after the call.
options.consequence: The auditor opens a follow-up request; you spend an hour that evening assembling the same backup you could have shown live, and the item stays open another day.

options.text: Tell the auditor the revenue was reviewed and approved by the controller, so the figure is reliable and the detail isn't needed right now.
options.consequence: Deflecting to approval instead of evidence reads as a red flag; the auditor expands the sample to five more projects, and your controller has you reconstruct support for all of them by Friday.

title: Financial Analyst
oneLineReality: You live inside Excel building forecasts and variance decks, turning messy company data into a number a VP will actually defend in a meeting.
typicalDay: 8:30am - Refresh the daily flash report: pull actuals from the ERP/GL, reconcile against yesterday's numbers, flag anything that moved more than ~5%.
9:30am - Update the monthly variance bridge: explain why marketing spend came in $180K over budget (timing? a misclassified vendor invoice?) before the controller asks.
11:00am - Build/maintain a three-statement or DCF model; sanity-check that the balance sheet still balances and growth assumptions tie to the sales pipeline.
1:30pm - Cross-functional meeting with a department head who insists their budget overrun was 'one-time' - you politely push back with the data.
3:00pm - Format a board/leadership deck: charts, footnotes, a one-line narrative per slide. Half the job is making the number legible.
4:30pm - Answer ad-hoc 'can you just quickly pull...' requests that are never quick, and document assumptions so next month is faster.
workStyle: Mostly onsite or hybrid, desk-bound and collaborative with finance peers plus business stakeholders. Heavy month-end and quarter-end deadline crunches; calmer mid-cycle. Corporate FP&A is more 9-to-6; investment banking / sell-side equity research runs far longer hours.
boringHardPart: Reconciliation and data cleanup. Before any 'analysis' happens you spend hours chasing why two systems disagree by $4,212, fixing broken Excel links, and re-keying numbers because a stakeholder sent a PDF instead of a file. Month-end close means the same deck, on a deadline, every single month.
keyTools: Microsoft Excel (advanced: pivot tables, XLOOKUP, INDEX/MATCH, modeling)
ERP/GL systems (SAP, Oracle, NetSuite, Workday Adaptive)
SQL for pulling data from warehouses
Power BI or Tableau for dashboards
Bloomberg Terminal / Capital IQ / FactSet (for markets-facing roles)
crashCourse: Build a 3-statement financial model (income statement, balance sheet, cash flow) that links and balances - the core skill.
Learn a discounted cash flow (DCF) valuation from scratch: free cash flow, WACC, terminal value.
Master Excel without the mouse: XLOOKUP/INDEX-MATCH, pivot tables, IF/SUMIFS, and keyboard shortcuts.
Learn to build a budget-vs-actual variance bridge and write the 2-sentence 'why' narrative behind each variance.
Pick up basic SQL SELECT/JOIN/GROUP BY so you can pull your own data instead of waiting on someone.

workSimulation.scenario: You're an FP&A analyst setting the run-rate EBITDA that next year's budget targets will be built on. Reviewing the trailing 12 months, you notice Q2 EBITDA was unusually high because the company booked a $3M one-time gain from a legal settlement. Your VP needs the normalized run-rate base by end of day.
workSimulation.task: What EBITDA base do you hand the VP to build next year's forecast on?

options.text: Use trailing-twelve-month EBITDA as-is, including the $3M settlement gain, since it's real cash that hit the books.
options.feedback: This inflates the run-rate. The $3M won't repeat next year, so every growth target built on this base starts ~$3M in the hole - you've baked a phantom into the plan and someone will miss their number because of it.

options.text: Exclude the $3M one-time settlement gain to get normalized run-rate EBITDA, and footnote it separately so the adjustment is transparent.
options.feedback: Correct. Run-rate / normalized EBITDA strips non-recurring items so the base reflects the ongoing business. Footnoting it keeps you auditable and lets leadership see exactly what you removed and why.

options.text: Spread the $3M evenly across all 12 months so it doesn't distort any single quarter.
options.feedback: Smoothing hides the problem instead of removing it. The gain is non-recurring; averaging it still leaves $3M of one-time money in your annual run-rate base.

options.text: Ask accounting to reclassify the settlement as operating revenue so the model treats it consistently.
options.feedback: This is both wrong and a red flag - you'd be distorting the financials to fit your model. Non-recurring items get normalized out, never relabeled to look recurring.

workSimulation.aiSuggestion: The AI coworker says: 'Easy - just pull the trailing-twelve-month EBITDA straight from the GL and annualize it. TTM is the standard run-rate base; the total is right there in the ledger.'
workSimulation.aiMistake: The AI grabbed the GL total mechanically and never scanned for non-recurring items. TTM is a fine starting point, but 'run-rate' specifically means normalized - the $3M legal settlement must be stripped out. The AI conflated 'what's in the ledger' with 'what will recur.'
workSimulation.correctHumanJudgment: A human analyst remembers that Q2 spiked, opens the detail, recognizes the settlement line as one-time, and ties it back to the legal footnote before trusting the total. The skill isn't pulling the number - it's knowing which numbers don't belong in it.

aiCatchOptions.text: It pulls the raw TTM total straight from the ledger without scanning for non-recurring items — leaving the $3M one-time legal settlement in the 'run-rate' base.
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Right. 'Run-rate' means normalized. Strip the one-time settlement before annualizing, or next year's targets sit on a number that won't repeat.

aiCatchOptions.text: It annualized TTM instead of using a simple quarterly average.
aiCatchOptions.feedback: The averaging method is minor. The real error is leaving a $3M non-recurring gain inside a 'normalized' base.

aiCatchOptions.text: It didn't adjust EBITDA for depreciation changes.
aiCatchOptions.feedback: EBITDA already excludes D&A. The miss is the one-time settlement inflating the recurring base.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Lock in Excel fundamentals
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Spend week 1 doing keyboard-only Excel: pivot tables, XLOOKUP/INDEX-MATCH, SUMIFS, IF logic. Use a free dataset and rebuild a P&L summary from raw transactions.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Build one 3-statement model
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Follow a free Corporate Finance Institute or Wall Street Prep intro and build a linked income statement, balance sheet, and cash flow from a real 10-K. Make the balance sheet actually balance.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Do a DCF on a public company
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Pick a company you understand (e.g. a retailer), pull its filings, and build a discounted cash flow valuation. Write down every assumption and why you chose it.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Mini project - budget vs actual
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Invent or download a department budget and actuals, build a variance bridge in Excel, and write a one-paragraph narrative explaining the three biggest variances. This is the literal daily job.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Learn basic SQL
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Do a free SQLBolt or Mode SQL tutorial through SELECT, WHERE, JOIN, GROUP BY so you can pull your own data instead of waiting on engineering.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Read the market's language

automates: Pulling and reconciling data across systems and refreshing recurring reports
First-draft Excel formulas, model scaffolding, and chart/deck formatting
Summarizing earnings calls, 10-Ks, and long financial documents
Writing the boilerplate narrative around routine variances
humanValue: Judgment on which adjustments/assumptions are defensible (normalizing one-time items, choosing a discount rate)
Reading organizational and business context AI can't see (a budget overrun that's really a strategic bet)
Pushing back on a department head's numbers in a live meeting
Owning and standing behind a forecast that real money and jobs depend on
aiImpact.riskNote: High exposure on the mechanical core - data pulls, model building, deck formatting - which AI does fast and well, squeezing the most junior tasks. But the judgment, stakeholder pushback, and accountability for the final number stay human. The risk is fewer pure-grunt analyst seats, not the role vanishing; analysts who only move data are far more exposed than those who interpret it.

shift.intro: It's 8:31am, your coffee is still too hot, and the daily flash report is already wrong: the ERP says cash is $4,212 off from what you closed last night.
shift.closer: You never built a single 'analysis' today and still left at 7pm exhausted, because the whole job was making one number defensible enough that a VP would say it out loud in a board meeting.

beats.title: The $4,212 ghost
beats.situation: Your daily flash report won't tie out: the GL cash balance is $4,212 higher than yesterday's reconciled close. The controller glances at flash before her 9am standup. You have twenty minutes.
beats.decision: How do you handle the variance before flash goes out?

options.text: Open the GL detail, sort by timestamp, and trace the $4,212 to its source before sending flash.
options.consequence: You find a wire that posted after midnight from a customer prepayment; you reclass it, flash ties out clean, and the controller forwards your note as the answer when the CFO asks the same question at 9:15.

options.text: Send flash on time with a footnote: '$4,212 unreconciled, investigating — likely timing.'
options.consequence: Flash goes out punctual but the controller pings you twice during her standup; you end up tracing it anyway by 9:40, now under pressure and in front of an audience.

options.text: Plug the $4,212 into a 'misc reconciling items' line so the report balances and move on.
options.consequence: Three weeks later at month-end the plug has grown to $19K of stacked timing differences nobody untangled, and you spend a Saturday rebuilding the cash recon from scratch.

beats.title: The $180K marketing overrun
beats.situation: The monthly variance bridge shows marketing $180K over budget. The controller will ask why in her 10:30 review. Marketing swears they didn't overspend.
beats.decision: How do you explain the $180K before the review?

options.text: Pull the GL detail for the marketing cost center and reconcile each large invoice against budget and vendor.
options.consequence: You find a $165K agency invoice miscoded to marketing that belongs in IT; you reclass it, the 'overrun' collapses to $15K of real timing, and the controller walks into review with a clean story.

options.text: Email the marketing director asking if they know what drove the $180K.
options.consequence: They reply at 10:25 — five minutes before review — with 'looks like timing on the Q3 campaign?' You repeat an unverified guess to the controller and look unsure when she pushes on it.

options.text: Write 'higher campaign spend, timing-related' in the bridge narrative and move to the next line.
options.consequence: The miscoded IT invoice rides in marketing all quarter; when IT under-runs its own budget, two department heads argue over phantom numbers and finance gets blamed for the mess.

beats.title: 'It was one-time'
beats.situation: You're in a room with the Ops director whose department blew budget by $90K. He insists it was 'a one-time equipment thing' and wants it excluded from his run-rate. You have the GL open on your laptop.
beats.decision: He's senior and annoyed. How do you respond?

options.text: Show him the GL detail: the 'one-time' equipment cost also appeared in two of the last three months — it's recurring.
options.consequence: He grumbles but concedes; the run-rate stays honest, and when his Q4 actuals land right on the un-adjusted number, your credibility with the controller climbs.

options.text: Agree to tag it 'one-time' for now but add a footnote that it recurred recently.
options.consequence: The footnote gets dropped when the deck is summarized upward; leadership budgets next year as if the $90K vanishes, and the gap resurfaces as a 'surprise' in Q2.

options.text: He outranks you and the meeting's tense — mark it one-time and move on.
options.consequence: His budget gets reset $90K too low; when the cost predictably returns, he's 'over' again every month and openly blames finance's numbers in front of the CFO.

beats.title: The run-rate base
beats.situation: Your VP needs the normalized run-rate EBITDA by end of day — it's the foundation next year's entire budget gets built on. You pull the trailing twelve months and notice Q2 EBITDA looks unusually high.
beats.decision: What EBITDA base do you hand the VP?
beats.aiSuggestion: The AI coworker says: 'Easy — just pull the trailing-twelve-month EBITDA straight from the GL and annualize it. TTM is the standard run-rate base; the total is right there in the ledger.'

options.text: Open the Q2 detail, find the $3M legal-settlement gain, strip it out, and tie the adjustment back to the legal footnote before handing over a normalized base.
options.consequence: Next year's targets are built on EBITDA that will actually recur; the VP defends the number to the board without a single follow-up, and you're handed the full model next quarter.

options.text: Use the TTM total but flag to the VP that Q2 'looked high' and may need a look.
options.consequence: The VP is in back-to-backs, skims your note, and ships the inflated base; the $3M phantom only surfaces in March when actuals miss and someone asks why the budget was 12% too high.

options.text: Follow the AI: pull TTM EBITDA from the GL, annualize it, and send it as the run-rate base.
options.consequence: The entire annual budget inflates by $3M of non-recurring gain; sales gets impossible quotas, bonuses are set against a fiction, and a Q1 reforecast scramble traces straight back to your number.

title: Creator / Content Strategist
oneLineReality: You are part marketer, part editor, part publicist: you plan what gets posted, write or shape most of it, and live or die by whether real audiences actually engage.
typicalDay: 8:30 - Check overnight analytics: which posts/emails performed, flag anything viral or any negative comment thread that needs a response
9:30 - Editorial standup: review the content calendar, reprioritize because a product launch or news event just shifted the week's plan
10:30 - Draft and edit: write captions, a blog post, a script outline, or a newsletter; route to a designer or video editor
13:00 - Stakeholder calls: brief a founder/executive on messaging, or align with sales/product on what the campaign must say
14:30 - Build or schedule: load posts into a scheduler, set UTM tracking links, brief a creator/influencer on deliverables
16:00 - Report and pitch: update a campaign dashboard, write a pitch email to a journalist or partner, propose next month's content bets
workStyle: Mostly hybrid or remote, highly collaborative (designers, video editors, founders, sales, sometimes legal). Deadline-driven and reactive: a news cycle, an algorithm change, or a viral comment can blow up your plan in an hour. Lots of context-switching, frequent off-hours monitoring during launches or a crisis.
boringHardPart: Most of the job is not the creative spark, it is the grind: rewriting the same caption five times for five platforms, chasing approvals from people who reply in three days, reformatting one idea into a post, a reel, an email, and a thread, and staring at flat engagement numbers you cannot fully explain. You also absorb the emotional whiplash of pouring days into something that gets 40 likes, then watching a throwaway post outperform it.
keyTools: Google Analytics 4 / native platform analytics (Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, LinkedIn)
Notion or Airtable for content calendars
Canva and Adobe Creative Cloud (Premiere, Photoshop)
Buffer / Later / Sprout Social for scheduling
SEO tools like Ahrefs or Semrush
crashCourse: Write one tight content brief: audience, goal, key message, channel, and the single metric that defines success
Learn to read a basic analytics dashboard: reach vs. engagement vs. conversion, and why each means something different
Repurpose one idea into four formats (long post, short video, email, carousel) without losing the core message
Master a hook: study why the first 3 seconds / first line decides whether anyone keeps watching or reading
Run a tiny A/B test on two headlines or thumbnails and let the data, not your taste, pick the winner

workSimulation.scenario: You run content for a mid-size skincare brand. A wellness influencer with 800k followers offers to post a glowing review of your new serum in exchange for a flat $6,000 fee. Their engagement looks strong and the founder is excited. You have three days to lock the campaign before a product launch.
workSimulation.task: Decide how to move forward with the influencer partnership.

options.text: Pay the $6,000, send the product, and let the influencer post their honest review without dictating the script or requiring any disclosure label
options.feedback: Wrong. A paid endorsement legally requires a clear, conspicuous disclosure (e.g. #ad) under FTC rules. 'Honest review' does not remove the paid relationship. You and the brand can both be liable for a deceptive endorsement.

options.text: Vet the influencer's audience quality and past brand work, agree on talking points and required claims limits, and contractually require a clear #ad disclosure plus FTC-compliant language
options.feedback: Correct. You protect the brand on three fronts: audience authenticity (are the 800k real and relevant?), claim safety (skincare 'results' claims can trigger regulatory issues), and disclosure compliance. This is exactly the judgment a strategist is paid for.

options.text: Negotiate the fee down to $3,000 and skip the contract to move faster, since the launch deadline is tight
options.feedback: Wrong. Saving money and time by skipping a contract removes your disclosure requirement, usage rights, and claim controls. One non-compliant or off-brand post can cause more damage than the entire campaign is worth.

options.text: Decline all paid influencer work because it is inherently deceptive and only use organic content
options.feedback: Wrong. Paid partnerships are standard and legitimate when disclosed properly. Refusing them outright is not principled, it just cedes the channel to competitors and misreads how the industry actually operates.

workSimulation.aiSuggestion: The AI assistant drafts the campaign and says: 'This influencer is a great fit. I analyzed their feed and engagement rate is 4.2%, well above average. I have written the post caption and a glowing testimonial script for them. Recommend moving forward at $6,000 to hit the launch.'
workSimulation.aiMistake: The AI optimized for surface metrics and speed but missed two real-world landmines: it never flagged the legal requirement for an #ad disclosure, and it wrote a scripted 'glowing testimonial' that puts specific efficacy words in the influencer's mouth, which can constitute an unsubstantiated skincare claim. It also took the 4.2% engagement at face value without checking for bought or bot followers.
workSimulation.correctHumanJudgment: A human strategist knows FTC disclosure is non-negotiable and that dictated efficacy claims create regulatory and reputational risk. They would require the #ad label, strip unverifiable 'results' claims, and manually spot-check the follower base (comment quality, follower growth spikes) before trusting that 4.2% number.

aiCatchOptions.text: It skips the legally required #ad disclosure and scripts specific 'glowing' efficacy claims for a skincare product, while taking 4.2% engagement at face value without checking for bot/bought followers.
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Right. FTC disclosure is non-negotiable, dictated efficacy claims create regulatory risk, and engagement rates need a manual authenticity check.

aiCatchOptions.text: The $6,000 fee is too high for an 800k-follower influencer.
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Price is negotiable and not the core risk. Missing FTC disclosure and unsubstantiated claims can trigger real legal and reputational damage.

aiCatchOptions.text: It didn't schedule the post for the optimal time of day.
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Timing optimization is minor. The landmines are legal: disclosure and unverifiable product claims.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Pick a niche and a real subject
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Choose one topic and one brand or creator (yourself, a local business, or a fictional but realistic brand) to make all your work concrete instead of theoretical.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Build a content calendar

thirtyDayPlan.title: Ship a 7-day mini campaign (mini project)

thirtyDayPlan.title: Write the analytics teardown
