typicalDegree: High school diploma plus a 4-5 year registered apprenticeship (paid). A college degree is not required; most electricians learn through apprenticeship and then pass a state/local licensing exam.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Lock down the fundamentals
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Spend the first week mastering Ohm's Law, series/parallel circuits, and wire-gauge-to-ampacity (14/15A, 12/20A, 10/30A). Use free Khan Academy circuit lessons or Mike Holt's free basic videos.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Buy and use a multimeter
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Get a cheap (~$30) multimeter and a non-contact voltage tester. Practice measuring voltage, continuity, and resistance on batteries, outlets, and a lamp cord (unplugged) until it's second nature.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Build a mini wiring project
thirtyDayPlan.detail: With a $25 wiring kit or hardware-store parts and a length of NM cable, wire a single-pole switch to a light, then a GFCI receptacle, then a 3-way switch pair on a board. This is your hands-on proof you actually like the work.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Read the apprenticeship landscape
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Compare a union JATC (NECA-IBEW Electrical Training Alliance, tuition-free + paid) vs. a merit-shop IEC apprenticeship in your state. Note application windows, aptitude test (math + reading), and physical requirements.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Knock out the math gate
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Most apprenticeship aptitude tests are algebra and reading comprehension. Spend a week on the free Electrical Training Alliance / IBEW aptitude prep and basic algebra (fractions, ratios, solving for a variable).

thirtyDayPlan.title: Make real contact
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Email or walk into 3 local electrical contractors and 1 JATC/IEC office. Ask about apprenticeship openings, pre-apprenticeship programs, and whether you can shadow a crew for a day. Getting on a real jobsite once beats a month of videos.

certificate.name: Registered Electrical Apprenticeship (NECA-IBEW Electrical Training Alliance JATC, or merit-shop IEC) - earn-while-you-learn, ~8,000 hrs OJT + classroom, ends in journeyworker credential

automates: Load calculations and panel schedules from a set of plans
Pulling NEC code references and flagging likely violations in a design
Generating material take-offs and conduit fill calculations
Estimating and bidding labor/material from blueprints
Documentation, as-builts, and inspection paperwork
humanValue: Physically pulling wire, bending conduit, and terminating devices in real, messy buildings
Troubleshooting live, undocumented systems where the as-built never matches reality
On-the-spot judgment when framing, plumbing, or HVAC conflicts with the planned routing
Carrying legal liability and a license that says the work is safe
Hands-on safety: lockout/tagout, working around energized equipment, protecting other trades
aiImpact.riskNote: Very low direct automation risk. The core work is physical, on-site, and requires a licensed human to legally sign off on safety. AI and robotics speed up design, estimating, and prefab, but someone still has to crawl the attic and make the connection. If anything, electrification (EVs, solar, data centers, grid upgrades) is expanding demand faster than AI is shrinking it.

shift.intro: It's 28 degrees in an unheated shell of a house, your breath fogging the prints as the foreman tells you the drywallers are coming Thursday whether you're ready or not.

beats.title: Laying Out the Floor
beats.situation: You're marking box locations down a long exterior wall. The print shows receptacles at the standard 12 inches, but the architect's elevation sheet shows a run of base cabinets and a countertop along this same wall that nobody flagged. If you set these boxes at 12 inches, they land behind the cabinet boxes, buried forever.
beats.decision: How do you set the rough-in heights on this wall?

options.text: Stop, pull the elevation sheet, and set the counter receptacles at 42-44 inches above the cabinet run while keeping the rest at 12 inches.
options.consequence: Three weeks later the granite goes in and every outlet sits clean above the backsplash; the GC name-drops you to the homeowner as the trade that actually reads the whole set.

options.text: Set everything at 12 inches like the power plan says and let the cabinet guys deal with it.
options.consequence: Cabinets land Thursday, four outlets vanish behind them; you spend a Saturday on your own dime cutting in old-work boxes and fishing wire through finished wall.

options.text: Set them at 12 inches but text the GC a heads-up that some may conflict with cabinets.
options.consequence: The text gets buried; two outlets are usable, two aren't, and you're back mid-finish relocating boxes while the painter waits on you.

beats.title: The HVAC Got There First
beats.situation: Your homerun path to the panel runs straight through a stud bay the HVAC crew just stuffed with a cold-air return boot. You need to get four circuits down to the basement. The framing is tight and the inspector hates drilled holes too close to the boot.
beats.decision: How do you route the homeruns?

options.text: Re-route one bay over, keep your holes centered in the studs and 1.25 inches off the edge, and add nail plates where needed.
options.consequence: Rough-in inspection passes clean; the drywall screws Thursday hit nothing, and no one ever calls you back about a screwed-through cable.

options.text: Notch the stud edges to squeeze cables past the boot and move on to keep pace.
options.consequence: Inspector red-tags the notched bearing studs; the GC has to call a framer for sistering, and your name is on the correction notice that delays drywall a week.

options.text: Drill through close to the boot but slap nail plates over everything to cover it.
options.consequence: It passes, but two cables run warm against the duct; a year later the homeowner reports a flickering circuit and you eat the callback diagnosing derating.

beats.title: The Bathroom Circuit
beats.situation: You're roughing in a new full bath. Prints call for a 20-amp GFCI-protected receptacle at the vanity, plus the homeowner wants the new ceiling light and exhaust fan wired. To save copper, the same homerun you're running also loops over and picks up the receptacle in the adjacent powder room. Now you have to pick conductor, breaker, and what loads ride this circuit.
beats.decision: How do you wire the bathroom receptacle circuit?
beats.aiSuggestion: Run 12 AWG on a 20-amp GFCI-protected circuit, and to save a homerun just put the new ceiling light and exhaust fan on that same 20-amp bathroom circuit.

options.text: Since this homerun feeds two bathrooms' receptacles, keep the 20A circuit receptacle-only and pull a separate 15A circuit for the light and fan.
options.consequence: Inspector checks the panel schedule, sees the receptacle-only 20A and the dedicated lighting circuit, and signs off in two minutes; the bath works flawlessly for years.

options.text: Follow the AI: 12 AWG, 20A GFCI, with the vanity receptacles, ceiling light, and fan all on the one circuit.
options.consequence: Because the homerun serves two baths, 210.11(C)(3)'s single-bath exception is void; inspector red-tags it, you re-pull a separate lighting homerun through insulated walls, blowing a full day.

options.text: Keep light and fan on the 20A receptacle circuit but quickly assume it only counts as one bathroom since it's the 'main' one.
options.consequence: You guessed wrong on the count; the inspector catches the powder-room tap on the same homerun and you're rewiring the lighting leg anyway, just a half-day instead of a full one.

beats.title: The Dead 3-Way
beats.situation: Make-up is done and you flip the stairwell circuit to test it. The 3-way switches do nothing; the light stays dead no matter the combination. The drywallers are 36 hours out and these boxes need to close. You've got a meter and two open switch boxes.
beats.decision: How do you troubleshoot it?

options.text: Meter it systematically: confirm power at the line box, check the travelers and common, and find the neutral or traveler that got landed wrong.
options.consequence: In fifteen minutes you find a traveler swapped onto the common screw, fix it, light works; boxes close on schedule and the drywall crew never even knows there was a problem.

options.text: Assume a bad switch, swap both 3-ways with new ones from the truck, and re-test.
options.consequence: New switches don't fix it because the wiring was the fault; you've burned 40 minutes and two devices before you finally pull the meter out anyway.

options.text: Call it close enough, tape the wires, and tell yourself you'll chase it at trim after drywall.
options.consequence: At trim the wall is closed; the fault is a miswired neutral deep in the buried box, and you're cutting open finished drywall and re-texturing to reach it.

shift.closer: You went home filthy, knees aching from concrete and shoulders cooked from overhead, having spent the whole day quietly catching the mistakes that would've burned you in three weeks.

title: Physician (Doctor)
oneLineReality: You spend a decade and six figures of debt earning the right to make life-and-death decisions on too little sleep, then half your day is fighting insurance forms and electronic charting instead of treating patients.
typicalDay: Pre-round and review overnight labs, vitals, imaging, and nursing notes on your patient list before the team huddle
See patients back-to-back: take history, examine, explain a diagnosis in plain language, and adjust the treatment plan
Document everything in the EHR and place orders for meds, labs, imaging, and consults (this eats hours)
Coordinate with nurses, pharmacists, specialists, and case managers; field pages and inbox messages between visits
Handle prior authorizations, refill requests, and phone calls to insurers to get a treatment approved
Break bad news, counsel a worried family, and sign discharge paperwork before finally heading home
workStyle: Mostly on-site in clinics, hospitals, and ORs; high-stakes, fast-paced, and team-based. Long shifts, frequent on-call and weekend coverage, and during residency 60-80 hour weeks are normal. Some specialties (radiology, dermatology, psychiatry) allow more telehealth and predictable hours.
boringHardPart: The EHR and the paperwork. Studies show physicians spend nearly half their workday on documentation, inbox messages, and prior authorizations rather than with patients. Add the slow grind of the path itself: years of memorization, board exams (USMLE/COMLEX), and residency before you ever practice independently, all while carrying ~$200k+ in debt.
keyTools: Electronic Health Record systems (Epic, Cerner/Oracle Health)
Stethoscope, otoscope, and bedside physical-exam skills
Point-of-care ultrasound and standard imaging (X-ray, CT, MRI)
Diagnostic decision support and order-entry (CPOE) systems
crashCourse: Master the language: learn anatomy, physiology, and medical terminology so you can read a chart and think in systems
Learn the diagnostic method: history-taking, differential diagnosis, and Bayesian reasoning (pretest probability, sensitivity/specificity)
Understand the pipeline: pre-med prerequisites + MCAT, then 4 years of med school, USMLE Steps 1-3, and 3-7 years of residency
Get comfortable with evidence-based medicine: how to read a clinical trial, interpret p-values, and apply guidelines to a real patient
Build the human skills: breaking bad news, shared decision-making, and clear plain-language communication

workSimulation.scenario: You are the physician at an urgent care clinic. A 58-year-old man walks in with 2 hours of pressure-like chest discomfort radiating to his left arm, sweating, and nausea. He has high blood pressure and is a smoker. He looks pale but his vital signs are currently stable.
workSimulation.task: What is the most appropriate immediate next step?

options.text: Get a 12-lead ECG within minutes, give aspirin to chew, and activate emergency transfer for suspected acute coronary syndrome
options.feedback: Correct. This is a textbook ACS presentation. Time is muscle: an ECG in under 10 minutes triages STEMI vs. non-STEMI, aspirin reduces clot burden, and he needs an ED with cath-lab capability, not an urgent care. You stabilize and move fast.

options.text: Reassure him it is likely acid reflux, prescribe a proton pump inhibitor, and send him home with primary-care follow-up
options.feedback: Dangerous. GERD can mimic cardiac pain, but you never anchor on the benign diagnosis in a 58-year-old smoker with diaphoresis and radiating pain. Missing an MI here can be fatal and is a classic malpractice scenario.

options.text: Order an outpatient stress test for next week and discharge him with instructions to rest
options.feedback: Wrong tempo. A stress test is for stable, low-risk chest pain workups, not an active, evolving presentation. Scheduling it for next week sends a possible heart attack home untreated.

options.text: Diagnose musculoskeletal strain, prescribe ibuprofen, and advise heat and stretching
options.feedback: No. Nothing in the history points to a muscle injury, and NSAIDs can worsen outcomes in acute coronary syndrome. This skips the must-not-miss diagnosis entirely.

workSimulation.aiSuggestion: The AI scribe assistant says: 'Classic ACS. Immediately give aspirin 325 mg, sublingual nitroglycerin for the chest pain, and start a beta-blocker now to lower cardiac workload before transport.'
workSimulation.aiMistake: The AI recommends giving sublingual nitroglycerin (and an immediate beta-blocker) reflexively, without first getting the ECG and without asking whether the patient recently took a PDE5 inhibitor such as sildenafil (Viagra). If he took one, or if the ECG shows an inferior/right-ventricular infarct, nitroglycerin can cause catastrophic, life-threatening hypotension. Early IV/oral beta-blockade in someone at risk of cardiogenic shock also increases harm (COMMIT trial).
workSimulation.correctHumanJudgment: The physician withholds nitroglycerin until the ECG is done and asks the patient directly about erectile-dysfunction medication use and signs of heart failure. Aspirin and rapid transfer stay; nitro and beta-blocker are given only after those checks. A human integrates the contraindications the AI glossed over.

aiCatchOptions.text: The AI told you to give nitroglycerin before checking the ECG for an inferior/right-ventricular infarct and before asking about recent PDE5 inhibitor (e.g., sildenafil) use, either of which can cause life-threatening hypotension
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Right. Nitroglycerin is not automatic in ACS. An inferior/RV MI or recent sildenafil makes it dangerous, and the immediate beta-blocker adds cardiogenic-shock risk. The ECG and a quick medication history must come first.

aiCatchOptions.text: The AI was wrong to recommend aspirin, which should be avoided in suspected heart attacks because it raises bleeding risk
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Incorrect. Chewable aspirin is a cornerstone of ACS care and improves survival. This part of the AI's advice was actually correct.

aiCatchOptions.text: The AI should have ordered a CT scan to rule out a pulmonary embolism before doing anything else
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Plausible-sounding but wrong. The presentation is classic cardiac, and a CT would dangerously delay the ECG, aspirin, and transfer. PE is a lower-priority consideration here, not the first move.

typicalDegree: Bachelor's degree with pre-med prerequisites + MCAT, then a 4-year M.D. (Doctor of Medicine) or D.O. (Doctor of Osteopathic Medicine) degree, followed by a 3-7 year residency and state medical licensure (USMLE/COMLEX).

thirtyDayPlan.title: Learn the language of medicine
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Spend week 1 on a free medical-terminology and basic anatomy/physiology course (Khan Academy Medicine or a free Coursera intro). Goal: read a basic chart and name body systems confidently.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Shadow or interview a real physician
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Email 5 local doctors or use a family connection to arrange a half-day of shadowing. Watch how much time goes to charting vs. patients, and write down 3 things that surprised you.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Understand the pipeline and the money
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Map the full path on one page: pre-reqs, MCAT, med school cost (use the tuition numbers above), USMLE Steps, residency match, and expected debt vs. salary by specialty. Decide if the 11+ year timeline fits your life.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Practice clinical reasoning
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Work through 10 free case studies (e.g., NEJM Healer or MedSchoolCoach case sets). For each, write a differential diagnosis and the one test you'd order first before checking the answer.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Mini project: present a patient case
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Pick one common condition (chest pain, diabetes, or appendicitis). Build a 1-page SOAP note (Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan) for a fictional patient and present it out loud in under 3 minutes, as if rounding with a team.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Pressure-test your interest
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Volunteer for a few shifts at a hospital, hospice, or free clinic. Honestly rate whether you're energized or drained by sick, scared people and long hours, this is the single best predictor of fit.

automates: Drafting clinical notes from ambient visit recordings (AI scribes)
Flagging abnormal labs and drug-interaction or dosing alerts
First-pass reads of imaging and ECGs to prioritize the worklist
Summarizing long chart histories and surfacing relevant prior results
Auto-populating prior-authorization and billing-code paperwork
humanValue: Physical examination and hands-on procedures (surgery, intubation, deliveries)
Weighing ambiguous, conflicting findings and accepting legal/ethical responsibility for the decision
Breaking bad news and guiding shared decisions with frightened patients and families
Catching the atypical presentation and the contraindication the algorithm misses
Earning trust and reading the unspoken cues that change a diagnosis
aiImpact.riskNote: AI is a powerful copilot, not a replacement. Licensure, malpractice liability, hands-on procedures, and the need for human accountability protect the core role. The real shift: doctors who use AI well (for documentation, triage, and decision support) will outpace those who don't, and some diagnostic/imaging tasks will be augmented or compressed. Demand also stays high from an aging population and physician shortages.

shift.intro: It's 6:40 a.m. and you're pre-rounding on twelve patients with a cold coffee and a pager that won't stop buzzing, knowing the team huddle starts in twenty minutes whether you're ready or not.
shift.closer: You made three good calls and one you'll second-guess for a week, but the truth is you spent more of the shift fighting an inbox and an insurer than touching a single patient.

beats.title: Pre-Round Triage
beats.situation: Overnight, one of your patients' labs flagged a potassium of 6.4 with peaked T-waves on a 4 a.m. ECG the night nurse quietly tucked into the chart. Huddle is in fifteen minutes and you still have eight charts unread.
beats.decision: How do you handle the hyperkalemia finding before huddle?

options.text: Go to the bedside now, repeat the ECG, and start emergent hyperkalemia treatment (calcium, insulin/glucose) before finishing the rest of pre-round
options.consequence: You stabilize the membrane and drop the K+ before he arrests; on rounds the attending notes you 'caught the one that mattered.' Two days later he's discharged home walking.

options.text: Order a stat repeat potassium to confirm it isn't a hemolyzed sample, and check the result before acting
options.consequence: Reasonable instinct, but the 40-minute lab turnaround burns time; the repeat confirms 6.3 and you treat late. He's fine, but the attending asks why you waited on a patient with ECG changes.

options.text: Flag it on your list to present at huddle so the team can decide together
options.consequence: By huddle he's in a wide-complex rhythm and a code is called. He survives the rapid response but lands in the ICU; the delay goes in the incident review.

beats.title: The Prior Auth Wall
beats.situation: A 34-year-old with poorly controlled diabetes needs a GLP-1 medication that's clearly indicated. Her insurer denied it and demands a prior authorization documenting two failed prior agents. Your waiting room has six patients stacked up.
beats.decision: How do you handle the denial?

options.text: Spend ten minutes now documenting her failed metformin and sulfonylurea trials and submit the prior auth with the specific clinical justification, then see the next patient
options.consequence: The auth clears in three days and she starts the drug. Your afternoon runs late, but she avoids an ER visit for hyperglycemia that month. The paperwork ate the time you'd budgeted for lunch.

options.text: Switch her to a cheaper, formulary-covered drug you know is less effective for her to avoid the paperwork entirely
options.consequence: She gets a prescription today, but her A1c barely moves over three months and you're having this same visit again in spring. Defensible under time pressure, suboptimal for her.

options.text: Tell her the insurance denied it and to call the insurer herself, and move on
options.consequence: She gives up, takes nothing, and returns six weeks later in DKA. The admission costs far more than the drug and a chart audit flags the abandoned plan.

beats.title: Chest Pain at Urgent Care
beats.situation: You're covering the urgent care side. A 58-year-old man walks in with 2 hours of pressure-like chest discomfort radiating to his left arm, sweating and nauseated. He's hypertensive and a smoker, pale but with stable vitals. Your AI scribe has already drafted orders.
beats.decision: What is the most appropriate immediate next step?
beats.aiSuggestion: The AI scribe assistant says: 'Classic ACS. Immediately give aspirin 325 mg, sublingual nitroglycerin for the chest pain, and start a beta-blocker now to lower cardiac workload before transport.'

options.text: Give chewable aspirin 325 mg and call EMS for emergent transfer now, but get a 12-lead ECG first and ask about sildenafil/ED meds and heart-failure signs before any nitroglycerin or beta-blocker
options.consequence: The ECG shows an inferior STEMI with right-ventricular involvement and he admits to taking sildenafil last night. Withholding nitro spares him a catastrophic crash; he reaches the cath lab and stents the RCA. The cardiologist later thanks you by name.

options.text: Give aspirin and arrange transfer, and give the sublingual nitroglycerin for pain but hold the beta-blocker until vitals are reassessed
options.consequence: Aspirin and transfer are right and you dodged the beta-blocker, but the nitro on an undiagnosed RV infarct drops his pressure to 70 systolic in the ambulance. EMS boluses fluids and he recovers, shaken, with a tougher pre-cath course.

options.text: Follow the AI: aspirin, sublingual nitroglycerin, and an immediate beta-blocker, then transport
options.consequence: Nitro plus recent sildenafil plus an RV infarct collapses his pressure; the early beta-blocker tips him into cardiogenic shock per the COMMIT data. He codes in your hallway before EMS arrives and the case becomes a morbidity-and-mortality conference.

beats.title: Breaking the News Before You Leave
beats.situation: Your shift technically ended an hour ago. The biopsy on a 61-year-old woman you admitted came back as metastatic pancreatic cancer. Her family is in the room, the night team hasn't met her, and you have eleven unsigned notes and a dark parking lot waiting.
beats.decision: How do you close out this patient?

options.text: Sit down with the patient and family, deliver the news in plain language without jargon, answer their questions, and hand off a clear plan to the night team before charting
options.consequence: It costs you another forty-five unpaid minutes and you finish notes at 8 p.m., but the family later writes that you were the one who made an unbearable day bearable. The night team inherits a clean, humane handoff.

options.text: Give the family the headline news briefly, promise the oncology team will explain details tomorrow, and leave the counseling to them
options.consequence: They get the truth but feel rushed and frightened overnight; the night nurse pages you twice at home with questions you could have pre-empted. Not wrong, but it leaves the family alone with the worst part.

options.text: Sign out 'biopsy results pending discussion' to the night team and head home, letting tomorrow's day team break the news
options.consequence: The family overhears 'cancer' from a phlebotomist before any physician speaks to them, and files a complaint about the handling. The dropped conversation erodes their trust in the whole team.

title: Dentist
oneLineReality: You run a small medical business with your hands inside nervous people's mouths all day — high pay and respect, but you graduate $300k+ in debt and your body pays the price for the precision.
typicalDay: Review the day's schedule and radiographs (X-rays) before the first patient, flagging anyone with complex medical histories or pending treatment plans
Numb and restore teeth: drilling out decay and placing composite fillings, crowns, or doing root canals while keeping the field dry and the patient calm
Perform exams and read new X-rays, diagnosing cavities, cracks, gum disease, and abscesses, then explaining findings to anxious patients in plain language
Handle one or two surgical procedures like an extraction or implant placement, watching for bleeding and anatomy near nerves and sinuses
Manage the business between patients: approve hygienist findings, sign off on insurance pre-authorizations, review lab cases, and handle a same-day emergency that breaks your schedule
Debrief with assistants and front desk, chart all treatment for legal and billing accuracy, and follow up on a post-op patient by phone
workStyle: Hands-on, detail-obsessed, and people-facing. You work standing or seated in fixed postures for hours, doing millimeter-precise work in a tiny wet space while simultaneously managing a frightened human and a small-business payroll. Highly autonomous once you own or run a practice, but relentlessly time-pressured.
boringHardPart: The grind nobody warns you about: hours of insurance paperwork and pre-authorization fights, narrow profit margins that mean you're effectively a small-business owner managing staff and supply costs, and the chronic neck, back, and hand strain from leaning over patients. Plus the emotional labor of treating people who are scared, in pain, or who ignored your advice and came back worse.
keyTools: Digital intraoral and panoramic X-ray / cone-beam CT imaging
Composite resins, dental amalgam, and curing lights
Intraoral scanners and CAD/CAM systems (e.g., CEREC) for same-day crowns
Practice management & EHR software (Dentrix, Eaglesoft, Open Dental)
Local anesthetic syringes, rubber dam isolation, loupes with headlight
crashCourse: Shadow a working dentist for 40+ hours and a specialist (oral surgeon or endodontist) for a day — admissions and your own sanity both demand you confirm you can stomach blood, drills, and saliva
Crush the prerequisite science stack: two semesters each of biology, general chem, organic chem, and physics with labs — these gate dental school and the DAT
Take the DAT (Dental Admission Test); aim for a 20+ academic average — practice the Perceptual Ability Test hard, it's the section that predicts hand skills
Learn the money math early: model 4 years of dental school debt (often $250k-$400k) against starting associate salaries before you commit
Practice fine-motor hobbies (carving, beading, sculpting) — dexterity is trainable and is literally graded in dental school waxing and prep labs

workSimulation.scenario: A 34-year-old patient comes in with sharp, lingering pain in the lower-right first molar (#30) that wakes them at night. The tooth has a large old filling. Cold testing produces pain that lingers 30+ seconds after the stimulus is removed. A bitewing X-ray shows recurrent decay deep under the filling, and the periapical X-ray shows a faint dark area (radiolucency) at the root tip.
workSimulation.task: What is the correct diagnosis and next step for tooth #30?

options.text: Irreversible pulpitis with apical periodontitis — the tooth needs root canal therapy (or extraction), not just a new filling
options.feedback: Correct. Lingering pain to cold (30+ seconds), spontaneous night pain, and a periapical radiolucency are classic signs the pulp is irreversibly inflamed/dying. Simply replacing the filling would trap the infection and the pain will worsen. Root canal or extraction is the standard of care.

options.text: Reversible pulpitis — remove the old filling, place a sedative dressing, and have the patient return if pain continues
options.feedback: This misreads the key sign. Reversible pulpitis causes brief pain that stops when the stimulus is removed. Pain that LINGERS 30+ seconds plus spontaneous night pain and a periapical radiolucency means the damage is irreversible — a sedative filling will fail.

options.text: Cracked tooth syndrome — place a crown to hold the tooth together and reassess
options.feedback: A crown might be needed eventually, but crowning a tooth with an already-dying pulp just seals infection inside. You must resolve the pulpal diagnosis (root canal) first; treating only the crack ignores the radiolucency and lingering pain.

options.text: Refer to an oral surgeon for immediate extraction since the tooth is non-restorable
options.feedback: Jumping to extraction is premature. A first molar with recurrent decay but intact root structure is usually restorable with root canal therapy plus a crown. Extraction is a fallback, not the first choice, and saving the natural tooth is generally better for the patient.

workSimulation.aiSuggestion: The clinical-AI assistant reads the chart and says: 'Diagnosis: irreversible pulpitis on #30. Recommend root canal therapy. I've drafted the treatment plan and pre-filled the anesthesia as 2 carpules of 2% lidocaine with 1:100,000 epinephrine — standard for a lower molar. Ready to proceed.'
workSimulation.aiMistake: The AI got the diagnosis right but blindly defaulted the anesthesia. A lower (mandibular) molar needs a nerve block, and dense mandibular bone plus an inflamed 'hot' tooth often resists standard lidocaine — many clinicians add articaine and/or supplemental intraligamentary or intraosseous injections. More importantly, the AI never checked the medical history: it didn't flag that epinephrine dose against the patient's cardiovascular status or possible drug interactions.
workSimulation.correctHumanJudgment: The dentist accepts the diagnosis but does NOT auto-accept the anesthesia plan. They check the medical history and meds, confirm there's no cardiac/epinephrine concern, and plan for a profound mandibular block with backup (extra articaine, intraligamentary injection) because hot lower molars are notoriously hard to numb. Anesthesia is a patient-specific clinical judgment, not a template field.

aiCatchOptions.text: It defaulted to a templated anesthesia plan without checking the medical history or that a hot lower molar often needs a supplemental block
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Right. The diagnosis was fine, but anesthesia is patient-specific: epinephrine must be checked against cardiovascular history, and inflamed mandibular molars frequently fail a single standard block. The AI treated a clinical judgment as a fill-in-the-blank.

aiCatchOptions.text: It misdiagnosed the tooth — it should have called this reversible pulpitis
aiCatchOptions.feedback: No, the AI's diagnosis of irreversible pulpitis was actually correct given the lingering pain and radiolucency. The flaw was downstream, in the anesthesia and safety check.

aiCatchOptions.text: It recommended a root canal when the tooth clearly needed extraction
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Extraction wasn't clearly indicated — a restorable first molar is usually saved with root canal therapy. The real error was the unchecked, templated anesthesia and missing medical-history review.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 1: Reality-check by shadowing
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Email 5 local dental offices and arrange to shadow at least 8 hours. Watch a filling, an extraction, and a hygiene exam. Honestly note: does the blood, drill noise, and saliva bother you, or fascinate you?

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 1-2: Map the real cost and timeline
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Build a simple spreadsheet: 4 years undergrad + 4 years dental school. Pull tuition from two schools above, add ~$25k/yr living costs, and project total debt vs. a $120k-$150k associate starting salary. Decide if the math works for you.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 2: Audit your science readiness
thirtyDayPlan.detail: List the prerequisites (bio, gen chem, orgo, physics, biochem). If you're in school, plan when you'll take each. If not, find a community college that offers them in-district for around $4k/year.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 3: Test your hands
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Mini project — buy a block of carving wax or soap and a cheap carving tool and sculpt a tooth (#8 central incisor) from a reference photo. Time yourself, then redo it. This is literally what dental school waxing labs grade; see if precise repetitive handwork energizes or drains you.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 3-4: Sample the DAT
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Download a free DAT practice test and take the Perceptual Ability and Quantitative sections cold. Don't judge the score — judge whether the spatial-reasoning puzzles feel learnable and interesting to you.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 4: Talk to someone in debt
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Find a dentist 2-5 years out of school (via shadowing contacts or LinkedIn) and ask three blunt questions: what's your debt, what do you actually earn, and would you do it again? Write down their answers and your gut reaction.

automates: Reading X-rays to flag suspected cavities, bone loss, and anomalies for the dentist to confirm
Drafting chart notes, treatment plans, and insurance pre-authorization paperwork
Scheduling, recall reminders, and patient intake/triage questions
Designing crowns and aligners from intraoral scans (CAD/CAM) and predicting tooth movement
humanValue: The actual physical procedure: drilling, suturing, extracting, and placing restorations with hands inside a moving, sensitive mouth
Real-time clinical judgment when anatomy, bleeding, or pain deviates from the textbook mid-procedure
Earning trust and calming a terrified or in-pain patient, and negotiating realistic treatment choices with them
Owning legal and ethical responsibility for the diagnosis and the irreversible thing you just did to someone's body
aiImpact.riskNote: Very low automation risk. AI is a genuinely useful second set of eyes on X-rays and a paperwork engine, but dentistry is a licensed, manual, surgical profession — someone has to physically do the procedure, exercise in-the-moment judgment, and hold legal liability. The bigger near-term shift is AI making each dentist faster and diagnostics more standardized, not replacing the chair.

shift.intro: It's 7:48 AM, your loupes are already fogging, the first patient is being seated, and a column of X-rays and a denied insurance claim are both glowing on your monitor before you've finished your coffee.
shift.closer: Eight hours of millimeter-precise work in a wet two-inch space while managing frightened people, a payroll, and an insurer who'd rather you fail — your hands and back ache, but the only mistakes that matter are the ones you didn't slow down to catch.

beats.title: The Pre-Flight Chart Review
beats.situation: Your 9:00 AM is a surgical extraction. The schedule note flags 'complex Hx.' You have ten minutes before the first restorative patient is numb and waiting, and the front desk wants you to just start the day on time.
beats.decision: How do you handle the flagged surgical patient before drilling on anyone?

options.text: Open the full medical history and med list now; you spot 'warfarin' and call to confirm a recent INR before touching them at 9.
options.consequence: INR comes back at 3.8 — too high to cut. You reschedule and loop in their physician. Avoids a post-extraction bleed that would have had them back in your chair, panicked, two days later.

options.text: Skim the flag, note 'on a blood thinner,' and plan to just ask them about it chairside.
options.consequence: You remember mid-numbing and stop to call the physician's office, sitting on hold while two other patients wait. The whole day runs 25 minutes behind from there.

options.text: Trust yesterday's hygienist note, keep the schedule, and deal with surprises when they come.
options.consequence: The socket won't stop oozing; they go home with a gauze pack and call your cell at 11 PM with a mouthful of clot. A preventable emergency you now own.

beats.title: Deep Decay, Live Nerve
beats.situation: Drilling out a large old filling on an upper bicuspid, the decay runs deeper than the X-ray showed. You're millimeters from the pulp and the tooth is still vital. The patient is gripping the armrests.
beats.decision: How do you finish this restoration?

options.text: Place a rubber dam for a dry field, excavate slowly, and do an indirect pulp cap with calcium silicate over the deepest spot, then restore and document.
options.consequence: The pulp stays vital and sealed. No callback. At the six-month recall the tooth tests normal and you never think about it again.

options.text: Work fast on cotton rolls, nick the pulp, and place a direct pulp cap on the tiny exposure.
options.consequence: Saliva likely touched the exposure. It holds for now, but there's a real chance it flares into irreversible pulpitis within six months and needs a root canal you'll do for free.

options.text: Pack and cure the composite quickly to stay on schedule, eyeballing the bite.
options.consequence: The filling sits high. Three days later they return with a cracked cusp and sharp bite pain — a remake plus an apology, and your morning blown open.

beats.title: The Denied Crown
beats.situation: Between patients you find the insurer denied pre-authorization for a crown on a cracked, root-canaled molar. The patient is in the chair now, the tooth genuinely needs full coverage, and the front desk is asking what to tell them about the cost.
beats.decision: How do you handle the denial?

options.text: Build the appeal: intraoral photos of the crack, the recent RCT, and a clinical narrative on fracture risk, then give the patient an interim plan while it's pending.
options.consequence: The appeal is approved two weeks later. The patient keeps the tooth and trusts you because you fought for them instead of billing them.

options.text: Skip the fight and just place a large filling instead to avoid the paperwork.
options.consequence: The unprotected tooth fractures under the filling in eight months. They're back needing the crown anyway — now angrier, and possibly needing an extraction.

options.text: Tell them the insurance said no and they'll need to pay the full crown fee out of pocket today.
options.consequence: They feel cornered, leave for a second opinion, and post a one-star review accusing you of upselling. You lose a patient over a fight you never started.

beats.title: The Hot Lower Molar
beats.situation: Your last slot is gone to a same-day emergency: a 34-year-old with sharp lower-right pain that wakes them at night. Tooth #30 has a large old filling, cold test lingers 30+ seconds, the bitewing shows recurrent decay deep under the filling, and the periapical shows a faint radiolucency at the root tip. The clinical-AI has already read the chart and drafted a plan.
beats.decision: You agree it needs a root canal — but do you run the AI's full plan as written?
beats.aiSuggestion: Diagnosis: irreversible pulpitis on #30. Recommend root canal therapy. I've drafted the treatment plan and pre-filled the anesthesia as 2 carpules of 2% lidocaine with 1:100,000 epinephrine — standard for a lower molar. Ready to proceed.

options.text: Accept the diagnosis, but open the medical history yourself — confirm no cardiac issue or epinephrine interaction — then plan a profound inferior alveolar nerve block with articaine and an intraligamentary backup, because hot lower molars resist standard lidocaine.
options.consequence: Anesthesia goes deep on the first try, the patient feels nothing, and the root canal finishes calm and clean. The right call was treating anesthesia as a patient-specific judgment, not a template field.

options.text: Take the diagnosis and lidocaine plan, but add a carpule of articaine as backup just in case — without reading the history.
options.consequence: The tooth does get numb, but mid-procedure you notice they're on a beta-blocker with borderline-high BP. It ends fine, but it was a near-miss you only avoided by luck, not by checking.

options.text: Click 'proceed' and deliver the two carpules of lidocaine exactly as the AI pre-filled them.
options.consequence: The inflamed tooth won't go numb — the patient jumps when you enter the pulp — and you realize too late their hypertension was uncontrolled. Palpitations, an aborted procedure, and a frightened patient you have to reschedule.

title: Pharmacist
oneLineReality: You are the last safety check between a prescriber's error and a patient's harm — paid six figures to catch the one interaction in a thousand, while standing for 10-hour retail shifts with no lunch break and a drive-thru line that never ends.
typicalDay: Verify and final-check 200-400 prescriptions per shift: confirm drug, dose, directions, and that the right pills are in the right bottle before they reach a patient
Run clinical screens for drug-drug interactions, duplicate therapy, allergies, and renal/age-based dosing, then call prescribers to resolve problems
Counsel patients at pickup on new meds — how to take them, side effects to watch for, what to do with a missed dose
Administer immunizations (flu, COVID, shingles, Tdap) and increasingly point-of-care test-and-treat visits
Manage insurance: adjudicate claims, fight prior-authorization rejections, find covered alternatives, handle DUR overrides
Supervise and direct pharmacy technicians, manage controlled-substance inventory and DEA recordkeeping, keep the workflow from collapsing
workStyle: On your feet behind a counter or in a hospital pharmacy for 8-12 hour shifts, often the only pharmacist on duty and legally responsible for everything that happens. High-interruption, high-stakes, deadline-dense. Retail means evenings, weekends, holidays and metrics pressure; hospital and clinical roles are calmer but require residency.
boringHardPart: The relentless interruption load. You are trying to perform a high-concentration legal verification on a controlled substance while the phone rings, a tech needs an override, the drive-thru buzzes, and an angry customer asks why their copay went up. Most of the day is not clinical brilliance — it's insurance battles, prior authorizations, and being held personally liable on a chronically understaffed floor with no scheduled break.
keyTools: Dispensing systems (Epic Willow, McKesson EnterpriseRx, BD Pyxis/Omnicell automated cabinets, ScriptPro)
Drug-interaction and clinical references (Lexicomp, Micromedex, Clinical Pharmacology)
Insurance claim adjudication / pharmacy benefit (PBM) portals and prior-auth platforms
Sterile/non-sterile compounding (USP 797/795) for hospital and specialty roles
crashCourse: Memorize the top 200 drugs cold: brand/generic, class, indication, key interactions, and counseling points — this is the spine of the job and the NAPLEX
Drill pharmaceutical calculations until flawless: mg/kg dosing, IV drip rates, alligation, mEq, and days-supply — a decimal error here can kill
Learn how insurance actually works: BIN/PCN, formularies, prior authorizations, and DAW codes — half your real day is this
Practice patient counseling out loud: explain a complex med to a scared 70-year-old in 60 seconds without jargon
Understand pharmacy law (federal DEA scheduling + your state's MPJE material): controlled-substance rules, refills, corresponding responsibility

workSimulation.scenario: You are the pharmacist on duty at a community pharmacy. An 82-year-old man drops off a new prescription for sildenafil 50 mg as needed. His active profile shows he is on isosorbide mononitrate 30 mg daily (a long-acting nitrate for chronic angina) and metoprolol.
workSimulation.task: Your software fires an interaction alert. What do you do before dispensing?

options.text: Hold the prescription, do not dispense, and call the prescriber — a PDE5 inhibitor (sildenafil) with any nitrate is a contraindicated combination that can cause life-threatening hypotension
options.feedback: Correct. Nitrate + PDE5 inhibitor is an absolute contraindication, not a manageable warning. The synergistic vasodilation can drop blood pressure catastrophically. You contact the prescriber to clarify intent and flag the nitrate before anything leaves the pharmacy.

options.text: Dispense it but counsel the patient to separate the sildenafil and his nitrate dose by at least several hours
options.feedback: Dangerous. This is not a timing or spacing problem — the combination is contraindicated regardless of how far apart the doses are taken, because the nitrate is long-acting and effects overlap. Spacing does not make it safe.

options.text: Dispense and counsel the patient to take sildenafil with food to reduce side effects
options.feedback: This treats a life-threatening interaction as a routine tolerability issue. Food does nothing about the additive hypotension risk with his nitrate. You ignored the actual alert.

options.text: Override the alert — sildenafil is commonly prescribed and the alert is probably noise
options.feedback: Alert fatigue is real, but this is one of the few interactions that is a true hard contraindication. Reflexively overriding it is exactly how a preventable death happens.

workSimulation.aiSuggestion: The clinical AI assistant says: 'Interaction confirmed: sildenafil + isosorbide mononitrate. Recommend dispensing with patient counseling to take the two medications at least 24 hours apart to minimize additive blood-pressure lowering.'
workSimulation.aiMistake: The AI correctly identifies the interacting pair but downgrades an absolute contraindication into a manageable dose-spacing problem. Because isosorbide mononitrate is long-acting and nitrate therapy is ongoing, there is no safe interval — the answer is 'do not combine,' not 'separate by 24 hours.' Its confident, specific number makes the wrong advice sound authoritative.
workSimulation.correctHumanJudgment: A pharmacist knows this pairing is a black-box contraindication, not a spacing nuance. You recognize the patient takes the nitrate daily for chronic angina, so 'space them 24 hours' is meaningless, and you hold the script and call the prescriber instead of dispensing.

aiCatchOptions.text: It treated an absolute contraindication as a manageable timing/spacing issue, suggesting a 24-hour separation when no safe interval exists
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Right. That is the precise flaw — the pairing should never be dispensed together, and a daily long-acting nitrate makes 'space them out' incoherent.

aiCatchOptions.text: It failed to detect the interaction between sildenafil and the nitrate at all
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Wrong — the AI did detect and name the interaction correctly. The error was in the recommended action, not the detection.

aiCatchOptions.text: It used the patient's age incorrectly and applied a geriatric dosing rule that doesn't exist
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Plausible-sounding but false. Age wasn't the issue; the AI never made an age-dosing claim. The failure was downgrading a contraindication to a spacing problem.

typicalDegree: Doctor of Pharmacy (PharmD) — a 4-year professional doctorate after ~2 years of undergraduate prerequisites; then pass NAPLEX + a state law exam (MPJE/CPJE) for licensure

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 1 — Map the real job
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Read the BLS OOH pharmacists page and 3-4 honest pharmacist accounts (retail vs. hospital vs. ambulatory). Write one page on why growth is only 5% and how AI/automation is reshaping the role.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 1-2 — Learn the language of drugs
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Start memorizing the top 50 drugs: brand/generic, class, main use, one key interaction, one counseling point. Use spaced-repetition flashcards (Anki) daily.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 2 — Get the calculations right
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Work through pharmaceutical math: days-supply, mg/kg dosing, IV drip rates, and alligation. Do 10 problems a day until you stop making decimal errors.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 3 — Shadow and verify the path
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Arrange to shadow a community and, if possible, a hospital pharmacist for a few hours each. Ask specifically about breaks, staffing, metrics, and what they'd change.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 3-4 — Understand the business
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Learn how a claim gets paid: formularies, prior authorizations, DAW codes, and PBMs. Summarize how insurance, not chemistry, drives much of the daily workload.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 4 — Mini project: build a counseling + safety sheet
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Pick 5 common high-risk drugs (warfarin, metformin, lisinopril, sildenafil, levothyroxine). For each, write a 60-second patient counseling script and list its top contraindication. Present one out loud as if to a real patient.

automates: High-speed barcode verification and automated counting/filling (robotic dispensing cabinets)
First-pass drug-interaction, duplicate-therapy, and allergy screening flags
Insurance claim adjudication and routine refill processing
Inventory forecasting and controlled-substance reconciliation
Drafting patient medication instructions and identifying formulary alternatives
humanValue: Final legal and clinical sign-off — a licensed human is accountable for every dispense
Resolving ambiguous or contraindicated orders by calling and negotiating with prescribers
Counseling frightened, low-health-literacy, or non-adherent patients with empathy
Judgment on edge cases AI gets confidently wrong (contraindications, off-label intent, renal dosing)
Administering vaccines and hands-on point-of-care services; managing a team under pressure
aiImpact.riskNote: Automation and AI will keep hollowing out the mechanical dispensing core — counting, claims, first-pass screening — which pressures retail headcount and is part of why growth is only ~5%. But the legally accountable final check, prescriber problem-solving, immunization, and patient counseling are hard to offload, and clinical/ambulatory roles are expanding. The risk is fewer pharmacists per pharmacy doing more clinical work, not the role vanishing.

shift.intro: It's 5:40 p.m. on a Friday, you're the only pharmacist on duty, 60 prescriptions deep in the verification queue, the drive-thru is buzzing, and a tech is waving an override slip in your face.
shift.closer: The job wasn't the one heroic catch — it was holding a legal-grade safety standard for ten hours while the phone, the drive-thru, and the queue all screamed that you were too slow.

beats.title: The Override Slip
beats.situation: A technician interrupts your verification to push through a DUR (Drug Utilization Review) 'refill too soon' alert on a patient's oxycodone — the insurance is rejecting it as a 4-days-early controlled-substance refill. The patient is at the window, frustrated, saying they're leaving town tomorrow. The tech has already typed the override code and just needs your sign-off.
beats.decision: How do you handle the early controlled-substance override?

options.text: Pull the patient's fill history and your state PDMP report yourself before deciding, then talk to the patient about the early date.
options.consequence: PDMP shows a second oxycodone fill from another prescriber 8 days ago — you catch an early-overlap pattern, counsel the patient, and document. Three weeks later that documentation protects you when a DEA audit reviews the store's controlled dispensing.

options.text: Approve the override but tell the tech to only fill a partial 3-day supply to cover the trip.
options.consequence: You bridge the gap and reduce exposure, but you never saw the duplicate prescriber. The full early pattern surfaces a month later when the patient overdoses-scares in the ER, and you realize you'd had the data and didn't pull it.

options.text: Sign the override — the tech already entered it and the line is backing up.
options.consequence: You authorize an early controlled refill you never reviewed. It posts against your license. At the next board inspection it's flagged as an undocumented early opioid override with your initials on it.

beats.title: The Prior-Auth Wall
beats.situation: A diabetic patient's insulin claim rejects: their plan now requires a prior authorization (PA), and the doctor's office closed an hour ago. The patient has roughly two days of insulin left at home and no way to pay the $340 cash price. The drive-thru is three cars deep behind them.
beats.decision: What do you do for the insulin patient?

options.text: Use your state's emergency-supply provision to dispense a short bridge supply, start the PA paperwork, and flag the prescriber for Monday.
options.consequence: The patient stays out of DKA over the weekend. Monday the PA clears and they thank you by name; the bridge dispense is fully legal and documented. Your manager notes the save in the next district review.

options.text: Find a cheaper covered alternative insulin and dispense that under your judgment without reaching the prescriber.
options.consequence: You keep them covered, but switching insulin types without prescriber sign-off risks a dosing mismatch. The patient runs high all weekend on an unfamiliar product and calls Monday confused about units.

options.text: Tell them it needs a PA, hand them the rejection, and say to come back when the doctor approves it.
options.consequence: The patient goes 48 hours rationing insulin and lands in the ER in early ketoacidosis Sunday night. The complaint that follows names the pharmacy that turned them away with two days of insulin left.

beats.title: The Sildenafil Script
beats.situation: An 82-year-old man drops off a new prescription for sildenafil 50 mg as needed. His active profile shows isosorbide mononitrate 30 mg daily — a long-acting nitrate for chronic angina — plus metoprolol. Your software fires an interaction alert and your clinical AI assistant weighs in instantly while two more scripts pile up behind it.
beats.decision: What do you do before dispensing the sildenafil?
beats.aiSuggestion: Interaction confirmed: sildenafil + isosorbide mononitrate. Recommend dispensing with patient counseling to take the two medications at least 24 hours apart to minimize additive blood-pressure lowering.

options.text: Recognize this as an absolute contraindication — the daily long-acting nitrate means there's no safe interval — so you hold the script and call the prescriber.
options.consequence: The prescriber didn't realize the man was on a chronic nitrate and cancels the sildenafil. You prevented a potentially fatal blood-pressure crash. The intervention is logged; months later it's cited as a model catch in a staff training.

options.text: Trust the pairing is real but cut the dose to 25 mg and counsel heavy spacing, dispensing a reduced quantity.
options.consequence: You sensed danger but treated a contraindication like a dosing problem. A lower dose still drops a nitrate patient's pressure dangerously; you got lucky he never took it because his wife questioned the combo and called the doctor herself.

options.text: Follow the AI: dispense with counseling to separate the two doses by 24 hours.
options.consequence: The 24-hour rule is meaningless for a daily long-acting nitrate — there is no off window. He takes sildenafil one evening, bottoms out his blood pressure, falls in the bathroom, and is found unresponsive. The dispense traces back to your final-check initials.

beats.title: Closing Alone
beats.situation: Ten minutes to close, no break taken since you clocked in. A walk-in wants a shingles shot, the closing tech has to leave for childcare, and there are still 9 prescriptions in the verification queue including a pediatric antibiotic suspension a worried parent is waiting on. You cannot do everything before lights-out.
beats.decision: How do you triage the final ten minutes?

options.text: Final-check the pediatric antibiotic now with full concentration, defer the non-urgent scripts to morning, and reschedule the vaccine rather than rush an injection alone.
options.consequence: The child gets a correctly verified dose tonight; nothing urgent is left unchecked. The deferred scripts are flagged clearly for the opening pharmacist, who thanks you for the clean handoff.

options.text: Bang through all 9 scripts fast to clear the queue, then give the vaccine right at close.
options.consequence: You clear the board, but rushing the pediatric suspension you miss that the concentration on the label doesn't match the mixed bottle. The parent calls Saturday confused about the dropper marks — a catch that should have happened at the counter.

options.text: Give the shingles shot first to make the metric, leave the queue for the morning shift, and start closing.
options.consequence: You chase the immunization number while a feverish child goes home with no antibiotic overnight. The parent's complaint and the unverified queue both land on the morning pharmacist — and on your name in the log.

title: Physical Therapist
oneLineReality: You spend your day on your feet coaching injured people through painful exercises, then spend your evenings fighting insurance documentation — it's deeply human work wrapped in productivity quotas.
typicalDay: Review the day's schedule and chart notes, then run an initial evaluation on a new patient: take history, measure range of motion and strength, and set functional goals
Lead 6-10 treatment sessions back-to-back, often overlapping two patients at once, cueing squats, gait drills, or shoulder mobilizations
Perform hands-on manual therapy: joint mobilizations, soft-tissue work, and guided stretching
Progress or regress each patient's home exercise program based on how they tolerated last visit
Document every visit in the EMR with billable CPT codes and skilled-care justification so the claim survives an insurance audit
Coordinate with physicians, PT assistants, and case managers on plan-of-care updates and discharge timing
workStyle: Mostly on your feet (15,000+ steps a day), physically hands-on, in a clinic, hospital, or home-health setting. High patient contact and emotional labor; you become a coach, motivator, and sometimes therapist-in-the-other-sense. Productivity expectations (units billed per day) create real time pressure.
boringHardPart: Documentation. Outpatient PTs routinely take work home or stay late charting, because every visit needs defensible 'skilled' language and correct billing codes or insurance denies the claim. Add the physical toll — back and wrist strain from manual therapy — and the productivity quotas that push you to double-book patients.
keyTools: Electronic medical record / documentation systems (WebPT, Epic, Raintree, Prompt)
Goniometer and dynamometer for measuring joint range and muscle force
Manual therapy / soft-tissue and mobilization techniques
Therapeutic exercise equipment: bands, dumbbells, balance boards, parallel bars
Modalities: ultrasound, electrical stimulation, dry needling (where licensed)
Standardized outcome measures (Berg Balance, LEFS, TUG) and CPT billing codes
crashCourse: Learn musculoskeletal anatomy and kinesiology cold — origin, insertion, action of major muscles and joints is the language of everything you do
Shadow a PT in two settings (outpatient ortho + a hospital or neuro/home-health) to see how different the job feels
Understand the business: insurance reimbursement, productivity units, and why documentation drives pay
Practice motivational communication — adherence to home exercise is the real outcome driver, not your fanciest technique
Map the path: prerequisites, GRE-optional DPT admissions, 3-year DPT, clinical rotations, then the NPTE licensure exam

workSimulation.scenario: You're an outpatient ortho PT. A 58-year-old patient is 4 weeks out from a total knee replacement. Your goal today is to restore knee extension (straightening). On the table, passive knee extension is stuck at -10 degrees (can't fully straighten), the joint feels firm but the end-feel is springy/elastic, not hard or bony. The patient reports moderate stiffness but minimal pain and no warmth, redness, or fever.
workSimulation.task: What is the most appropriate action this session?

options.text: Apply low-load prolonged stretch into extension plus manual mobilization, then progress the home program — the springy end-feel and absence of red flags point to soft-tissue and capsular tightness that responds to graded loading
options.feedback: Correct. A springy/elastic end-feel with no warmth, redness, or fever is classic soft-tissue/capsular restriction. Low-load prolonged stretch and joint mobilization are the evidence-based response, and reinforcing the home program drives the real gains between visits.

options.text: Stop all extension work and refer back to the surgeon immediately for suspected infection
options.feedback: Over-reaction. There's no warmth, redness, fever, or hard end-feel — none of the infection or hardware red flags are present. Reflexively referring out abandons the patient and delays the exact loading they need.

options.text: Aggressively force the knee into full extension with maximal overpressure to break up the restriction in one session
options.feedback: Dangerous. Ballistic high-force manipulation on a healing post-surgical joint risks tissue damage, pain flare-ups, and guarding that worsens stiffness. Loss of extension responds to graded, low-load stretch over time, not force.

options.text: Skip manual work and just give more quad-strengthening exercises
options.feedback: Incomplete. Strengthening matters, but you can't strengthen your way out of a mechanical extension restriction. If the joint won't passively straighten, you must address the soft-tissue/capsular limitation first or the deficit becomes permanent.

workSimulation.aiSuggestion: The clinical-documentation AI assistant drafts your note and flags: 'Patient progressing well. Recommend discharge planning within 1-2 visits — knee flexion is 0-118 degrees, nearly full range, and strength is improving. Goals largely met.'
workSimulation.aiMistake: The AI anchored on the flexion number (118 degrees, which is excellent) and the general 'improving' trend, and completely ignored the extension deficit (-10 degrees). For a total knee replacement, a lingering extension lag is the more functionally damaging problem — it causes a limp, quad inhibition, and long-term gait issues — and it is nowhere near resolved. Discharging now would lock in a permanent deficit.
workSimulation.correctHumanJudgment: A human PT reads the whole picture: great flexion does not equal a met goal when extension is still -10 degrees. You keep the patient on, prioritize extension restoration, and document the specific lingering deficit and why continued skilled care is justified — the opposite of discharge.

aiCatchOptions.text: It recommended discharge based on flexion while ignoring the unresolved -10 degree extension deficit, which is the more functionally critical goal after a knee replacement
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Exactly. The AI fixated on one good number and missed that residual extension loss causes a permanent limp and quad inhibition — this patient is not ready for discharge.

aiCatchOptions.text: It used degrees instead of converting range of motion to a percentage of normal
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Wrong. Degrees are the correct, standard unit for documenting joint range of motion — there's nothing wrong with the AI's units. The real error is ignoring the extension deficit entirely.

aiCatchOptions.text: It failed to flag signs of post-surgical infection in the joint
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Wrong. The scenario explicitly notes no warmth, redness, or fever — there were no infection signs to flag. The AI's actual error was clearing the patient for discharge despite an unresolved extension limitation.
