thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 1: Learn the body's language
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Drill major muscles and joints — origin, insertion, action — and the planes of movement. Use a free kinesiology playlist; quiz yourself on shoulder, knee, hip, and spine until you can name what moves what.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 1-2: Shadow a real PT
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Email 5 local outpatient ortho clinics and one hospital or home-health agency to arrange observation hours (you'll need them for DPT applications anyway). Watch how they cue, document, and juggle two patients at once.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 2: Understand the money and the gatekeeping
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Read up on how insurance reimbursement and 'productivity units' work, what the NPTE licensure exam is, and DPT prerequisites. Build a one-page reality sheet on cost, debt, and time-to-license.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 3: Mini project — design and test a home exercise program
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Pick a common issue (e.g., a desk worker's stiff neck or a runner's tight hip). Build a 4-exercise progressive program with sets, reps, and clear cues, then teach it to a willing friend or family member and adjust based on how they actually tolerate it.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 4: Document like a clinician
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Write a SOAP note for your mini-project 'patient' — Subjective, Objective (measure their range of motion with a phone protractor app), Assessment, Plan. Notice how hard it is to justify 'skilled' care in writing; that's the daily grind.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 4: Decide and map the path
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Reflect honestly on the on-your-feet, documentation-heavy reality. If still in, map your DPT prerequisite courses, target 3 programs by cost, and schedule the observation hours and GRE (if required) you still need.

automates: Drafting and auto-coding visit documentation from voice or templated notes
Generating and printing personalized home-exercise handouts with videos
Scheduling, reminders, and insurance authorization paperwork
Flagging outcome-measure trends and suggesting standard exercise progressions
Motion analysis from a phone video to estimate joint angles
humanValue: Skilled hands-on manual therapy and palpation that reads tissue response in real time
Clinical judgment integrating contradictory findings, red flags, and patient context
Motivating and building trust so an anxious or discouraged patient actually does the work
Adapting a plan live when a patient flares up, plateaus, or surprises you
Physically guarding and safely progressing a fall-risk or post-surgical patient
aiImpact.riskNote: Low automation risk. The core of the job — hands-on assessment, manual treatment, in-person motivation, and split-second safety judgment with fall-risk and post-surgical patients — requires physical presence and trust AI can't replace. AI will offload documentation and exercise-prescription busywork, making PTs more clinical rather than redundant. The honest risk is AI-driven productivity pressure, not job loss.

shift.intro: It's 7:48 AM, your first patient is already gowned in Bay 2, your EMR has 11 unsigned notes from yesterday glowing red, and your wrists still ache from last night's manual therapy block.
shift.closer: You walked 16,200 steps, touched a dozen aching bodies with real skill, and still drove home with two unfinished notes riding shotgun — the work that heals people and the work that pays for it are never the same eight hours.

beats.title: The New Eval
beats.situation: A 64-year-old woman arrives for an initial evaluation after a rotator cuff repair. The front desk booked her into a standard 30-minute slot, but a real eval — history, goniometry, manual muscle testing, functional goals — needs 45. Your 8:30 treatment patient is already checking in.
beats.decision: How do you run this initial evaluation?

options.text: Do the full eval properly — take the history, measure every plane of motion and strength, set functional goals — and absorb running 15 minutes behind all morning.
options.consequence: You catch that she's also guarding from undiagnosed cervical radiculopathy; you adjust the plan and flag it to the surgeon. Three weeks later her referral note thanks you for catching it early.

options.text: Measure shoulder range and strength quickly, skip the cervical screen and skip writing formal goals, plan to backfill the note tonight.
options.consequence: The visit fits the slot, but without documented baseline goals the insurer later questions medical necessity, and you spend an unpaid evening reconstructing measurements from memory.

options.text: Eyeball her range, copy a goal template from the last rotator cuff patient, and start exercises to stay on schedule.
options.consequence: The cloned goals don't match her actual deficits; at re-eval there's no real baseline to show progress, the claim gets denied as not skilled, and the clinic eats the visit.

beats.title: Double-Booked
beats.situation: Your productivity target is 9 billable units by noon. The scheduler just slid a walk-in into your 11:30, meaning you'd be running two patients at once: a deconditioned post-op in parallel bars who needs guarding, and a teen athlete doing plyometrics. One needs your hands, the other needs your eyes.
beats.decision: How do you handle the overlap?

options.text: Keep the fall-risk post-op patient under your direct hands-on guarding and have the stable athlete do a supervised self-managed warm-up until you can cue her safely.
options.consequence: Both stay safe and you bill honestly for the skilled time. The post-op, never let to wobble, gains confidence and is off the walker a week ahead of plan.

options.text: Bounce between both bays every couple of minutes, hoping your timing holds and nobody loses balance.
options.consequence: You hit the unit quota, but during one trip across the room the post-op patient grabs the bar hard and tweaks her shoulder — a minor setback and an incident note you didn't want to write.

options.text: Park the post-op on a stationary bike unsupervised and run the athlete's plyometric drills to bank the higher-value units.
options.consequence: The post-op pedals with terrible compensatory form for ten minutes, flares her knee, and reports it to the surgeon — who calls the clinic questioning your supervision.

beats.title: The Knee That Won't Straighten
beats.situation: Your 58-year-old patient is 4 weeks out from a total knee replacement. Flexion looks great at 0-118 degrees and strength is climbing. But on the table, passive knee extension is stuck at -10 degrees — he can't fully straighten. The end-feel is springy and elastic, not hard or bony; he reports moderate stiffness, minimal pain, no warmth, redness, or fever. Your documentation AI has already drafted today's note.
beats.decision: What is the most appropriate action this session?
beats.aiSuggestion: Patient progressing well. Recommend discharge planning within 1-2 visits — knee flexion is 0-118 degrees, nearly full range, and strength is improving. Goals largely met.

options.text: Reject the discharge suggestion. Prioritize restoring extension this session — low-load prolonged stretch, extension mobilizations, prone hangs, quad re-education — and document the specific -10 degree extension lag as the deficit justifying continued skilled care.
options.consequence: Because the springy end-feel meant the contracture was still mobile, six more visits drive extension to zero. He walks without a limp. Had you discharged, the lag would have ossified into a permanent gait deficit.

options.text: Note that extension still needs work but accept the AI's optimistic trend, keep flexion-and-strength as the focus, and plan a soft discharge in a few visits.
options.consequence: Extension creeps from -10 to -7 but never closes before the plan-of-care expires. He keeps a subtle limp and quad lag that nags him on stairs for years.

options.text: Accept the AI's note, sign off on discharge planning — flexion and strength are clearly the big wins and the numbers look done.
options.consequence: Discharged at -10 degrees, the extension lag becomes fixed. Months later he returns with chronic anterior knee pain and an antalgic gait that now needs a far longer, harder course of care.

beats.title: The Charting Wall
beats.situation: The last patient left at 6. You're alone in a quiet clinic facing 8 unfinished notes, each needing defensible skilled-care language and correct CPT codes or insurance denies the claim. You're exhausted, your back is stiff, and dinner was three hours ago. Tomorrow's caseload is already full.
beats.decision: How do you close out the day's documentation?

options.text: Write each note now while the sessions are fresh — specific skilled interventions, objective measures, and clear justification — even though it means leaving at 7:40.
options.consequence: Every claim clears the payer's audit clean. Two months later when this insurer audits the clinic, your notes are the ones the billing manager holds up as the standard.

options.text: Write the three complex notes now and dash off five with quick generic phrases like 'therapeutic exercise as tolerated,' planning to be more careful tomorrow.
options.consequence: Tomorrow never has spare time. Two of the thin notes get flagged for lacking skilled justification, and you're pulled into a denial appeal that costs an afternoon weeks later.

options.text: Copy-forward yesterday's notes for everyone, change the date, and go home — you'll fix anything that bounces.
options.consequence: The cloned notes show identical 'progress' on patients who plateaued; the payer denies a batch as not skilled, claws back paid visits, and your name is on every one during the compliance review.

title: Physician Assistant
oneLineReality: You practice medicine — diagnose, prescribe, suture, manage patients — at near-physician scope but under a collaborating physician, for roughly a third of the schooling and half the pay of an MD.
typicalDay: Pre-chart the day's panel: review labs, imaging, and prior notes before the first patient so you walk in knowing why they're there
See patients back-to-back (often 18-30/day in primary care, fewer but sicker in specialty/surgery) — take a history, examine, order tests, diagnose, and write prescriptions
Perform procedures hands-on: suturing lacerations, joint injections, skin biopsies, incision and drainage, or first-assisting in the OR depending on specialty
Staff complex or new-medication cases with your collaborating physician — a 60-second curbside, not a sign-off on everything
Document every encounter in the EHR and close out billing codes; chart notes follow you home if you fall behind
Call patients with results, refill requests, and follow-up instructions between or after scheduled visits
workStyle: Team-based clinical work inside a hospital, clinic, or surgical practice. High patient contact, on your feet, frequent decisions under time pressure. Strong lateral mobility — PAs can switch from dermatology to emergency medicine without re-doing school, which is rare in medicine. Many roles are M-F outpatient; ER, surgery, and hospitalist roles add nights, weekends, and call.
boringHardPart: The charting and prior-authorization grind. You'll spend a real chunk of every day fighting the EHR, justifying medications to insurers, and clearing inbox baskets of results and refills. Plus the structural ceiling: you always practice under a collaborating physician, so even with 15 years of expertise you can be overruled, and reimbursement/scope rules vary by state and employer.
keyTools: Electronic Health Record systems (Epic, Cerner/Oracle Health)
Diagnostic tools: otoscope, stethoscope, point-of-care ultrasound
Procedure kits: suture trays, biopsy punches, injection sets
ICD-10 / CPT coding and billing workflows
crashCourse: Shadow a PA for a full clinical day — outpatient AND a procedural/ER setting — before committing; the job varies wildly by specialty
Rack up direct patient-care hours (CNA, EMT, medical assistant, scribe); most PA programs require 1,000-2,000 hours to even apply
Nail the prerequisite science gauntlet: anatomy, physiology, microbiology, biochemistry, statistics — your GPA in these decides admission
Learn the SOAP note and clinical reasoning framework (Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan) — it's how every encounter is structured
Understand the PA-physician collaboration model and your state's scope-of-practice laws so you know the real boundaries of the job

workSimulation.scenario: You're a PA in a busy urgent care. A healthy-looking 24-year-old man comes in with 3 days of a sore throat, fever to 101.5°F, no cough, and tender swollen lymph nodes in his neck. He wants antibiotics so he can get back to work.
workSimulation.task: Decide your next step before reaching for the prescription pad.

options.text: Apply the Centor/McIsaac criteria, do a rapid strep test, and prescribe antibiotics only if it's positive (or treat empirically only if the score is high and testing isn't available)
options.feedback: Correct. This is evidence-based stewardship: fever + tender nodes + no cough + age all raise his Centor score, which justifies TESTING, not automatic antibiotics. You confirm strep before committing him to a drug — and you protect against over-prescribing that breeds resistance.

options.text: Prescribe amoxicillin immediately — he has classic strep symptoms and wants to get back to work
options.feedback: Too fast. Many sore throats are viral, and amoxicillin given to someone who actually has mononucleosis (which mimics strep at this age) causes a dramatic rash. You test before you treat.

options.text: Tell him it's definitely viral, send him home with ibuprofen, and don't test
options.feedback: Too dismissive. His symptom cluster actually scores HIGH for strep. Skipping the rapid test risks missing a treatable bacterial infection that can progress to complications like rheumatic fever.

options.text: Order a throat culture and have him wait 48 hours for results before any decision
options.feedback: Impractical for urgent care. A rapid strep test gives an answer in minutes; a 48-hour culture delays care and isn't the first-line tool when point-of-care testing is available.

workSimulation.aiSuggestion: The clinical-decision AI reviews the chart and recommends: 'High Centor score with positive rapid strep — prescribe azithromycin 500mg day 1 then 250mg daily, a convenient 5-day Z-pack that improves compliance for this working patient.'
workSimulation.aiMistake: Azithromycin is the wrong first-line drug for strep pharyngitis. Guidelines call for penicillin or amoxicillin first-line; macrolides like azithromycin are reserved for documented penicillin allergy because Group A strep has meaningful macrolide resistance and azithromycin has higher treatment-failure rates. The AI optimized for convenience over the correct antibiotic.
workSimulation.correctHumanJudgment: A human PA checks the allergy field — the chart shows NO penicillin allergy — so the right call is penicillin VK or amoxicillin. The PA overrides the AI, reserving azithromycin for true penicillin-allergic patients, avoiding a resistance-prone, higher-failure choice.

aiCatchOptions.text: It chose azithromycin when penicillin/amoxicillin is first-line for strep in a non-allergic patient; macrolides are reserved for penicillin allergy due to resistance
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Exactly right. The AI skipped straight to a second-line macrolide despite no documented penicillin allergy — that risks treatment failure and fuels resistance. The fix is penicillin VK or amoxicillin.

aiCatchOptions.text: It should not have prescribed any antibiotic because all sore throats are viral
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Wrong — a confirmed positive rapid strep test means a bacterial infection that genuinely warrants antibiotics. The error is the CHOICE of drug, not the decision to treat.

aiCatchOptions.text: The dose of azithromycin was too low to treat strep effectively
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Wrong — the 500mg-then-250mg regimen is a standard azithromycin dosing. Dosing isn't the problem; azithromycin being the wrong first-line agent here is.

typicalDegree: Master's degree from an ARC-PA accredited PA program (after a bachelor's plus prerequisite sciences and patient-care hours)

thirtyDayPlan.title: Shadow two PAs in different settings
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Arrange to follow a PA in primary care and one in a procedural/ER or surgical role. Log hours and note how scope, pace, and physician collaboration differ — this is your reality check and counts toward applications.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Audit the prerequisite gauntlet
thirtyDayPlan.detail: List the science prerequisites (anatomy, physiology, microbiology, biochem, statistics) for 3 target PA programs on the PAEA program directory. Map which you've done and which you still need, with target grades.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Start banking patient-care hours
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Apply for a CNA, EMT, medical-assistant, or scribe job. Programs typically want 1,000-2,000 direct-care hours; starting now is the single biggest admissions lever.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Learn the SOAP note (mini project)
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Watch a free clinical-reasoning intro, then write 3 practice SOAP notes from sample cases (e.g., chest pain, sore throat, ankle sprain). Get them critiqued by a PA you shadowed — you'll learn how clinicians actually think.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Build a CASPA-ready snapshot
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Create a spreadsheet tracking GPA, prerequisite grades, patient-care hours, shadowing hours, and target programs' GRE/PA-CAT requirements. This becomes your application command center.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Pressure-test the finances
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Compare total cost (tuition + ~2 years of lost income) against a $95k-$133k starting salary for 2-3 programs. Decide whether in-state public, MEDEX, or a private like Duke makes financial sense for you.

automates: Drafting clinical notes from ambient conversation (AI scribes like DAX/Abridge)
Surfacing differential diagnoses and drug-interaction or dosing checks
Pre-populating prior-authorization paperwork and inbox triage
Flagging abnormal labs and imaging for review
humanValue: Physical examination and hands-on procedures (suturing, injections, surgical assisting) that require touch and dexterity
Building trust, breaking bad news, and reading the unspoken cues a patient gives
Integrating messy, conflicting real-world findings into a judgment call AI can't be liable for
Owning the legal and ethical accountability for the diagnosis and treatment plan
aiImpact.riskNote: Low automation risk. AI will reshape the documentation and decision-support parts of the job, but the core — physically examining patients, performing procedures, and carrying clinical/legal responsibility — requires a licensed human. Demand is structurally rising as healthcare expands access; AI more likely makes PAs faster than it replaces them.

shift.intro: It's a Saturday urgent care shift, the waiting-room board already shows nine red names before you've finished your first coffee, and every one of them thinks they're your only patient.
shift.closer: The medicine was the easy part — the real shift was holding the line on the correct call while a clock, an insurer, an algorithm, and twelve unfinished notes all pulled you toward 'good enough.'

beats.title: The Walk-Up
beats.situation: Your board is full and you're mid-suture when a diaphoretic 58-year-old man leans on the front desk saying he's had 'bad indigestion' and left-arm heaviness for an hour. Front desk wants to hand him a number like everyone else.
beats.decision: He isn't on your schedule and you have a half-closed laceration in the other room. What do you do with him right now?

options.text: Stop, pull him straight to a room, and get a 12-lead EKG within 10 minutes while treating it as possible heart attack.
options.consequence: The EKG shows an inferior STEMI; you activate EMS transfer and push aspirin. Two days later the interventional cardiologist calls to say your door-to-EKG time made the cath lab catch.

options.text: Tell the nurse to bump him up next, but finish closing your current laceration first so you don't break sterile field.
options.consequence: A 14-minute delay; the EKG still catches the STEMI, but the receiving ED documents the door-to-EKG lag and it lands in your clinic's quality review as a near-miss.

options.text: Hand him a clipboard — sweaty middle-aged guy with indigestion, he can wait his turn like the rest.
options.consequence: He collapses in the waiting room 20 minutes later; you run a code on the floor. The root-cause review names you, and the story circulates through the regional medical group for a year.

beats.title: The Z-Pack Request
beats.situation: A healthy-looking 24-year-old has 3 days of sore throat, fever to 101.5°F, no cough, and tender swollen neck nodes. He's blunt: he needs antibiotics today to get back to work. You open the chart and the clinical-decision AI has already weighed in.
beats.decision: Decide your next step before you reach for the prescription pad.
beats.aiSuggestion: High Centor score with positive rapid strep — prescribe azithromycin 500mg day 1 then 250mg daily, a convenient 5-day Z-pack that improves compliance for this working patient.

options.text: Check the allergy field — no penicillin allergy — and prescribe penicillin VK (or amoxicillin) first-line, reserving azithromycin only for true PCN allergy.
options.consequence: He's cured uneventfully. A month later the antibiotic-stewardship audit flags your panel's low macrolide rate as a model, and your collaborating physician cites it in the quarterly meeting.

options.text: Reject the azithromycin and write amoxicillin — correct drug — but trust the AI's 'positive rapid strep' line without confirming the swab actually resulted.
options.consequence: Right antibiotic, but the rapid strep was still pending when you signed; it does come back positive, so you got lucky treating on data you never verified — a habit that burns you the day a result flips negative.

options.text: Accept the AI's recommendation — it sounds evidence-based and the patient is happy — and send the azithromycin Z-pack.
options.consequence: He's back on day 5 still febrile with a swelling toward peritonsillar abscess; the macrolide-resistant strep failed. Your supervisor pulls the chart and asks why you used a second-line drug in a patient with no penicillin allergy.

beats.title: The Deep Cut
beats.situation: A line cook has a 3 cm laceration across the back of his hand from a falling knife. It's bleeding but looks closeable. As you irrigate, you notice he can't quite fully straighten his middle finger — and he's begging you to just stitch it so he can finish his double shift.
beats.decision: It's busy and a simple closure takes five minutes. How do you handle the wound?

options.text: Test extensor tendon function and explore the wound under good light before closing — and act on what you find.
options.consequence: You find a 40% extensor tendon laceration hiding under the skin, splint it, and get him to hand surgery within 48 hours. The tendon is repaired in time and he keeps full extension.

options.text: Close the skin neatly, splint the hand, and refer him to ortho follow-up without formally exploring the wound bed.
options.consequence: The partial tendon injury is missed today and only caught at follow-up four days later. It's repairable, but the delayed fix leaves him with a stiff finger and a stack of therapy visits.

options.text: Suture it, tell him to keep it clean, and discharge — it's just a skin cut and your board is full.
options.consequence: The cut tendon retracts and scars down; he loses the ability to extend the finger and can't grip a knife. Eight months later a malpractice claim names you for failure to assess an obvious extensor injury.

beats.title: The Basket at Closing
beats.situation: Doors are locked but your EHR inbox isn't: 12 notes unsigned and a stack of results. Buried in the basket is a urine culture from a woman you treated this morning for a UTI — it's growing E. coli resistant to the exact antibiotic you started her on. You've been on your feet for ten hours.
beats.decision: You want to be home. How do you close out the day?

options.text: Triage the basket first: call her tonight, switch her to an antibiotic the bug is sensitive to, document it, then finish notes — taking the routine ones home.
options.consequence: She starts the right drug that evening and never progresses to a kidney infection. You chart until 8 pm, but nothing falls through the cracks and the loop is closed.

options.text: Sign your routine notes now to stay current, and flag the abnormal culture for the morning provider to handle at open.
options.consequence: An 18-hour delay; she's sicker by the time she's called but recovers as an outpatient. Your supervisor notes the lag on a result you saw but deferred.

options.text: Bulk-sign the whole basket to hit inbox-zero and get out the door — you'll sort real issues tomorrow.
options.consequence: The resistant culture gets marked reviewed and vanishes. Three days later she's admitted with pyelonephritis; the chart shows you closed the result without acting, and it becomes a formal incident.

title: Nurse Practitioner
oneLineReality: You diagnose, prescribe, and manage patients like a junior physician for a fraction of the training time, but you carry real clinical liability while drowning in charting and prior-authorization paperwork.
typicalDay: Review the day's patient panel and overnight lab/imaging results before the first appointment, flagging abnormal values that need same-day callbacks
See 16-24 patients in 15-20 minute slots: take history, examine, diagnose, order labs/imaging, and write prescriptions
Document each encounter in the EHR (Epic or Cerner) with billing-compliant notes plus ICD-10 and CPT codes during or right after the visit
Work the 'in-basket': refill requests, patient portal messages, prior-authorization fights with insurers, and results that arrived during clinic
Coordinate care: refer complex cases to specialists, call pharmacies about formulary issues, and consult the collaborating physician on borderline cases
Finish charting after the last patient leaves (the dreaded 'pajama time' of documenting from home)
workStyle: Clinical, fast-paced, and people-facing. Mostly outpatient clinics, urgent care, or hospital units; on your feet between exam rooms with constant context-switching. High autonomy in full-practice-authority states, more physician oversight in restricted states. Emotionally demanding and documentation-heavy.
boringHardPart: The mountain of non-clinical paperwork: insurance prior authorizations, refill queues, and EHR notes that must be coded correctly or the visit does not get paid. You can spend 1-2 unpaid hours a night charting, and a single missed abnormal lab can become a malpractice claim.
keyTools: Epic and Cerner electronic health records (EHR)
UpToDate and Epocrates clinical decision and drug-reference tools
Stethoscope, otoscope, and basic point-of-care exam equipment
ICD-10 and CPT coding systems for diagnosis and billing
E-prescribing systems with state PDMP (prescription drug monitoring) lookups
crashCourse: Shadow an NP or PA for a full clinic day and count how much time is charting versus patient contact
Learn the SOAP note format (Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan) and write three practice notes on mock patients
Memorize first-line treatments for the 10 most common primary-care complaints (hypertension, UTI, strep, diabetes, etc.)
Take a free intro pharmacology MOOC and master 20 high-frequency drugs, their doses, and major interactions
Read your target state's scope-of-practice rules: full, reduced, or restricted practice authority changes the whole job

workSimulation.scenario: You are an NP in a busy family-practice clinic. A 58-year-old man comes in for a 'medication refill' on his blood pressure pill. He mentions in passing that he has had 'some indigestion and tiredness' for two days that gets worse when he walks to his mailbox and eases when he rests.
workSimulation.task: You have 15 minutes. What do you do?

options.text: Refill the blood pressure medication, recommend an over-the-counter antacid for the indigestion, and book a routine follow-up in two weeks
options.feedback: Dangerous. Exertional 'indigestion' with fatigue that improves with rest is a classic atypical presentation of cardiac ischemia (angina), especially in a 58-year-old hypertensive man. Treating it as reflux can send a heart attack home.

options.text: Stop the refill agenda, get an immediate 12-lead ECG and vital signs, and evaluate for acute coronary syndrome before anything else
options.feedback: Correct. Exertional symptoms relieved by rest plus cardiac risk factors demand you rule out ACS first. An ECG and focused cardiac workup take minutes and can be life-saving; the refill can wait.

options.text: Order an outpatient stress test and a GI referral, then refill the medication and send him home to await appointments
options.feedback: Too slow. Outpatient referrals take days to weeks. If this is unstable angina, sending him home without an ECG risks a fatal event in the parking lot. Acute symptoms need same-visit evaluation.

options.text: Prescribe a proton-pump inhibitor for presumed GERD and tell him to return if it does not improve
options.feedback: This anchors on the least dangerous diagnosis. The exertional pattern is the red flag; treating empirically for reflux without ruling out the heart is exactly how missed MIs happen.

workSimulation.aiSuggestion: The clinic's AI scribe summarizes the visit and suggests: 'Chief complaint: indigestion. Plan: refill lisinopril, start omeprazole 20mg daily for dyspepsia, routine follow-up 2 weeks. Symptoms most consistent with GERD given the burning quality and post-meal timing.'
workSimulation.aiMistake: The AI latched onto the word 'indigestion' and the burning quality but ignored the exertional pattern (worse with walking, better with rest) buried in the patient's offhand comment, which is the hallmark of angina, not reflux. It pattern-matched to the most common benign cause and never flagged cardiac risk.
workSimulation.correctHumanJudgment: A human NP hears 'worse when I walk, better when I rest' and immediately reframes this as possible cardiac ischemia regardless of the word 'indigestion.' The exertion-rest relationship overrides the burning sensation; you get an ECG before accepting any GI explanation.

aiCatchOptions.text: The AI ignored the exertional pattern (worse with walking, relieved by rest) that points to angina rather than reflux
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Right. That exertion-rest relationship is the single most important clue, and the AI dropped it in favor of the word 'indigestion.'

aiCatchOptions.text: The AI chose the wrong drug; pantoprazole would be more appropriate than omeprazole for this patient
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Wrong focus. The PPI choice is irrelevant when the real problem is that GERD itself may be the wrong diagnosis. Quibbling over which acid blocker misses the life-threatening issue.

aiCatchOptions.text: The AI forgot to document the patient's blood pressure reading in the note
aiCatchOptions.feedback: A vitals omission is minor charting hygiene. The actual error is diagnostic: failing to recognize a possible heart attack masquerading as indigestion.

typicalDegree: Master of Science in Nursing (MSN) or Doctor of Nursing Practice (DNP), plus an active RN license and national NP board certification

thirtyDayPlan.title: Map the real pipeline
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Write out your exact path: BSN, then NCLEX-RN license, 1-2 years of RN experience, then an accredited MSN/DNP NP program. Confirm prerequisite courses (anatomy, physiology, microbiology, statistics).

thirtyDayPlan.title: Talk to two working NPs
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Do informational interviews with one primary-care NP and one acute-care/specialty NP. Ask about charting hours, scope-of-practice frustrations, and collaborating-physician relationships.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Shadow a clinic day
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Arrange to shadow an NP or PA for a full shift. Tally minutes spent on patient care versus documentation and in-basket work so you understand the real ratio.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Learn the foundational note
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Master the SOAP format and write five practice notes on mock cases. Learn three common primary-care algorithms (hypertension, type 2 diabetes, UTI).

thirtyDayPlan.title: Mini project: build a one-patient workup
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Pick a fictional patient with two chronic conditions. Produce a full problem list, differential diagnosis, medication plan with doses and interactions, and a follow-up schedule. Have an NP critique it.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Decide your state and specialty
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Research whether your target state grants full, reduced, or restricted practice authority, and pick a population focus (family, adult-gero, psych, acute care). This shapes which program you apply to.

automates: Drafting visit notes and SOAP summaries from ambient recordings (AI scribes)
Surfacing drug-interaction and dosing alerts at the point of prescribing
Pre-populating differential diagnosis lists and order sets from the chief complaint
Automating prior-authorization paperwork and routine refill triage
humanValue: Physical examination and reading non-verbal cues a patient cannot put into words
Catching the atypical presentation where the obvious diagnosis is the wrong one
Building trust so patients disclose the embarrassing or scary detail that changes the plan
Owning legal and ethical accountability for the final clinical decision
Breaking bad news and shared decision-making at the bedside
aiImpact.riskNote: Low automation risk. AI accelerates documentation and decision support, but hands-on exam, procedures, prescriptive authority, and personal legal liability for diagnoses keep the human NP central. The bigger threat is AI making lazy clinicians over-trust a confident wrong summary.

shift.intro: It's 7:48 AM and your in-basket already shows 41 unread results, your first patient is roomed, and you have not yet finished charting on yesterday's last three visits.

beats.title: The Overnight Result
beats.situation: Before your first appointment you scan the overnight labs. A 64-year-old woman's potassium came back at 6.1 (critical high) on a sample drawn yesterday afternoon. She's on lisinopril and spironolactone. Her chart shows no callback yet. Your 8:00 patient is waiting and the schedule is already double-booked.
beats.decision: A critical potassium is sitting unaddressed. What do you do before clinic swallows you?

options.text: Call her now, tell her to hold both meds, and get her into an open urgent slot or the ED for a repeat K+ and ECG today.
options.consequence: Repeat K+ is 6.4 with peaked T-waves on ECG; she's treated same-day and avoids a fatal arrhythmia. Your 8:00 patient waits 12 extra minutes and complains, but the chart note documents you acted within the hour.

options.text: Message the patient through the portal to stop spironolactone and recheck labs 'this week,' then start clinic.
options.consequence: She doesn't open the portal for two days. The repeat draw happens Thursday, still 6.0. No harm this time, but the gap is exactly the kind of delay a malpractice attorney highlights, and your collaborating physician asks why a critical value wasn't phoned.

options.text: Flag it to recheck after your morning patients so you don't fall behind on the schedule.
options.consequence: Clinic buries you; you don't circle back until 1 PM. She's home, nauseous and weak, and her husband calls an ambulance. The unaddressed critical value drawn yesterday becomes the centerpiece of a complaint to the board.

beats.title: The 'Quick Refill'
beats.situation: A 58-year-old man is here for a blood-pressure med refill. While you reconcile his lisinopril he mentions, almost as an aside, that he's had 'some indigestion and tiredness' for two days that gets worse when he walks to his mailbox and eases when he sits down. The clinic's AI scribe has already drafted your note. You have 15 minutes and four patients stacked behind him.
beats.decision: The AI's note is ready to sign. Do you accept its tidy story or chase the detail it glossed over?
beats.aiSuggestion: Chief complaint: indigestion. Plan: refill lisinopril, start omeprazole 20mg daily for dyspepsia, routine follow-up 2 weeks. Symptoms most consistent with GERD given the burning quality and post-meal timing.

options.text: Stop, get a 12-lead ECG now, and work up the exertional pattern as possible angina before accepting any GI explanation.
options.consequence: ECG shows ST depression; troponin is elevated. He's having unstable angina and goes to the cath lab the same afternoon for a 90% LAD lesion. The 'mailbox' detail he almost didn't mention is what you stented before it became a widow-maker.

options.text: Refill the lisinopril and start omeprazole, but tell him to return immediately if it worsens or spreads to his arm.
options.consequence: He goes home reassured about 'reflux.' Two nights later the chest pressure wakes him; he calls 911 in time, but it's now a full NSTEMI with heart muscle lost. The ER physician's note pointedly quotes the exertional history that was in your chart.

options.text: Sign the AI scribe's note as written; the burning quality and timing clearly point to GERD, and you're behind schedule.
options.consequence: He collapses in his driveway Saturday with a massive anterior MI. The AI summary you co-signed never flagged 'worse with walking, better with rest.' Your signature is on a note that missed textbook angina, and the family's attorney calls within the month.

beats.title: The Prior-Auth Standoff
beats.situation: A diabetic patient with an A1c of 10.2 needs the GLP-1 agonist you started, but the insurer denied it and demands a prior authorization: documented failure of metformin plus a step-therapy trial. The portal form will take 25 minutes you don't have, the pharmacy is holding, and the patient is in the waiting room asking why his medication 'got cancelled.'
beats.decision: The denial is on your desk and the clock is bleeding into your charting. How do you handle it?

options.text: Pull his metformin history into the PA form now, submit it with the A1c trend, and set a tickler to call the insurer if there's no answer in 72 hours.
options.consequence: Approved in two days. He starts the GLP-1, and at the next visit his A1c is trending toward 8. The 25 minutes cost you a later night, but the documented step-therapy makes the appeal airtight.

options.text: Switch him to a cheaper formulary sulfonylurea to avoid the PA fight entirely.
options.consequence: He's covered immediately, but the sulfonylurea drops his sugars too hard; he has a hypoglycemic episode while driving the next week. Avoiding the paperwork shifted the risk onto the patient.

options.text: Tell the patient to pay cash or appeal it himself, and move on to stay on schedule.
options.consequence: He can't afford $900/month, stops the med, and disappears for four months. He returns with an A1c of 12 and new neuropathy. The lapse is documented as a care-coordination failure during your next chart audit.

beats.title: Pajama Time
beats.situation: The last patient left at 5:30. You have 11 unfinished encounter notes, six in-basket results, and a borderline chest-CT incidentaloma (a 7mm lung nodule) that landed at 4 PM on a patient you saw this morning. You're unpaid for every minute from here on, and your own kid's bedtime is in 50 minutes.
beats.decision: You're exhausted and off the clock. What gets done tonight versus tomorrow?

options.text: Document the nodule with a Fleischner-guideline follow-up plan and message the patient tonight, then finish the remaining notes from home after bedtime.
options.consequence: The nodule gets a tracked 6-month CT and a flag so it can't fall through. You lose 90 minutes of family time, but nothing slips, and the audit trail shows same-day action on the incidental finding.

options.text: Handle the nodule now but batch the 11 notes to finish over the weekend.
options.consequence: The clinical risk is covered, but three notes miss the 24-hour billing window and get kicked back; two visits go unpaid and you redo them Monday. The nodule is safe; your productivity numbers and the clinic's revenue take the hit.

options.text: Go home now and deal with all of it, nodule included, tomorrow when you're fresh.
options.consequence: Tomorrow buries you the same way and the nodule note sits untouched for nine days. When you finally order the follow-up, the patient has moved; the nodule isn't re-imaged for a year and has grown. The delayed-diagnosis exposure is yours.

shift.closer: The shift wasn't dramatic codes and heroics; it was 19 patients, a hundred small judgment calls under a clock, and the quiet knowledge that the one detail you almost skipped is the one that can end a career or a life.

title: Veterinarian
oneLineReality: You diagnose patients who can't talk, console owners who can, and carry six figures of debt while doing the emotional labor of life-and-death decisions ten times a day.
typicalDay: Morning appointments back-to-back: wellness exams, vaccines, ear infections, limping dogs, and the cat that 'just isn't acting right'
Reading your own radiographs and in-house bloodwork (IDEXX/Abaxis) between rooms and deciding treatment on the spot without a specialist down the hall
A surgery block: spays, neuters, dental cleanings with extractions, or a mass removal you scoped that morning
At least one hard conversation about money, because the right diagnostic costs more than the owner can pay, and one euthanasia where you hold the room together
Charting, callbacks, and refill approvals that pile up; you finish records after the last patient leaves
Squeezing in a walk-in emergency (blocked cat, hit-by-car, suspected bloat) that blows up the schedule everyone else is waiting on
workStyle: On your feet in a clinic or barn, hands-on with animals and people all day; mix of fast-paced exam rooms, focused surgery, and emotionally heavy client conversations. Often on-call or working weekends in GP and emergency settings.
boringHardPart: The crushing routine isn't the medicine, it's the unfinished medical records at 8pm, the insurance-free clients choosing between the gold-standard workup and what they can afford, and the compassion fatigue from doing euthanasias and angry online reviews while carrying ~$200k in student debt against a salary that took years to catch up.
keyTools: In-house chemistry/CBC analyzers (IDEXX, Abaxis) and reference lab portals
Anesthesia machines and multiparameter patient monitors
Surgical instrument packs, electrocautery, dental units
Plumb's Veterinary Drug Handbook for dosing
Practice management/EMR software (Cornerstone, ezyVet, Avimark) and VIN for case lookups
crashCourse: Volunteer or work as a kennel/vet assistant first - 200+ shadowing hours is what admissions and reality both demand
Build the science base: general/organic chemistry, biology, biochem, anatomy and physiology (the pre-vet prereqs)
Get a VIN (Veterinary Information Network) student account and read real case discussions
Keep Plumb's Veterinary Drug Handbook nearby and learn to actually calculate doses by body weight
Read Ettinger's or a clinical small-animal medicine text and follow AVMA/myvetlife resources on debt and wellbeing

workSimulation.scenario: A 6-year-old male Labrador is rushed in: restless, hypersalivating, retching unproductively, and with a visibly distended, tympanic (drum-tight) abdomen. Gums are pale and tacky, heart rate is 160. The owner says it came on within the last hour after dinner.
workSimulation.task: This is a classic presentation of GDV (gastric dilatation-volvulus, 'bloat'), a surgical emergency. What is your immediate first action?

options.text: Place a large-bore IV catheter, start shock-rate isotonic crystalloid fluids, then decompress the stomach
options.feedback: Correct. GDV patients are in distributive/obstructive shock; you stabilize the cardiovascular system first (IV access, aggressive fluids) and decompress to relieve pressure. Imaging and surgery follow once the dog can survive them.

options.text: Take abdominal radiographs to confirm GDV before doing anything else
options.feedback: Wrong order. The right-lateral radiograph confirms volvulus, but a shocky dog can arrest while you're positioning it. Stabilize first, image second. Treatment of a dying patient never waits on a picture.

options.text: Induce vomiting to relieve the gas and distension
options.feedback: Dangerous. In GDV the stomach is twisted, so it can't empty that way; making the dog retch raises the risk of aspiration and rupture. This can kill the patient.

options.text: Give oral simethicone and send the dog home with instructions to monitor overnight
options.feedback: Fatal mistake. GDV kills within hours through shock, gastric necrosis, and arrhythmias. There is no outpatient version of this disease - it needs IV stabilization and surgery now.

workSimulation.aiSuggestion: This is textbook GDV. Place a large-bore IV and run shock-rate fluids, then pass an orogastric tube to decompress. If the tube passes into the stomach and you get a rush of gas and fluid out, the volvulus is relieved - you can downgrade from emergency surgery to overnight monitoring and recheck in the morning.
workSimulation.aiMistake: The AI claims that successfully passing an orogastric tube relieves the volvulus and removes the need for surgery. It does not. Tube passage (or trocharization) only decompresses gas; a tube can slide past a twisted stomach, so successful passage neither rules out nor corrects the rotation. The stomach is still volvulated, will re-bloat, and the dog can die overnight from necrosis or arrhythmia.
workSimulation.correctHumanJudgment: Use decompression only as temporary stabilization, then confirm with a right-lateral abdominal radiograph (look for the 'double bubble'/compartmentalization) and take the dog to surgery for derotation and a gastropexy regardless of how well the tube passed. Decompression buys time; only surgery fixes GDV and prevents recurrence.

aiCatchOptions.text: It treated successful orogastric tube passage as proof the volvulus was relieved, when tube passage only decompresses gas and the stomach is still twisted and needs surgery
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Exactly right. This is the subtle, dangerous error: decompression is stabilizing, not curative, and a tube can pass alongside a volvulus. The dog still needs radiographic confirmation and surgical derotation plus gastropexy.

aiCatchOptions.text: It chose the wrong fluid - GDV shock should be treated only with hypertonic saline, never isotonic crystalloids
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Wrong. Large-bore IV access with shock-rate isotonic crystalloids is standard initial resuscitation for GDV; hypertonic saline is an adjunct, not the only acceptable choice. The AI's fluid advice was fine.

aiCatchOptions.text: It skipped radiographs that must be taken before the IV catheter is placed
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Wrong. Stabilization (IV, fluids, decompression) correctly comes before imaging in a shocky patient. The AI's sequencing of IV-then-decompress was appropriate; the error was calling decompression definitive.

typicalDegree: Doctor of Veterinary Medicine (DVM or VMD) - a 4-year professional doctorate after a bachelor's, plus passing the NAVLE licensing exam

thirtyDayPlan.title: Get inside a real clinic
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Call 5-10 local GP, emergency, and large-animal practices and line up shadowing or a paid vet-assistant/kennel role. Hours here are non-negotiable for vet school and for finding out if you can stomach the work.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Audit the prereq science
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Map the pre-vet course list (gen/organic chem, biology, biochem, physics, anatomy/physiology, statistics) against any classes you have. Start one free course now - Khan Academy chemistry or biology - and build the study habit.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Learn the language and the math
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Get a VIN student account, follow AVMA myvetlife, and practice weight-based drug dose calculations from a Plumb's-style reference until mg/kg conversions are automatic. This is daily clinic math.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Mini project - work up a case end to end
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Pick one common condition (e.g., GDV, diabetic cat, or parvo puppy) and write a one-page workup: presenting signs, top 3 differentials, the diagnostics you'd run and why, treatment plan, and an honest cost estimate for the owner. Show it to a vet you shadow and ask where your reasoning breaks.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Run the money math honestly
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Use the AVMA salary estimator and a student-loan calculator to model a realistic debt-to-income scenario (e.g., $200k debt against a $130k new-grad salary). Decide if in-state DVM tuition or a service-payback program (military, USDA, rural) changes your plan.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Talk to two working vets about burnout
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Ask specifically about compassion fatigue, hours, on-call, and what they'd do differently. Going in clear-eyed about the emotional load is part of the qualification, not a detour.

automates: Drafting medical record notes and discharge instructions from your dictation
Flagging abnormal bloodwork values and suggesting differential lists to consider
Triage chatbots and symptom checkers that screen owner questions before a visit
Reminder/recall scheduling, inventory, and billing workflows
First-pass screening of radiographs and cytology images for common abnormalities
humanValue: Physically examining, restraining, and reading a non-verbal patient that can't describe its symptoms
Performing surgery, dentals, and hands-on procedures
Weighing diagnostics against an owner's real budget and emotions, then making the call
Delivering euthanasia and end-of-life conversations with compassion
Taking legal and ethical responsibility for the diagnosis and the controlled-drug prescriptions
aiImpact.riskNote: The diagnostic and paperwork side is increasingly AI-assisted, but the core job - physically handling animals, surgery, judgment under uncertainty, and legal/prescribing responsibility - cannot be automated. AI changes the tools, not the need for the veterinarian. Bigger near-term threats to the job are debt and burnout, not replacement.

shift.intro: It's 7:48am, your coffee is already cold, the waiting room is full, and the first chart on the door just says 'Cat — not acting right,' which could mean anything from a hairball to kidney failure.
shift.closer: The medicine was the easy part; what wrecked you was choosing between the right thing and the affordable thing all day, then charting it all alone at 8pm while a one-star review pinged your phone.

beats.title: The cat that 'just isn't acting right'
beats.situation: A 9-year-old neutered male cat, indoor-only, hasn't eaten since yesterday and keeps going to the litter box without producing. The owner thinks he's constipated. On your exam his bladder feels like a hard lemon and he cries when you touch his belly.
beats.decision: What do you do first with this 'constipated' cat?

options.text: Palpate the bladder, then immediately confirm a urethral obstruction and check an in-house potassium before sedating to unblock
options.consequence: You catch a blocked cat with a potassium of 7.2; you stabilize the heart, unblock him, and he walks out alive in three days. The owner sends cookies a week later.

options.text: Give a stool softener and an enema, send him home as constipation, recheck in 48 hours
options.consequence: He ruptures his bladder overnight and dies in agony before the 48-hour recheck; the owner files a board complaint and the case haunts your records review.

options.text: Take an X-ray first to look for stool, then decide once you see the films
options.consequence: The radiograph delays unblocking by 40 minutes and shows a huge bladder you already felt; he's fine, but his potassium climbed and the morning schedule is now 30 minutes behind.

beats.title: The workup nobody can afford
beats.situation: A limping, lethargic 11-year-old Golden has a firm swelling above the wrist. You suspect osteosarcoma — bone cancer. The gold-standard is radiographs plus referral for biopsy and staging. The owner, near tears, says she has maybe $300 to her name and no credit.
beats.decision: How do you handle the money wall?

options.text: Shoot the two-view leg radiograph now (within her budget), explain the likely diagnosis honestly, and lay out a tiered plan from palliative pain control to referral
options.consequence: The films show the classic lytic lesion. She can't afford amputation but starts pain meds and gets six good months; she later writes that you treated her like a person, not a wallet.

options.text: Recommend full referral, staging CT and biopsy only — tell her anything less is substandard
options.consequence: Overwhelmed and shamed, she declines everything and walks out; the dog suffers untreated for weeks and she never comes back to any vet.

options.text: Skip imaging, dispense pain meds empirically, and tell her to 'see how he does'
options.consequence: You ease his pain today but never confirm the cancer; when his leg fractures pathologically two weeks later, she's blindsided because nobody named the real risk.

beats.title: The Lab that came in retching
beats.situation: Mid-surgery block, a 6-year-old male Labrador is rushed in: restless, hypersalivating, retching unproductively, abdomen visibly distended and drum-tight. Gums are pale and tacky, heart rate 160. Owner says it hit within the last hour after dinner. Your clinic's AI triage assistant flashes a recommendation on the screen.
beats.decision: After shock fluids and decompression, what determines whether this dog goes to surgery?
beats.aiSuggestion: This is textbook GDV. Place a large-bore IV and run shock-rate fluids, then pass an orogastric tube to decompress. If the tube passes into the stomach and you get a rush of gas and fluid out, the volvulus is relieved — you can downgrade from emergency surgery to overnight monitoring and recheck in the morning.

options.text: Use the tube only to buy time, then shoot a right-lateral abdominal radiograph for the 'double bubble' and take him to surgery for derotation and gastropexy regardless of how well the tube passed
options.consequence: The X-ray confirms a compartmentalized, twisted stomach. You derotate and pexy that night; he recovers and never bloats again. The gastropexy means this exact emergency can't recur.

options.text: Follow the AI: the tube passed and gas rushed out, so downgrade to overnight monitoring and recheck in the morning
options.consequence: The tube slid past a still-twisted stomach. He re-bloats at 3am, the gastric wall goes necrotic, he throws a fatal arrhythmia, and dies in the ICU cage before your morning recheck.

options.text: Tube him, get partial decompression, then keep him on fluids and pain meds and reassess his comfort in a few hours before deciding on imaging
options.consequence: He looks better for an hour, so you lose time; you eventually X-ray and operate, but the delay means a splenectomy and a far rougher recovery that could have been avoided.

beats.title: The room you have to hold together
beats.situation: Last appointment of a 10-hour day: a 14-year-old dog in heart failure, the family chose euthanasia. The kids are sobbing, the husband is angry and quiet, and you still have nine unfinished records waiting. The catheter placement matters and the family is watching everything.
beats.decision: How do you run the euthanasia?

options.text: Slow down, give a sedative first so he's relaxed and pain-free, explain each step in plain words, and let the family say goodbye on their timeline
options.consequence: It's peaceful; the dog drifts off in the kids' arms. Months later the family returns with a new puppy and asks for you by name — they trust you with the next fourteen years.

options.text: Skip the sedation to save time and go straight to the IV injection so you can get to your charts
options.consequence: The vein blows, the dog vocalizes, the family's last memory is panic, and a raw one-star review about 'a vet who rushed our dog's death' is up by morning.

options.text: Sedate and proceed, but stay clinical and brief to keep your composure and protect yourself from the weight of it
options.consequence: It's medically clean and the family is okay, but your flat affect reads as cold; they don't complain, yet they quietly switch clinics, and the bottled-up grief adds to the fatigue you'll carry home.

title: Clinical Psychologist
oneLineReality: You spend years earning a doctorate and a license to sit with people in their worst moments — the work is profound, the paperwork and insurance battles are relentless, and the path is one of the longest in healthcare.
typicalDay: Run 5-7 back-to-back 50-minute therapy or assessment sessions, resetting your attention completely between each client
Write progress notes and treatment plans in an EHR after each session — often the most time-consuming part of the day
Administer or score psychological tests (e.g., WAIS-IV, MMPI-2) and integrate results into a diagnostic formulation
Handle insurance pre-authorizations, justify continued care, and chase down reimbursement denials
Consult with a psychiatrist, PCP, or school about a shared client and coordinate care
Do a risk check-in on a high-acuity client and document a safety plan
workStyle: Mostly solo, high-focus 1-on-1 work in an office or teletherapy setup, broken by consults and a heavy documentation load; emotionally demanding and requires strict boundary-keeping.
boringHardPart: The clinical work is meaningful, but the grind is documentation and insurance: notes for every session, treatment-plan updates, pre-authorizations, and appeals on denied claims. Add the unpaid years of training — a 4-7 year doctorate, a full-time internship, ~1,500-3,000 supervised postdoc hours, and the EPPP licensing exam — before you can independently bill.
keyTools: Standardized assessments (WAIS-IV, MMPI-2-RF, PHQ-9, GAD-7, C-SSRS)
Evidence-based treatment manuals (CBT, DBT, ACT, EMDR)
crashCourse: Earn a strong undergrad psych GPA + research experience; a doctorate (PhD or PsyD) in clinical psychology is non-negotiable for the title
Learn the difference between a PhD (research-funded, longer) and a PsyD (practice-focused, often self-funded) before you pick a path
Master at least one evidence-based modality deeply (CBT or DBT) rather than dabbling in many
Understand licensure: APA-accredited internship, supervised hours, and passing the EPPP — rules vary by state
Get comfortable with risk assessment and ethics early; they define real clinical practice more than any theory

workSimulation.scenario: It's an intake session with a new adult client referred for depression. Twenty minutes in, while describing months of low mood and poor sleep, she says quietly, 'Honestly some mornings I just wish I didn't have to wake up.' She has not mentioned this before and there's nothing about it in the referral.
workSimulation.task: What is the appropriate next clinical step?

options.text: Pause the intake flow and conduct a structured suicide risk assessment — ask directly about ideation, plan, intent, access to means, and prior attempts (e.g., using the C-SSRS).
options.feedback: Correct. A direct verbal disclosure of a passive death wish is a clinical signal you must explore in the moment. Asking directly does not 'plant the idea' — it's the standard of care. You stratify risk first, then decide on a safety plan, level of care, or continued assessment.

options.text: Reassure her that wishing you could sleep through a hard time is completely normal, and continue gathering the depression history.
options.feedback: Unsafe. Normalizing and moving on means you never learn whether there is active ideation, a plan, or intent. You cannot rule out risk by reassurance; you rule it out (or in) by assessing it.

options.text: Immediately call 911 and arrange involuntary hospitalization to be safe.
options.feedback: Premature and harmful. A passive death wish is not the same as imminent danger. Escalating to involuntary hospitalization before assessing intent, plan, and means can destroy the therapeutic alliance and is clinically and ethically disproportionate.

options.text: End the session early and refer her out to a higher level of care since this is beyond an intake.
options.feedback: Abandoning the assessment is itself a risk. Risk evaluation IS core clinical work, not something to offload before you even understand the severity. Refer only after you've assessed and have a clinical reason.

workSimulation.aiSuggestion: Your AI scribe drafts the intake note and concludes: 'Client completed the PHQ-9 at check-in, scoring 8 (mild range) and answering 0 on item 9 (thoughts of being better off dead or self-harm). Suicide risk is therefore low; no further risk assessment indicated. Recommend weekly CBT for depression.'
workSimulation.aiMistake: The AI used a self-report screener score to rule out suicide risk, directly contradicting the client's in-session verbal disclosure of a passive death wish. PHQ-9 item 9 is a coarse, narrow-window self-report that frequently under-detects risk, and a clinical verbal disclosure overrides a screener every time. The 'risk is low, no assessment needed' conclusion is clinically dangerous.
workSimulation.correctHumanJudgment: The clinician notices the note's conclusion conflicts with what was actually said in the room. A screener supplements but never replaces a clinical risk assessment. The human keeps the disclosure front-and-center, performs a structured C-SSRS assessment regardless of the PHQ-9 score, and documents the discrepancy and the assessment outcome.

aiCatchOptions.text: It treated a low PHQ-9 item-9 score as ruling out suicide risk, ignoring the client's verbal disclosure — a screener supplements, it can never replace a clinical risk assessment.
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Right. The screener said one thing, the client said another, and the client's disclosure wins. Self-report instruments under-detect risk and must never override what's revealed in the room.

aiCatchOptions.text: It used the PHQ-9 when the GAD-7 is the correct instrument for assessing depression.
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Wrong. The PHQ-9 is the appropriate, validated depression measure; the GAD-7 screens anxiety. The instrument choice was fine — the error was using its score to dismiss a verbal risk disclosure.

aiCatchOptions.text: It miscalculated the score: a PHQ-9 of 8 is actually moderate-to-severe and should trigger a medication referral.
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Wrong. A PHQ-9 of 8 genuinely falls in the mild range, and severity alone wouldn't be the safety issue here. The danger is the conclusion that no risk assessment is needed despite the disclosure.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Map the real path before you commit years
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Read the APA's guide to clinical psychology training and write a one-page comparison of PhD (funded, research) vs PsyD (self-funded, practice) and what licensure requires in your target state (internship, supervised hours, EPPP).

thirtyDayPlan.title: Test whether you actually like the work
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Volunteer or apply for a crisis-line / peer-support role (e.g., a local hotline or 988). A few shifts tells you more about your fit for emotional labor than any book.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Learn one evidence-based model deeply
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Take a free or low-cost intro to Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (e.g., Beck Institute resources or a Coursera CBT course) and learn how a thought record actually works.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Shadow and interview a licensed psychologist
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Email 5 local clinical psychologists asking for a 20-minute informational interview; ask specifically about caseload, income reality, and how much time goes to insurance/notes.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Mini project: run a structured intake roleplay
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Using a public C-SSRS and PHQ-9, write a mock intake script and have a friend roleplay a client. Practice asking risk questions directly and writing a clean, defensible session note.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Build the research/GPA foundation
thirtyDayPlan.detail: If you're pre-doctorate, line up a research assistant position or psych lab volunteer role — clinical PhD admissions are research-driven and brutally competitive.

automates: Drafting first-pass progress notes and intake summaries from session transcripts
Scoring standardized assessments and flagging out-of-range scores
Insurance pre-authorization paperwork and claim-denial appeal letters
Scheduling, reminders, and routine outcome-measure tracking between sessions
Psychoeducation handouts and homework worksheets for clients
humanValue: Building therapeutic alliance — the trust and attunement that actually drives outcomes
In-the-moment clinical judgment on risk, crisis, and ambiguity that screeners miss
Reading nonverbal cues, ruptures, and what a client is NOT saying
Ethical and legal responsibility for diagnosis, treatment decisions, and safety
Tailoring an intervention to a specific person, culture, and history rather than a protocol
aiImpact.riskNote: AI chatbots are eating into low-acuity self-help and journaling, and will automate notes and billing — but the core of clinical psychology is a regulated, relationship-based, liability-bearing human act. Risk assessment, diagnosis, and the therapeutic alliance are hard to automate and legally must be owned by a licensed human. The realistic threat is AI handling intake/admin and reshaping the job, not replacing the clinician.

shift.intro: It's 8:52 a.m., your first client is already in the waiting room, and your inbox shows three insurance denials and an unsigned note from yesterday you forgot to close.
shift.closer: The hours with clients were the realest, most human part of your day — and most of the day was spent typing, justifying, and fighting a system that pays you to prove people still deserve care.

beats.title: The 50-minute reset
beats.situation: Back-to-back is the job: a grieving widower at 9, a panic-disorder teen at 10, a couple in crisis at 11. Your 9:00 runs hot and emotional, ending with him in tears about his late wife. It's 9:51. Your 10:00 — a 16-year-old you've never met — is checking in at the desk, and you can still feel the weight of the last hour in your chest.
beats.decision: You have nine minutes before the next intake. What do you do with them?

options.text: Take 4 minutes to jot the core note, then deliberately reset — water, two slow breaths, re-read the teen's intake form — before opening the door.
options.consequence: You walk in present, not leaking grief into a scared kid's first session. She opens up about school refusal in week one; rapport holds for months.

options.text: Skip the break and write the full, detailed 9:00 note now while it's fresh, letting the teen wait 10 extra minutes.
options.consequence: Your note is excellent, but you greet the teen flustered and 12 minutes late; she reads it as 'I don't matter here' and no-shows the next two weeks.

options.text: Just open the door on time — push the grief down, you'll 'deal with it later,' and wing the intake cold.
options.consequence: By client #5 the unprocessed sessions stack into a fog; you misremember which client said what and have to call one back to re-confirm her meds. Burnout creeps in by Thursday.

beats.title: The denial on the screen
beats.situation: Between the couple and lunch, the EHR flags it: your long-term OCD client's insurer denied authorization for continued sessions, calling her 'sufficiently improved.' She is not — she's mid-exposure work and a cutoff now risks relapse. The appeal needs a clinical justification letter, and the portal deadline is today.
beats.decision: Your lunch break is the only open slot. How do you handle the denial?

options.text: Eat at your desk and write a specific appeal: cite her Y-BOCS scores over time, the active ERP protocol, and the documented relapse risk of premature termination.
options.consequence: Eight days later the appeal is approved with six more sessions. You lost a lunch, but she finishes her exposure hierarchy instead of crashing.

options.text: Send a quick generic appeal — 'client still symptomatic, requests continued care' — without the score data.
options.consequence: The vague letter gets a second denial two weeks later; now you're in a peer-to-peer phone review, burning another hour you didn't have.

options.text: Let it ride — tell her at the next session that insurance stopped and she can pay out of pocket or pause.
options.consequence: She can't afford private rates, drops out mid-treatment, and relapses by fall. You document a termination you know was clinically wrong, and it sits with you.

beats.title: The intake and the AI scribe
beats.situation: New adult client, referred for depression. Twenty minutes in, describing months of low mood and broken sleep, she says quietly: 'Honestly, some mornings I just wish I didn't have to wake up.' It's not in the referral; she's never said it before. After session, your AI scribe has already drafted the intake note.
beats.decision: The AI's note is on your screen, ready to sign. What is your next clinical step?
beats.aiSuggestion: Client completed the PHQ-9 at check-in, scoring 8 (mild range) and answering 0 on item 9 (thoughts of being better off dead or self-harm). Suicide risk is therefore low; no further risk assessment indicated. Recommend weekly CBT for depression.

options.text: Stop. The note contradicts what she said out loud. Keep her in the room, run a structured C-SSRS regardless of the PHQ-9, then document the disclosure, the assessment outcome, and the screener discrepancy.
options.consequence: The C-SSRS surfaces passive ideation without plan or intent; you build a safety plan and schedule a 3-day check-in. She later says that was the moment she trusted you. The signed note is clinically defensible.

options.text: Note the comment in a line you add to the AI draft, ask her one quick 'are you safe?' question, get a yes, and sign off with weekly CBT.
options.consequence: A single yes/no isn't a risk assessment; you missed that she's been giving away belongings. No safety plan exists. It surfaces in week three as a near-miss you should have caught at intake.

options.text: Accept the AI's logic — the validated screener scored her low-risk on item 9 — sign the note as drafted and book her for CBT next week.
options.consequence: You let a self-report number override a spoken death wish. No safety plan, no documented assessment. If she deteriorates, the chart shows you were told and did nothing — clinically and medico-legally indefensible.

beats.title: The note backlog vs. the consult
beats.situation: Last client's out. You have nine unwritten progress notes, two treatment plans overdue for the audit, and a WAIS-IV to score. Then the phone rings: the psychiatrist co-managing your bipolar client wants to talk now about a med change and a discharge plan — she's only reachable for the next 20 minutes before she's off for a week.
beats.decision: Twenty minutes, one phone window, and a wall of documentation. What gets your attention?

options.text: Take the consult now — align on the lithium change, flag the early-warning signs you've seen, and agree on the discharge timeline; write the notes after, even if it means staying late.
options.consequence: Coordinated care catches a hypomanic shift two weeks later before it spikes; the psychiatrist adjusts the dose early. You leave at 6:40 with notes done but the client stayed safe.

options.text: Let it go to voicemail and grind out the notes — documentation is overdue and the audit is real; you'll catch the psychiatrist next week.
options.consequence: Your charts are pristine, but the uncoordinated med change confuses the client about her plan; she stops lithium for four days and ends up in a crisis appointment you have to squeeze in.

options.text: Do neither well — half-listen to the psychiatrist while typing notes, agreeing to things you're not really tracking.
options.consequence: You mishear the new dose, document it wrong, and the error rides into the chart. The pharmacy catches the mismatch and pages you at 8 p.m. to untangle it.

title: Web Developer
oneLineReality: You build and maintain the websites and web apps people actually use — which is 20% writing fresh code and 80% fixing why a button works on Chrome but not Safari, chasing a CSS bug, and shipping someone else's design pixel-for-pixel by Friday.
typicalDay: Pull the latest code, read overnight bug tickets, and pick up a task from the sprint board in Jira
Turn a Figma design into responsive HTML/CSS/React components that look right from a phone to a wide monitor
Wire the frontend to a backend API, handle the loading/error/empty states nobody put in the mockup
Debug why something breaks only in Safari or only on a slow connection, using browser DevTools
Open a pull request, respond to code-review comments, fix what a teammate flagged
Join a 15-minute standup and a meeting about why the form submission is double-charging users
workStyle: Mostly solo focused coding in 2-4 hour blocks, punctuated by standups, code reviews, and Slack questions. Heavily remote or hybrid. Collaborative with designers and backend devs but you own your tickets. Deadline-driven in sprints (usually 2 weeks); occasional crunch before a launch.
boringHardPart: Cross-browser and cross-device compatibility: the same code renders differently in Safari, on an old Android, or at an odd screen width, and you burn hours hunting a one-pixel misalignment or a CSS quirk no tutorial covers. Add to that maintaining old codebases nobody documented and fixing flaky bugs you can't reproduce.
crashCourse: Learn HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript first — frameworks come later and rest on these
Master the browser DevTools: inspect elements, read the console, debug the network tab
Get fluent in Git: branch, commit, pull request, resolve a merge conflict
Learn one frontend framework deeply (React) plus how to call an API and handle errors
Build and deploy 3 real projects to a live URL — a portfolio matters more than any certificate

workSimulation.scenario: You're a frontend developer at a mid-size e-commerce company. QA filed a bug: on the checkout page, the 'Place Order' button can be clicked multiple times in a row on a slow connection, and some customers are getting charged twice. You can reproduce it by throttling your network in DevTools.
workSimulation.task: What is the correct, robust fix to ship?

options.text: Disable the button (set a loading/disabled state) the instant it's clicked, AND make the order endpoint idempotent on the backend using a unique request key
options.feedback: Correct. Disabling the button stops the common case immediately, but a determined or glitchy client can still fire duplicate requests, so the backend must reject duplicates via an idempotency key. Defense in depth is what prevents real double-charges.

options.text: Just add CSS 'pointer-events: none' to the button after the first click
options.feedback: CSS can be bypassed, doesn't cover keyboard/Enter submissions, and does nothing if the first request is still in flight when a retry fires. It hides the symptom, not the cause, and gives no server-side protection.

options.text: Add a 3-second setTimeout that ignores clicks after the first one
options.feedback: A fixed timer is a guess: on a truly slow connection the request may take longer than 3 seconds, so the window reopens and the double-charge returns. Tie the lock to the request lifecycle, not the clock.

options.text: Show a confirmation modal asking 'Are you sure?' before charging
options.feedback: Adds friction and still doesn't prevent a double-submit — a user can confirm, see no response on a slow connection, and click again. It treats UX as a substitute for correctness.

workSimulation.aiSuggestion: The AI coding assistant suggests: 'Simple fix — add a useState `isSubmitting` flag. Set it true on click, disable the button while true, and the duplicate charges stop. Here's the component code.'
workSimulation.aiMistake: The AI's fix is purely client-side. It correctly disables the button but never addresses the backend — if the same request reaches the server twice (retries, two devices, a network hiccup, or any client that bypasses the UI), the order endpoint will still charge the customer twice because there's no idempotency check.
workSimulation.correctHumanJudgment: A human who understands the system knows money-handling endpoints must be idempotent on the server. The button flag is necessary but not sufficient; you add a unique idempotency key per checkout so the backend safely ignores duplicates. The client can never be the only line of defense for a financial transaction.

aiCatchOptions.text: The fix is client-side only — it never makes the order endpoint idempotent, so duplicate requests reaching the server can still double-charge
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Right. The UI flag stops the common case but a financial endpoint needs server-side duplicate protection (an idempotency key). The AI solved the symptom in the browser and ignored the source of truth.

aiCatchOptions.text: useState is the wrong hook — it should have used useRef so the flag doesn't trigger a re-render
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Wrong. A re-render is exactly what you want here so the button visibly disables; useState is appropriate. This is a plausible-sounding nitpick that misses the real, dangerous gap (no server-side protection).

aiCatchOptions.text: It forgot to add a loading spinner, so users won't know the order is processing
aiCatchOptions.feedback: A spinner is a nice UX touch but it's not the bug. Even with a perfect spinner the double-charge can still happen server-side. This names a cosmetic miss, not the correctness flaw.
