thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 1: HTML & CSS foundations
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Build 3 static pages by hand (no framework): a profile card, a pricing page, and a responsive nav bar. Learn flexbox and grid. Goal: make them look right on phone and desktop.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 2: JavaScript & the DOM
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Learn variables, functions, arrays, and DOM manipulation. Build an interactive to-do list that adds/deletes items and saves to localStorage. Live entirely in the browser console and DevTools.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 3: React + an API
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Learn components, props, state, and useEffect. Build a small app that fetches from a free public API (e.g. weather or movies) and handles loading and error states.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 4: Mini project + deploy
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Ship a real portfolio site that lists your 3 projects, then deploy it live to Vercel or Netlify with a custom-looking URL. Put the code on GitHub with a clean README.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Ongoing: Git habit
thirtyDayPlan.detail: From day one, commit every project to Git with meaningful messages and practice one pull request. Recruiters look at your GitHub activity and your live links far more than any certificate.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Stretch: read real code
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Find a small open-source repo, read an issue, and try to reproduce one bug locally. Understanding someone else's codebase is the skill that separates hobbyists from hireable juniors.

automates: Scaffolding boilerplate components, forms, and config files
Writing first-draft CSS and converting designs to markup
Generating unit tests and regex
Explaining error messages and suggesting fixes
Translating between frameworks or refactoring repetitive code
humanValue: Judging whether a fix is actually correct and safe (e.g. idempotent payments, security, edge cases)
Understanding the real business goal behind a vague ticket
Debugging weird cross-browser and production-only issues AI can't reproduce
Architecture decisions and trade-offs across a whole codebase
Collaborating with designers/stakeholders and owning accountability for what ships
aiImpact.riskNote: AI dramatically speeds up routine frontend work and is shrinking demand for pure 'turn this design into HTML' junior roles — that's real and already happening. But someone still has to integrate, debug, secure, and take responsibility for production systems, and AI confidently produces subtly wrong code (see the double-charge bug). The risk is highest for low-skill template work and lowest for developers who understand systems end-to-end. BLS still projects 7% growth (2024-2034), faster than average.

shift.intro: It's 9:15, your coffee's still hot, and the overnight bug queue has 11 new tickets — two of them flagged 'customer-impacting' in angry red.
shift.closer: You wrote maybe forty lines of original code all day; the rest was reading other people's code, fighting a browser that hates you, and being the last person between a customer and a double charge.

beats.title: Standup and the sprint board
beats.situation: You pull main, the build is green. Standup is in 5 minutes. The board has your committed ticket (a product-card redesign) but overnight QA also filed a P1: search returns zero results on the live site for any query with an apostrophe. Your lead is out sick and didn't reassign it.
beats.decision: What do you bring to standup and pick up?

options.text: Flag the apostrophe P1 in standup, grab it, and reproduce it first thing — customer-facing breakage outranks your planned card work.
options.consequence: You find an unescaped query string within the hour; search is back by lunch and the team reprioritizes your card ticket to next sprint without drama.

options.text: Stick to your committed card ticket and drop a Slack note that 'someone should look at the P1.'
options.consequence: The card ships on time but the search bug sits untouched till afternoon; support logs 30+ tickets and a manager asks in standup why nobody owned it.

options.text: Say nothing about the P1 in standup, assume the on-call backend dev will catch it.
options.consequence: Two days later it surfaces in a postmortem that the bug was visible at 9am and ignored; conversions dipped 4% and your name is on the ignored ticket.

beats.title: Figma to a real responsive component
beats.situation: You're building the product card from a pixel-perfect Figma. The mockup shows one happy state: short title, in-stock badge, a price. Nothing for long titles, out-of-stock, missing image, or the slow API that feeds it.
beats.decision: How do you build it?

options.text: Build the happy state, then add loading skeletons, an out-of-stock variant, image fallback, and clamp long titles — and screenshot the edge cases for the designer.
options.consequence: In review the designer thanks you and approves clamp behavior; QA finds zero state bugs and the card ships clean across the catalog.

options.text: Match the Figma exactly, pixel for pixel, and handle states later if a ticket comes in.
options.consequence: It looks gorgeous in the demo, but a 90-character title from a real SKU blows the layout in prod three days later and you reopen the work mid-sprint.

options.text: Hardcode the sample title and price from the Figma to get it looking right fast.
options.consequence: It passes your local check, then ships showing 'Sample Product / $19.99' on live category pages; a customer tweets a screenshot and you hotfix under pressure.

beats.title: It only breaks in Safari
beats.situation: Your card looks perfect in Chrome. QA says on Safari and on an older iPhone the price overlaps the badge and a sticky filter bar jumps on scroll. You can't reproduce it on your machine until you open a real device via BrowserStack.
beats.decision: How do you chase it?

options.text: Reproduce on a real iOS device, isolate it to a flexbox gap and a 100vh quirk, fix with tested fallbacks, and re-verify on Safari plus old Android.
options.consequence: The fix holds across browsers; you add the two quirks to the team's cross-browser checklist and the next dev avoids the same trap.

options.text: Apply a Stack Overflow `-webkit-` snippet that sounds right and push it without retesting on a device.
options.consequence: It fixes the overlap but the sticky bar still jitters on real iOS; QA bounces the ticket back and you lose another afternoon you'd called done.

options.text: Add `!important` overrides until it looks fine in your Chrome window and mark it resolved.
options.consequence: Chrome's fine, Safari's still broken, and now the specificity war means the next person's style fix silently does nothing — two bugs from one.

beats.title: The double-charge button
beats.situation: QA's last ticket: on checkout, a slow connection lets users click 'Place Order' several times and some get charged twice. You throttle your network in DevTools and reproduce it instantly. Finance wants a fix shipped tonight.
beats.decision: What fix do you ship?
beats.aiSuggestion: Simple fix — add a useState `isSubmitting` flag. Set it true on click, disable the button while true, and the duplicate charges stop. Here's the component code.

options.text: Disable the button with the submitting flag AND have the client send a unique idempotency key per checkout so the payment endpoint safely ignores duplicate requests.
options.consequence: Duplicates die at the server too; a week later a retry storm from a flaky mobile network hits the same key and zero customers are double-charged.

options.text: Ship the button-disable flag now and file a backend ticket to 'consider idempotency later.'
options.consequence: UI clicks stop, but a customer on two devices and an automated retry still double-charge that month; the backlog ticket is still untriaged at the postmortem.

options.text: Take the AI's component as-is — `isSubmitting` flag disables the button, charges stop, done.
options.consequence: A network hiccup resends the same request server-side; 60 customers get charged twice over the weekend, finance issues refunds and a chargeback report lands on your lead's desk.

title: DevOps / Cloud Engineer
oneLineReality: You are the plumber of the cloud: you keep code flowing to production through pipelines and infrastructure-as-code, and you get paged at 3am when it leaks. BLS files this work under "Network and Computer Systems Administrators" ($96,800 median), but real DevOps/Cloud titles routinely pay $120k-$160k+ because the bar is coding + ops + on-call nerves.
typicalDay: Check overnight alerts in Datadog/Grafana and the on-call queue, triage anything red before standup
Review and merge teammates' Terraform/Kubernetes pull requests, watching for changes that could take down production
Build or fix a CI/CD pipeline so a developer's code ships to staging automatically and safely
Investigate why a deployment is slow or a pod is in CrashLoopBackOff, reading logs and metrics to find root cause
Right-size cloud resources and chase down a surprise AWS bill spike
Write a postmortem or update runbooks so the same incident does not page you twice
workStyle: Mostly remote or hybrid, deep-focus solo work punctuated by high-stakes incident firefighting. You rotate through on-call (often 1 week in every 4-6) where your phone can wake you. Heavy async collaboration with developers, security, and SRE teams over Slack, tickets, and PRs.
boringHardPart: The glamorous-sounding 'automation' is mostly debugging YAML indentation, IAM permission errors, and flaky pipelines at the worst possible time. On-call burnout is real: a single bad deploy or expired certificate can eat your evening, and the work is invisible when it goes right and very visible when it goes wrong.
keyTools: Git + GitHub Actions / Jenkins / GitLab CI
crashCourse: Get comfortable in a Linux terminal: file system, permissions, processes, and writing a Bash script that does something useful
Containerize a small app with Docker, then run it on a local Kubernetes cluster (kind or minikube)
Learn Terraform by spinning up and tearing down a real AWS resource (an S3 bucket, then an EC2 instance) from code
Build a CI/CD pipeline in GitHub Actions that tests and deploys a repo automatically on every push
Set up basic monitoring (Prometheus + Grafana) and trigger an alert on purpose so you understand observability

workSimulation.scenario: It is Tuesday afternoon. A developer asks you to add a `backup` cost-allocation tag to the company's primary production PostgreSQL database, managed in Terraform. You make the one-line change and run `terraform plan` before applying.
workSimulation.task: The plan output does NOT show a simple in-place update. Instead it reads: `# aws_db_instance.prod must be replaced` and lists `-/+ destroy and then create replacement`, with `~ engine_version: "15.4" -> "15.7" # forces replacement` buried in the diff. What do you do?

options.text: Apply it — it's just a tag, and Terraform knows what it's doing.
options.feedback: Catastrophic. 'must be replaced' means Terraform will DESTROY the production database and build a new empty one. The tag is harmless, but something else in the plan is forcing a full replacement. Applying blindly would wipe live customer data.

options.text: Read the plan carefully, spot that `engine_version` is forcing replacement, revert that unintended version bump, take a manual snapshot, and re-plan until it shows only an in-place tag update.
options.feedback: Correct. The tag was safe; an unrelated engine_version drift was the real culprit forcing destroy/create. You found the line annotated 'forces replacement', removed the unintended change, and protected yourself with a snapshot before touching prod. This is the core DevOps discipline: never apply a plan you don't fully understand.

options.text: Run `terraform apply -auto-approve` to skip the confirmation and save time.
options.feedback: Worse than applying normally — you're removing the one human checkpoint that lets you catch the 'must be replaced' warning. Auto-approve on production state is how databases get deleted.

options.text: Delete the Terraform state file and re-import the database so the plan looks clean.
options.feedback: Destructive and superstitious. Deleting state doesn't fix the underlying version drift, and a botched re-import can leave the resource unmanaged or duplicated. You'd be hiding the warning, not resolving it.

workSimulation.aiSuggestion: The AI pair-programming assistant says: 'Easy fix — add a `lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }` block to the aws_db_instance resource and re-run terraform apply. That guarantees the database can never be destroyed, so your tag change is now safe to apply.'
workSimulation.aiMistake: `prevent_destroy = true` does not make the change safe — it makes `terraform apply` HARD-ERROR and abort the moment a plan would replace the resource. Because the engine_version drift still forces replacement, the apply fails and the deploy is now stuck, while the actual root cause (the unintended version bump) is never addressed. It's a guardrail, not a fix.
workSimulation.correctHumanJudgment: A human reads the plan and notices the `~ engine_version ... # forces replacement` line, understands that the replacement — not the tag — is the danger, removes the drift so the plan reduces to an in-place tag update, and snapshots before applying. prevent_destroy can stay as a permanent guardrail, but it is never the thing that 'fixes' a replacement plan.

aiCatchOptions.text: prevent_destroy only blocks the apply with an error; it never resolves WHY Terraform wants to replace the DB, so the deploy stays stuck and the engine_version drift is left unfixed.
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Exactly right. prevent_destroy is a safety brake that aborts the apply, not a fix. The root cause — the unintended engine_version change forcing replacement — is still there, so the human still has to read the plan and remove that drift.

aiCatchOptions.text: prevent_destroy will silently delete the database anyway because tags always force recreation in AWS.
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Wrong on both counts: prevent_destroy does the opposite of silently deleting (it errors out and blocks), and tags are an in-place update, not a forced recreation. This misnames the real flaw.

aiCatchOptions.text: The AI's only mistake is putting the lifecycle block in the wrong file; it works fine once moved to the module root.
aiCatchOptions.feedback: File location is irrelevant — Terraform reads the whole module regardless. The real problem is conceptual: prevent_destroy blocks the apply instead of resolving the version drift that forces replacement.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 1: Live in the Linux terminal
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Install WSL2 or a Linux VM. Learn navigation, permissions, processes, SSH, and write three Bash scripts (backup a folder, parse a log, health-check a URL). Set up a GitHub account and commit them.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 1-2: Containerize something real
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Take any small web app, write a Dockerfile, build and run it locally, then push the image to Docker Hub. Understand images vs containers, ports, and environment variables.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 2: Touch real cloud (free tier)
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Open an AWS free-tier account, set a billing alarm immediately, and manually create an S3 bucket and a t2.micro EC2 instance. Then learn IAM basics so you understand permissions before automating.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 3: Infrastructure as code
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Rebuild that same S3 bucket and EC2 instance with Terraform instead of clicking. Run plan, apply, and destroy until you trust the workflow and can read a plan's 'forces replacement' warnings.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 4: Mini capstone project
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Deploy your Dockerized app to AWS via a GitHub Actions pipeline that builds the image, runs a test, and deploys on every push to main — all infra defined in Terraform. Add a Grafana/CloudWatch dashboard and one alert. Write a short README explaining the architecture.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Ongoing: Start a cert track
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Begin studying for the AWS Certified Solutions Architect – Associate ($150). It forces you to learn cloud fundamentals systematically and is the most recognized entry credential for cloud/DevOps roles.

automates: Generating first-draft Terraform, Dockerfiles, and CI pipeline YAML from a prompt
Writing and explaining Bash/Python glue scripts
Summarizing noisy logs and suggesting likely root causes
Recalling exact kubectl / aws-cli command syntax
Drafting runbooks and postmortem templates
humanValue: Judgment under pressure during a live production incident
Assessing blast radius and risk before running a destructive change
Designing secure, cost-aware architecture and the tradeoffs behind it
Deciding when NOT to deploy and owning the on-call call
Coordinating humans across dev, security, and leadership during an outage
aiImpact.riskNote: AI accelerates the keystroke-heavy parts (writing configs, scripts, recalling commands) and will shrink demand for pure 'click-ops' admins — which is partly why BLS projects a 4% decline for the underlying admin occupation. But production ownership, incident judgment, security tradeoffs, and accountability for destructive changes stay firmly human. The risk is less 'job vanishes' and more 'the boring 40% gets automated, raising the bar on the hard 60%.'

shift.intro: Your laptop is barely open and your coffee still steaming when the on-call dashboard flares red and Slack starts buzzing with the words 'is staging down for anyone else?'

beats.title: Triage Before Standup
beats.situation: Datadog shows a 5xx error-rate spike on the checkout service that started at 04:12 and self-recovered by 04:40. The on-call queue has one auto-resolved PagerDuty alert nobody acknowledged. Standup is in 20 minutes and a teammate is asking in Slack if they can start a big deploy.
beats.decision: The spike already healed itself. What do you do with the next 20 minutes?

options.text: Pull the 04:12 logs and traces, find the trigger, and post a 3-line summary in the incident channel before standup
options.consequence: You discover a nightly batch job briefly exhausted the DB connection pool. Two weeks later that same job tries to scale up and your pool-size fix is the reason checkout doesn't fall over during the Friday sale.

options.text: Ack the alert, note 'self-recovered, monitoring' and tell the teammate to go ahead with their deploy
options.consequence: Standup stays on schedule, but the connection-pool exhaustion recurs the following Tuesday at peak traffic and this time it doesn't self-heal — you eat a 40-minute partial outage that the morning logs would have predicted.

options.text: Close the auto-resolved alert as noise and start your day; if it mattered it would still be firing
options.consequence: The silent failure mode goes undocumented. A month later a new hire hits the identical spike, finds zero runbook history, and pages you at midnight to rediscover what you already saw this morning.

beats.title: The PR That Looks Harmless
beats.situation: A teammate's Terraform PR is tagged 'tiny, just a Kubernetes resource limit bump' and they want it merged before lunch. Reading the diff, you notice it also lowers the production deployment's readinessProbe initialDelaySeconds from 30 to 5 and drops replicas from 4 to 2 — changes the PR description never mentions.
beats.decision: CI is green and they're waiting. How do you handle the review?

options.text: Request changes: flag the undeclared probe and replica edits, ask them to split those out so each change is reviewable and reversible
options.consequence: Turns out the replica drop was an accidental rebase artifact from an old branch. Catching it saves you a 2am page when 2 pods couldn't have absorbed the evening traffic the service normally needs 4 for.

options.text: Approve the limit bump but leave a comment asking them to double-check the probe timing later
options.consequence: The merge ships. The 5-second readiness delay marks pods Ready before the JVM finishes warming up, so the next deploy routes traffic into cold pods and users see a burst of timeouts — exactly the question your comment asked but nobody actioned.

options.text: Stamp approve — CI passed and it's labeled tiny, you trust them
options.consequence: Production quietly runs on 2 replicas for nine days until one node drains for maintenance, leaving a single pod that gets crushed during peak — a self-inflicted outage that a 90-second read of the diff would have stopped.

beats.title: One-Line Tag, Full Plan Carnage
beats.situation: A developer asks you to add a 'backup' cost-allocation tag to the primary production PostgreSQL database in Terraform. You make the one-line change and run terraform plan. The output is not an in-place update — it reads '# aws_db_instance.prod must be replaced' with '-/+ destroy and then create replacement', and buried in the diff: '~ engine_version: "15.4" -> "15.7" # forces replacement'. Your AI pair-programmer is already typing in the IDE.
beats.decision: The plan would destroy and recreate prod Postgres. What do you actually apply?
beats.aiSuggestion: Easy fix — add a lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true } block to the aws_db_instance resource and re-run terraform apply. That guarantees the database can never be destroyed, so your tag change is now safe to apply.

options.text: Read the diff, see the engine_version 15.4->15.7 is forcing the replacement, pin engine_version back to 15.4 so the plan collapses to a pure in-place tag update, take a manual snapshot, then apply
options.consequence: Plan shrinks to '~ tags' only. The tag lands with zero downtime. You also file a ticket about the upstream version drift so the real upgrade gets scheduled with a maintenance window instead of ambushing the next person who touches this file.

options.text: Add prevent_destroy = true as the AI suggests, but instead of applying, treat the hard error as a stop sign and dig into why the plan wants a replacement before doing anything else
options.consequence: The guardrail is correct and now permanent, but you've spent an hour wrestling an aborting apply before realizing the engine_version drift was the culprit all along — the tag ships late, and you got there the slow way around the actual fix.

options.text: Drop in prevent_destroy = true and run terraform apply — the AI says the DB can never be destroyed now, so the change is safe
options.consequence: terraform apply hard-errors and aborts the instant it hits the replacement plan; the engine_version drift is untouched, the deploy is wedged, and the on-call pipeline is now blocked for everyone until someone reads the line you skipped. A guardrail is not a fix.

beats.title: The Page You Were Dreading
beats.situation: You're on the couch when your phone screams: payments API returning 503, pods in CrashLoopBackOff. kubectl logs show 'x509: certificate has expired'. The cert that fronts the internal mTLS between payments and the auth service expired at 21:30. Renewals were supposed to be automated by cert-manager, but this one was a hand-rolled secret from before that existed.
beats.decision: Money is not moving and the customer-status page is about to flip red. What's your move at 10pm?

options.text: Reissue the cert and rotate the secret to restore service now, then before logging off open a PR to bring this cert under cert-manager and write the postmortem with the renewal gap as the action item
options.consequence: Payments recover in 15 minutes. The follow-up PR merges Thursday and cert-manager now auto-renews it 30 days early — this exact expiry can never page anyone again, which is the only kind of fix that actually buys back your evenings.

options.text: Manually generate a new cert with a 1-year expiry, drop it in the secret, restart the pods, and go back to bed — it works, ship it
options.consequence: Service is back in 12 minutes and you sleep, but you've just planted the identical landmine 365 days out with no alert and no runbook. Next year's on-call, possibly you, gets the same 10pm page with even less context.

options.text: Roll back the payments deployment to last week's image hoping it had a longer-lived cert, and escalate to the team channel if it doesn't clear
options.consequence: The cert lives in a Secret, not the image, so the rollback changes nothing — you burn 25 minutes and a real outage while the status page goes red, then have to do the actual cert rotation anyway, now with an angry incident bridge watching.

shift.closer: Nobody thanked you for the four times nothing broke, but you spent the day standing between a one-line diff and a destroyed production database, and you ended it renewing a certificate in your pajamas — that's the job.

title: Machine Learning Engineer
oneLineReality: You spend most of your time cleaning data and plumbing pipelines so a model can run reliably in production; the glamorous modeling is maybe 10% of the job.
typicalDay: Pull and clean a fresh batch of training data; write or fix feature-engineering code in Python and SQL.
Run training experiments, tune hyperparameters, and compare runs in MLflow or Weights & Biases.
Debug why a deployed model's predictions drifted or its latency spiked overnight.
Review a teammate's model-serving pull request and discuss an upcoming A/B test with product.
Write unit tests and data-validation checks so a bad upstream table doesn't silently poison the model.
Attend a short stand-up to align with data engineers and product managers on priorities.
workStyle: Mostly heads-down individual coding and experimentation, punctuated by cross-functional collaboration with data, product, and infra teams. Very remote-friendly, but you may be on-call when a model is in production.
boringHardPart: Roughly 80% of the work is data wrangling and pipeline plumbing, not inventing clever models. The painful part is chasing silent data-quality bugs and reproducing flaky training runs that fail for no obvious reason, which can eat days before you write a single line of model code.
crashCourse: Andrew Ng's Machine Learning Specialization (DeepLearning.AI on Coursera)
Read 'Hands-On Machine Learning with Scikit-Learn, Keras & TensorFlow' by Aurelien Geron
fast.ai 'Practical Deep Learning for Coders'
Get fluent in SQL plus the Python data stack (pandas, numpy)
Build and deploy one model end-to-end: Docker container behind a cloud API endpoint

workSimulation.scenario: You're an ML engineer at a fintech. You built a fraud-detection classifier that scores 0.97 AUC on a random 80/20 test split. Fraud is about 0.5% of all transactions. Product wants to ship it this week.
workSimulation.task: What is the most important thing to verify before deploying?

options.text: Re-split the data with a time-based split (train on past, evaluate on future) and re-measure, because a random split can leak future information and inflate offline metrics.
options.feedback: Correct. Random splits on time-ordered transaction data routinely leak signal from the future into training, producing offline AUC that collapses in production. A temporal split is the honest test of how the model will actually perform.

options.text: Just deploy. A 0.97 AUC is excellent and every day of delay costs the company money.
options.feedback: A high offline AUC on a leaky random split is exactly the trap that ships broken fraud models. Shipping without a temporal validation is how you discover the metric was fiction after the losses pile up.

options.text: Add more features until AUC climbs above 0.98 before doing anything else.
options.feedback: Chasing a higher offline number on a flawed evaluation just makes you more confident in a possibly leaky result. More features cannot fix an invalid validation setup.

options.text: Swap the gradient-boosted trees for a deep neural network, which will generalize better.
options.feedback: Model choice is not the issue here, and deep nets rarely beat gradient-boosted trees on tabular fraud data. This ignores the real risk: an evaluation that may be leaking future information.

workSimulation.aiSuggestion: Your 0.97 AUC is strong. To launch safely, set the classification threshold at the default 0.5 and monitor accuracy in production. Accuracy is the clearest, most intuitive metric for stakeholders to track for a fraud model.
workSimulation.aiMistake: It recommends accuracy as the production metric (with a default 0.5 threshold) for a severely imbalanced problem where fraud is only ~0.5% of transactions. A model that flags nothing scores ~99.5% accuracy while catching zero fraud, so accuracy hides whether the model actually works. The threshold must be tuned to the business cost of false positives versus missed fraud, using precision/recall or PR-AUC.
workSimulation.correctHumanJudgment: A human recognizes the class imbalance, throws out accuracy in favor of precision/recall (or PR-AUC), and tunes the decision threshold to the dollar cost of a missed fraud versus a false alarm rather than accepting the arbitrary 0.5 default.

aiCatchOptions.text: It recommended accuracy as the key metric, which is misleading on a highly imbalanced fraud dataset where the non-fraud class dominates and a do-nothing model still scores ~99.5%.
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Right. On imbalanced data accuracy is dominated by the majority class and tells you nothing about caught fraud. Precision/recall or PR-AUC at a cost-tuned threshold is the correct lens.

aiCatchOptions.text: It chose AUC over log-loss, the only valid metric for probability calibration.
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Wrong target. AUC is a perfectly reasonable ranking metric here, and log-loss is not the 'only valid' metric. The real flaw is recommending accuracy on imbalanced data, not the AUC versus log-loss choice.

aiCatchOptions.text: It assumed gradient-boosted trees when fraud detection requires deep learning.
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Incorrect and irrelevant: the AI never specified a model family, and deep learning is not required for tabular fraud. The actual mistake is the accuracy metric on an imbalanced problem.

Suggesting hyperparameter search spaces and writing config
Auto-producing documentation and unit-test scaffolding
Spinning up AutoML baseline models for quick comparison
humanValue: Framing a fuzzy business problem into a learnable task and picking the right metric
Spotting data leakage, bias, and subtle distribution shifts
Owning trade-offs: latency vs accuracy, cost of false positives vs missed cases
Being accountable for production reliability, fairness, and failure modes
aiImpact.riskNote: AI coding tools make ML engineers much faster but don't replace them: someone must define the problem, validate the data, choose metrics, and own deployment and accountability. The pure glue-code junior work is shrinking, while judgment-heavy and production-ownership roles keep growing.

shift.intro: It's 9:02 a.m., your coffee is still cold, and Slack already has a red alert: last night's fraud model started timing out and product wants the new classifier shipped by Friday.
shift.closer: You wrote zero lines of clever model code today and still did the most important ML work of the week: stopping a confident, broken model from silently waving fraud through.

beats.title: Stand-up triage
beats.situation: In the 15-minute stand-up, the data engineer mentions the upstream `transactions` table reran overnight and a few columns 'might look different.' Product is pushing for the new fraud model this week. You have one day of focus before meetings eat the rest.
beats.decision: What do you make your first priority after stand-up?

options.text: Diff today's `transactions` schema and row counts against yesterday's baseline before touching anything downstream.
options.consequence: You catch that `amount` switched from cents to dollars overnight; fixing it now prevents every feature built on it from being silently wrong for the rest of the week.

options.text: Start retraining on the fresh data right away so you have a model ready for product by lunch.
options.consequence: Training runs fine, but two days later metrics look 'off' and you waste an afternoon discovering the schema drift you could have caught in 10 minutes.

options.text: Assume the data team handled it and jump straight into the model code product is asking for.
options.consequence: The cents-to-dollars shift poisons your features unnoticed; the model ships with garbage inputs and you're debugging a 'mystery' regression on Friday night.

beats.title: The flaky run
beats.situation: Your feature pipeline is fixed, but the same training script gives AUC 0.94 one run and 0.89 the next with identical code and data. The clock is burning and you need a number you can trust.
beats.decision: How do you handle the non-reproducible runs?

options.text: Pin every random seed, log data/version hashes to MLflow, and isolate the source of variance before trusting any score.
options.consequence: You find an unseeded train/test shuffle leaking rows across splits; fixing it gives stable, honest scores you can defend in review.

options.text: Run it five times and just report the average AUC to product.
options.consequence: The average hides a real leakage bug; the model looks decent now but behaves unpredictably once retrained next sprint.

options.text: Take the 0.94 run as the 'real' number and move on—it's the better result anyway.
options.consequence: You cherry-picked a lucky split; production performance lands near 0.89 and a stakeholder asks why the model underdelivers versus your slide.

beats.title: Reviewing the serving PR
beats.situation: A teammate's pull request adds the model-serving endpoint. It loads the model, returns a score, and has one happy-path test. Product wants to merge today to start the A/B test.
beats.decision: What do you push for in review?

options.text: Request input-validation and a fallback for malformed/missing features, plus a test for the bad-input path before merge.
options.consequence: Week two, an upstream null storm hits; the endpoint degrades gracefully instead of 500-ing the checkout flow during peak traffic.

options.text: Approve but file a follow-up ticket to add validation 'next sprint.'
options.consequence: The ticket slips twice; an unhandled null eventually crashes serving for 20 minutes before anyone links it back to the deferred work.

options.text: Approve—tests pass and the latency looks good, ship it.
options.consequence: A malformed feature payload throws an unhandled exception in prod; on-call pages you at 2 a.m. for a bug a single review comment would have caught.

beats.title: The 0.97 AUC deploy call
beats.situation: Your fraud classifier hits 0.97 AUC on a random 80/20 split. Fraud is ~0.5% of transactions. Product wants it live this week and asks the AI assistant how to launch safely.
beats.decision: What is the most important thing to verify before deploying?
beats.aiSuggestion: Your 0.97 AUC is strong. To launch safely, set the classification threshold at the default 0.5 and monitor accuracy in production—accuracy is the clearest, most intuitive metric for stakeholders to track for a fraud model.

options.text: Reject accuracy: evaluate precision/recall and PR-AUC on the imbalanced classes, then tune the threshold to the dollar cost of a missed fraud vs. a false alarm.
options.consequence: You discover the 'great' model catches only 30% of fraud at the 0.5 default; tuning the threshold to business cost turns it into something that actually saves money, not just looks good.

options.text: Keep AUC as the headline but add a precision/recall check at the default 0.5 threshold before shipping.
options.consequence: You spot weak recall but never tune the threshold to cost; the model ships flagging too few frauds, and finance asks in a month why losses barely moved.

options.text: Follow the AI: ship at threshold 0.5 and track accuracy in production as the success metric.
options.consequence: A model flagging almost nothing scores ~99.5% accuracy while letting fraud through; the dashboard glows green for weeks until a chargeback spike exposes that it never worked.

title: Game Developer
oneLineReality: You spend 90% of your time fixing bugs, tuning numbers, and waiting for builds so that players never notice the work you did.
typicalDay: Pull the latest build from Perforce/Git, read overnight QA bug reports, and triage which crashes block today's playtest
Write and debug C# (Unity) or C++ (Unreal) gameplay code: a new enemy behavior, an inventory screen, a save system
Sit in a 15-minute standup, then spend an hour in Jira/Hansoft updating ticket status and estimating tasks
Profile a level that's dropping below 60 FPS and hunt the spike in the frame using the engine profiler
Iterate on 'feel': tweak jump height, camera lag, or hit-stun by 0.05s, rebuild, playtest, repeat a dozen times
Sync with artists and designers on why an asset broke the build, and merge code without stepping on a teammate's branch
workStyle: Mostly collaborative studio or remote team work in sprints; deep solo focus blocks for coding interrupted by frequent cross-discipline syncs with artists, designers, and producers. Heavy reliance on version control and code review.
boringHardPart: The fun ideas are 5% of the job. The other 95% is reproducing a bug that only happens on one player's hardware, waiting 20 minutes for a build to cook, merging branches without conflicts, and re-tuning the same mechanic 40 times because it still doesn't feel right.
keyTools: Blender / Maya (reading and importing art assets)
RenderDoc and the engine frame profiler
crashCourse: Learn one engine deeply: do the official Unity 'Junior Programmer' pathway or Unreal's 'Your First Hour' then build, don't just watch
Master one language for it (C# for Unity, C++ for Unreal) including memory, references vs values, and collections
Understand the game loop: Update vs FixedUpdate, delta time, and why frame-rate-independent code matters
Learn version control early (Git for solo, Perforce for studios) so you don't lose work or break the team build
Finish small games end-to-end (Pong, then a platformer) and ship them on itch.io. A finished tiny game beats an unfinished epic

workSimulation.scenario: You are a gameplay programmer on a 3D platformer. QA files a bug: when the player does a max-height jump and lands on the thin floor of a moving elevator, they occasionally fall straight through it and die. It only happens on fast landings, maybe 1 in 8 times.
workSimulation.task: The player Rigidbody uses default physics settings and the elevator floor is a thin box collider. What is the correct root-cause fix?

options.text: Increase the world's gravity value so the player accelerates downward faster and 'sticks' to the floor sooner.
options.feedback: Wrong direction. More gravity means a HIGHER landing speed, which makes tunneling through the thin collider MORE likely, not less. You'd see the bug more often.

options.text: Switch the player Rigidbody's collision detection from Discrete to Continuous (and/or add a downward raycast for ground), because a fast body skips past a thin collider between fixed physics steps.
options.feedback: Correct. This is classic tunneling: at high velocity the body moves more than its own width in one FixedUpdate, so discrete collision never registers an overlap with the thin floor. Continuous collision detection sweeps the path between steps and catches it.

options.text: Add more polygons to the elevator floor mesh so the collision surface is denser and easier to hit.
options.feedback: Mesh density doesn't change physics stepping. The issue is the body teleporting past the collider between frames, not the collider being too coarse. This wastes memory and fixes nothing.

options.text: Disable the floor collider while the player is airborne and re-enable it on the way down.
options.feedback: Fragile and buggy: timing 'airborne' is exactly what's unreliable here, and a disabled collider means anything else (NPCs, items) also falls through. This trades one race condition for another.

workSimulation.aiSuggestion: Your AI coding assistant says with full confidence: 'Easy fix. Just lower Time.fixedDeltaTime globally to 0.005 so physics runs more often. With a smaller timestep the player can't move far enough to skip the floor, and tunneling is eliminated everywhere in the game.'
workSimulation.aiMistake: Lowering the global fixedDeltaTime is a brute-force mitigation, not a fix. It triples the physics workload for EVERY rigidbody in the game, which tanks frame rate on target hardware (consoles, phones) and can destabilize gameplay feel. It also still doesn't guarantee a fix at very high velocities. The correct fix is targeted Continuous Collision Detection on the one fast body.
workSimulation.correctHumanJudgment: A human runs the engine profiler on the actual target hardware, sees the global timestep change spike CPU time and drop the whole game below 60 FPS, and instead applies Continuous Collision Detection locally to the player Rigidbody, leaving everyone else's physics cheap.

aiCatchOptions.text: Shrinking the global physics timestep multiplies CPU cost for every physics object and still won't reliably stop tunneling at extreme speeds; the right fix is Continuous Collision Detection on just the fast body.
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Right. The AI optimized the wrong scope. It solved a local problem with a global setting, paying a frame-rate tax across the entire game to patch one collider.

aiCatchOptions.text: The AI is wrong because Time.fixedDeltaTime cannot be changed at runtime, so its suggestion won't even compile.
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Incorrect. fixedDeltaTime can be set at runtime. The AI's idea runs fine; the problem is its performance cost, not its legality.

aiCatchOptions.text: The AI is wrong because a smaller timestep reduces effective gravity, so the player would slowly float upward off the elevator.
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Incorrect. A correct physics integrator is timestep-independent for gravity; the player won't float. The real flaw is the global performance hit.

shift.intro: It's 9:14 AM, your coffee is still hot, and overnight QA has filed 23 new bugs with three of them tagged BLOCKER for the 2 PM publisher playtest.
shift.closer: You shipped nothing visible today: you fixed a fall-through bug nobody will ever see, and that invisible save is the whole job.

beats.title: Triage Before Standup
beats.situation: You pull the latest from Perforce and the overnight bug list is a wall of red. Three blockers: a crash on the boss arena load, a save-corruption report from one tester, and a 'player falls through elevator' repro. Standup is in 30 minutes and you can realistically own one before then.
beats.decision: Which blocker do you claim and start reproducing first?

options.text: Repro the boss-arena load crash first, since a crash hard-blocks the entire 2 PM playtest from starting
options.consequence: You catch a null material reference from a bad asset merge; playtest boots clean at 2 PM and the publisher never sees a crash dialog.

options.text: Grab the save-corruption bug because data loss feels scariest, even though only one tester hit it once
options.consequence: Three days later it turns out to be that tester's full disk, not your code; meanwhile the boss crash you skipped ate two hours of the morning.

options.text: Start with the elevator fall-through because it looks the most fun to debug
options.consequence: Playtest opens, the boss arena crashes on load in front of the publisher, and the producer pulls you aside about reading the BLOCKER tags.

beats.title: Merge Without Blood
beats.situation: Your crash fix is ready, but an artist pushed a 400-file scene change to the same branch an hour ago and the inventory designer is mid-merge on overlapping prefabs. You need your one-line fix in before the playtest build cooks at 12:30.
beats.decision: How do you land your fix without breaking the build for everyone?

options.text: Pull latest, resolve conflicts locally, run the scene and a quick smoke test, then commit only your changed files
options.consequence: Clean integration; the 12:30 build cooks green and three teammates keep working without ever noticing your change.

options.text: Ping the artist and designer to pause, then commit, but skip the local smoke test to save ten minutes
options.consequence: It merges fine but a prefab reference silently breaks; QA flags it tomorrow morning and you spend an hour re-bisecting your own commit.

options.text: Force your version over theirs with 'accept yours' on all conflicts to push it through fast
options.consequence: You clobber the artist's scene work; the build cooks without their assets, the playtest looks unfinished, and the artist redoes a morning of work.

beats.title: The Elevator That Eats Players
beats.situation: Playtest survived, but the elevator bug is now yours. On a max-height jump landing on the thin floor of a moving elevator, the player Rigidbody falls straight through and dies, about 1 in 8 fast landings. The Rigidbody uses default physics and the floor is a thin box collider. Your AI assistant has an instant answer.
beats.decision: What is the correct root-cause fix for the tunneling?
beats.aiSuggestion: Easy fix. Just lower Time.fixedDeltaTime globally to 0.005 so physics runs more often. With a smaller timestep the player can't move far enough to skip the floor, and tunneling is eliminated everywhere in the game.

options.text: Set the player Rigidbody's Collision Detection to Continuous and leave every other body's physics untouched
options.consequence: Tunneling stops at any velocity, frame budget is unchanged, and the fix survives certification on console and phone hardware.

options.text: Try the global timestep first but profile on target hardware before committing it
options.consequence: The profiler shows physics CPU time tripling and the game dropping under 60 FPS on console, so you back it out and burn an afternoon arriving at CCD anyway.

options.text: Trust the AI and lower Time.fixedDeltaTime to 0.005 globally because it claims to fix tunneling everywhere
options.consequence: Bug seems gone on your beefy PC, but the console build tanks to 38 FPS; QA reopens it as a perf blocker two weeks before cert and you re-do the fix under pressure.

beats.title: Forty Takes for One Jump
beats.situation: Bug closed, but the lead says the jump still 'feels floaty.' You've already rebuilt and re-tuned jump height, gravity scale, and hang-time eleven times this week. Each tweak is a 6-minute rebuild and a playtest lap, and it's the end of the day.
beats.decision: How do you handle the feel iteration without burning out or shipping mush?

options.text: Expose jump height, gravity, and hang-time as live-tunable values so you adjust in play mode without a rebuild, then lock the numbers with the lead
options.consequence: You nail the feel in 20 minutes of live tuning; the designer reuses the same sliders next sprint and your rebuild count drops to near zero.

options.text: Keep doing full rebuild-and-playtest laps but write down every value you try so you don't loop
options.consequence: You land a decent jump by 7 PM, but you're an hour late and tomorrow's coast-time tweak means another round of slow rebuilds.

options.text: Bump jump height a flat 20%, call it 'snappier,' and commit without a playtest because you're tired
options.consequence: The higher arc now clips players into a low ceiling in two levels; QA files a fresh blocker overnight and you start tomorrow undoing today's shortcut.

title: Product Manager
oneLineReality: You own the "what" and "why" of a product but have authority over none of the people who build it — so most of the job is influence, trade-off decisions, and saying no with a smile.
typicalDay: Stand-up with engineering and design to unblock the current sprint and re-clarify scope on the two tickets that drifted overnight
Read raw user feedback, support tickets, and a Mixpanel/Amplitude funnel to decide whether last week's release actually moved the metric it was supposed to
Write or refine a PRD (product requirements doc) and an Eng+Design review to pressure-test the spec before anyone writes code
Stakeholder management: a 30-minute meeting where sales wants Feature X for one big client, marketing wants Y for launch, and you say no to both with data
Prioritization: re-rank the backlog against the quarter's goal because a competitor shipped something and a key assumption just broke
Demo prep and a written update to leadership translating engineering progress into business outcomes
workStyle: Hybrid desk-and-meeting job inside a cross-functional team (engineers, designers, data, marketing, sales). You have responsibility for outcomes but no direct reports building the product, so you lead through writing, data, and persuasion. Heavy context-switching; calendar is fragmented; the real thinking work often happens before 10am or after 5pm.
boringHardPart: The unglamorous core is endless prioritization and saying no — to good ideas, loud stakeholders, and your own pet features — while documenting the reasoning so nobody relitigates it next week. You get blamed for missed dates you didn't control and rarely get credit for the features you killed that would have wasted six engineer-months.
keyTools: SQL (pulling your own usage data instead of waiting on a data team)
Slack + a roadmap tool like Productboard or Aha!
crashCourse: Read 'Inspired' by Marty Cagan to learn how strong product teams actually decide what to build
Learn one analytics tool well enough to build a funnel and read retention curves (Amplitude has a free academy)
Learn enough SQL to answer your own 'how many users did X' questions in 10 minutes
Write one real PRD for a feature of an app you use daily: problem, users, success metric, scope, non-goals
Understand A/B testing fundamentals: statistical significance, guardrail metrics, novelty effects, and why a 2-week test can't measure 30-day retention

workSimulation.scenario: You're an Associate PM on a subscription mobile app (8M monthly users). You ran a 2-week A/B test on a redesigned onboarding flow. Results: Variant B raised signup conversion from 8.0% to 9.2% (statistically significant, p=0.03). But the dashboard also shows 30-day retention for Variant B at 38% versus 42% for the control, and the experiment has only been live for 14 days.
workSimulation.task: Leadership wants a recommendation by end of day. What do you do with Variant B?

options.text: Ship Variant B to 100% now — conversion is the north-star metric and the lift is statistically significant.
options.feedback: Tempting, but you'd be acting on a retention number that literally cannot exist yet, and trading a real top-of-funnel gain for a possibly larger downstream loss. More signups at lower retention can mean fewer net active users.

options.text: Hold the rollout, extend the experiment so real cohorts can reach a full 30 days, and dig into why early retention looks lower before deciding.
options.feedback: Correct. The conversion win is real and worth pursuing, but no test cohort has actually been around 30 days, so the retention figure is incomplete, not a verdict. Extending the test and investigating protects long-term value (LTV) instead of optimizing a vanity step.

options.text: Kill Variant B entirely and move on to the next item in the backlog.
options.feedback: Premature. A statistically significant conversion lift is a genuine signal; throwing it away because of an unmeasurable retention number wastes a promising result. The right move is more data, not abandonment.

options.text: Ship Variant B to 50% of traffic and leave both versions running indefinitely.
options.feedback: This dodges the decision. Running forever dilutes your test power, doubles maintenance and QA surface, and you still never get a clean 30-day read. Indecision is itself a (costly) decision.

workSimulation.aiSuggestion: Your AI copilot writes: 'Ship Variant B. You lifted conversion 1.2 points at p=0.03 — that's a ~15% relative gain, which at your traffic is thousands of extra signups per month. The 4-point retention dip is small and almost certainly statistical noise; conversion is the metric leadership reports, so the EV is clearly positive. Roll it out.'
workSimulation.aiMistake: The AI labels the 30-day retention drop as 'statistical noise,' but the experiment has only run 14 days — no user in the test has been enrolled long enough to have a real 30-day retention outcome. That 38% is an incomplete/extrapolated figure, not noise, so it cannot be dismissed on statistical grounds the way the AI implies.
workSimulation.correctHumanJudgment: A human PM notices the timeline contradiction: you can't measure 30-day retention in a 14-day test. Instead of dismissing the number, they treat it as 'unknown, possibly bad,' weigh a 1.2-point conversion gain against a potential 4-point retention loss spread over a larger base (which can be net-negative for active users and LTV), and choose to extend the test rather than ship.

aiCatchOptions.text: The AI dismissed the retention drop as noise, but 30-day retention can't be measured at all after only a 14-day test — the number is incomplete data, not noise.
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Right. The flaw is the timeline: the AI applied a statistical-noise argument to a metric that has no valid value yet, which is the exact trap a careful PM catches.

aiCatchOptions.text: The AI was wrong that p=0.03 is significant; that p-value fails the standard 0.05 threshold.
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Incorrect. p=0.03 is below 0.05, so the conversion result is statistically significant. The real problem is the retention claim, not the significance of conversion.

aiCatchOptions.text: The AI was wrong to treat conversion as a meaningful metric; conversion is a vanity metric with no business value.
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Incorrect. Signup conversion is a legitimate, valuable metric. The error isn't caring about conversion — it's mischaracterizing the unmeasurable retention figure as noise.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 1: Learn the language
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Read 'Inspired' (Cagan) and Lenny's Newsletter archives. Write down the difference between outputs (features shipped) and outcomes (metrics moved) until it's second nature.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 1-2: Pick a product and teardown
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Choose an app you use daily. Write a 2-page teardown: who the users are, the core job-to-be-done, the funnel, and three weaknesses you'd fix first and why.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 2-3: Learn the data tools
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Complete Amplitude Academy's free analytics course and a beginner SQL course (Mode or SQLZoo). Goal: build one funnel and answer one 'how many users did X' question yourself.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 3: Write a real PRD (mini project)
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Spec one new feature for your chosen app: problem statement, target user, success metric + guardrail metric, scope, explicit non-goals, and an A/B test plan. This is your portfolio centerpiece.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 4: Pressure-test and network
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Get your PRD critiqued by two people (a developer friend and a designer if possible). Do 3 informational interviews with working PMs; ask what they'd cut from your spec.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 4: Apply the AI edge
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Use AI to draft user stories and summarize reviews for your feature, then document where it was wrong — bring that 'here's how I catch AI mistakes' story to interviews.

certificate.name: Product School — Product Manager Certification (PMC)

automates: Drafting first-pass PRDs, release notes, and meeting summaries from notes
Summarizing hundreds of support tickets and reviews into themes
Writing and even debugging SQL queries for ad-hoc data pulls
Generating user-story drafts, edge cases, and competitive-feature comparison tables
Producing first drafts of stakeholder updates and launch announcements
humanValue: Deciding what NOT to build and owning that trade-off when stakeholders push back
Reading the room: aligning sales, eng, design, and leadership who all want different things
Judging whether a metric move is real, causal, and worth a strategic bet
Setting product vision and sequencing a roadmap against shifting market reality
Taking accountability when a launch fails — a responsibility AI cannot hold
aiImpact.riskNote: AI is a powerful accelerator for the writing, data-pulling, and synthesis parts of PM work, and it is compressing the number of junior PMs a team needs. But the core — cross-functional judgment, prioritization under ambiguity, stakeholder trust, and owning outcomes — resists automation. The risk is less 'PMs replaced' and more 'fewer entry-level seats, higher bar to break in,' so the AI-literate PM has an edge over one who ignores it.

shift.intro: It's 8:52am, your coffee is still too hot, and Slack already has 14 unreads — two sprint tickets quietly mutated overnight and leadership wants an onboarding call by 5pm.
shift.closer: You shipped nothing, wrote three paragraphs, and said no four times — and the day's real win was a number you refused to trust.

beats.title: Stand-up, and two tickets drifted
beats.situation: In stand-up, the lead engineer says the 'save filters' ticket grew overnight — design quietly added a sync-across-devices requirement nobody scoped. Eng estimates it now eats half the sprint. Six people are staring at you waiting to know if that's okay.
beats.decision: How do you handle the scope that crept in overnight?

options.text: Cut sync out of this sprint, ship local-only saved filters now, and log sync as its own ticket with a one-line rationale in the PRD.
options.consequence: The team hits the sprint date; three weeks later when sync comes up again, your written note kills a re-litigation in 30 seconds.

options.text: Keep the bigger scope — sync is clearly better — and let the sprint slip a few days to do it right.
options.consequence: Quality is fine but the slip cascades into the next sprint; in retro you eat the 'why did we commit to a date we missed' question.

options.text: Tell engineering to 'just figure out how to fit it all in' and move on to the next ticket.
options.consequence: Eng silently cuts test coverage to make the date; a sync bug ships to 8M users and the on-call hates you by Thursday.

beats.title: Did last week's release actually work?
beats.situation: Last week you shipped a streamlined checkout. Support tickets are up slightly and three loud users hate the new layout. But the Amplitude funnel for checkout completion looks flat-to-up. Marketing is already asking if they can 'announce the win.'
beats.decision: What do you tell marketing about the release?

options.text: Pull the funnel yourself, segment by new-vs-returning users, and say 'completion is up 0.4pt for new users, flat for returning — not announce-worthy yet, give it a week.'
options.consequence: You catch that the gain is real but tiny; marketing holds the blog post and avoids a credibility hit when the lift doesn't hold.

options.text: The funnel's up and tickets are just a vocal minority — tell marketing to go ahead and announce.
options.consequence: The announcement ships; the 'win' is within noise and a competitor's data-savvy PM subtweets your inflated number.

options.text: The three angry users scared you — tell marketing to hold and quietly consider rolling it back.
options.consequence: You rollback a release that was actually fine, burning an eng day and signaling to the team that loud feedback beats data.

beats.title: The onboarding A/B test, due at 5
beats.situation: Your 2-week A/B test on the redesigned onboarding is in. Variant B lifted signup conversion 8.0% to 9.2% (p=0.03). But the dashboard also shows Variant B's 30-day retention at 38% vs control's 42% — and the test has only been live 14 days. Leadership wants a ship/no-ship by end of day.
beats.decision: What's your recommendation on Variant B?
beats.aiSuggestion: Ship Variant B. You lifted conversion 1.2 points at p=0.03 — that's a ~15% relative gain, which at your traffic is thousands of extra signups per month. The 4-point retention dip is small and almost certainly statistical noise; conversion is the metric leadership reports, so the EV is clearly positive. Roll it out.

options.text: Flag that a 14-day test can't have a real 30-day retention number — that 38% is incomplete, not noise. Recommend extending the test to read true retention before shipping.
options.consequence: Two weeks later the matured cohort shows retention really did drop to 39%; your hold saves an LTV hit across millions of users and leadership trusts your judgment.

options.text: Ship B but instrument a retention guardrail and commit to rolling back if 30-day retention stays below control after a month.
options.consequence: You ship a possibly-harmful change to all users first and measure later; the rollback is messy and you spend a sprint cleaning up cohorts.

options.text: Follow the copilot — conversion's the headline metric, the retention dip is noise. Ship Variant B today.
options.consequence: A month later matured data shows real retention erosion; churn quietly rises, the conversion 'win' is net-negative on LTV, and you own it.

beats.title: Sales and marketing both want a yes
beats.situation: A 30-minute stakeholder meeting: Sales wants Feature X promised to a whale client by next month; Marketing wants Feature Y for the launch campaign. Both block the quarter's retention goal. You have 20 minutes and a leadership update to write after.
beats.decision: How do you close the meeting?

options.text: Say no to both with the quarter goal on screen, show how X and Y each trade against retention, and offer Sales a lightweight workaround for the one client instead.
options.consequence: Both leave unhappy but unable to argue; the whale gets unblocked without derailing the roadmap, and your written rationale ends the debate.

options.text: Take both as 'maybe next quarter' and promise to 'look into it' to keep the room calm.
options.consequence: You dodge the conflict now but both stakeholders escalate to your VP Friday, and you defend a non-decision you never made.

options.text: Give Sales the whale feature — it's real revenue — and quietly bump a retention item to make room.
options.consequence: You miss the quarter's retention goal you're measured on, and the whale churns anyway after the contract; you get the blame for both.

title: Marketing Manager
oneLineReality: You own a number (leads, revenue, signups) and spend your days fighting to move it with limited budget, while defending every dollar to a CFO who thinks marketing is "just the logo people."
typicalDay: Open dashboards (GA4, ad platforms, CRM) and check yesterday's numbers against the monthly target before the inbox swallows you
Run a campaign stand-up: review what's live, what's stuck in design/legal review, and what's launching this week
Sit in a budget or pipeline meeting defending spend and explaining why a channel did/didn't perform to sales and finance
Review creative drafts, ad copy, and landing pages — sending most back with notes because the CTA or message is off
Pull a performance report, find the one metric that moved, and decide where to shift next week's budget
Field a last-minute 'can you make this go viral' request from an executive and translate it into something measurable
workStyle: Hybrid office work, heavy in meetings and shared docs; cross-functional (sales, product, design, finance, agencies). Deadline-driven around launches and quarter-ends. Mostly collaborative, but you carry a number alone.
boringHardPart: Attribution and reporting. Proving which channel actually caused a sale is messy, never clean, and you spend hours reconciling numbers across tools that disagree — then explaining the gap to people who want one simple answer that doesn't exist.
keyTools: Google Looker Studio / Tableau for dashboards
crashCourse: Learn the funnel: awareness to consideration to conversion to retention, and which metric matters at each stage
Master one analytics tool (GA4) until you can read a report without panicking
Understand CAC and LTV — customer acquisition cost vs lifetime value is the math that gets you taken seriously
Run a real A/B test on something (email subject line, ad creative) and read the result honestly
Learn paid vs organic vs owned channels and what each realistically costs and returns

workSimulation.scenario: You're a marketing manager at a mid-size B2B SaaS company. Last month you launched a paid LinkedIn campaign and a big SEO/blog content push in the same week. Total inbound leads jumped 40% month-over-month. The CEO is thrilled and emails you: 'LinkedIn is clearly working — double its budget next month.'
workSimulation.task: LinkedIn shows 1,200 clicks and 80 leads last month. SEO traffic also rose sharply in the same period. Before you reallocate next month's budget, what's the right first move?

options.text: Double the LinkedIn budget immediately — leads are up 40%, ride the momentum while it's hot
options.feedback: This is exactly the trap. Two channels launched at once, so you can't credit the lift to LinkedIn alone. Doubling spend on an unproven assumption is how marketing budgets get torched.

options.text: Pull multi-touch attribution and lead-quality data to see which channel actually drove the lift, and whether those leads convert, before reallocating
options.feedback: Correct. You isolate contribution (did SEO assist or drive these leads?) and check lead quality (MQL vs SQL, pipeline created). Reallocation decisions follow evidence, not correlation or the loudest stakeholder.

options.text: Cut the SEO budget entirely and move it all to LinkedIn since LinkedIn is the obvious winner
options.feedback: You have zero proof SEO didn't drive most of the lift — and SEO compounds over time. Killing it on a hunch could remove the very thing that caused the surge.

options.text: Split the budget increase evenly across every channel to stay safe
options.feedback: Spreading money evenly with no evidence isn't safe, it's just indecision. You'd under-fund whatever is actually working and over-fund what isn't.

workSimulation.aiSuggestion: The AI marketing assistant says: 'Based on the data, LinkedIn delivered 80 leads from 1,200 clicks — a 6.7% conversion rate, which is strong. To maximize ROI, reallocate 80% of next month's budget to LinkedIn and scale the winning campaign.'
workSimulation.aiMistake: The AI credits all 80 leads to LinkedIn using single-channel (last-touch) volume, ignoring that the SEO push ran simultaneously and likely assisted or drove many of those same leads via multi-touch journeys. It also treats raw leads as the goal, ignoring lead quality (MQL vs SQL) and downstream pipeline/revenue — so its 6.7% looks impressive but may be low-intent traffic.
workSimulation.correctHumanJudgment: A human pulls a multi-touch attribution report and the CRM to see how many of those 80 leads also touched SEO content and how many became real sales-qualified pipeline. Only then do you size the budget — often you find SEO assisted most conversions and LinkedIn's true incremental contribution is far smaller than the headline number.

aiCatchOptions.text: It relied on single-channel/last-touch numbers and ignored that the simultaneous SEO push likely assisted or drove many of the same leads, overcrediting LinkedIn
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Right. The fatal flaw is attribution: with two channels launched together, last-touch volume can't prove LinkedIn caused the lift, and it ignores assisted conversions plus lead quality.

aiCatchOptions.text: It miscalculated the conversion rate — 80 leads from 1,200 clicks is not 6.7%
aiCatchOptions.feedback: The math is actually correct (80 / 1,200 = 6.7%). The problem isn't arithmetic, it's what that number is being credited to.

aiCatchOptions.text: It failed to include the cost-per-click, so ROI can't be calculated at all
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Plausible-sounding but not the core flaw. Even with perfect CPC data, the attribution and lead-quality blind spot would still make the recommendation wrong.
