typicalDegree: Bachelor's degree in interior design (CIDA-accredited program strongly preferred); many states require licensure/registration tied to the NCIDQ exam

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 1 — Learn the tools
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Install SketchUp (free) and start AutoCAD's free student license. Complete a beginner tutorial and draw one room of your home to scale with accurate dimensions.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 1-2 — Master human dimensions & code basics
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Study clearance and ergonomic standards (accessible 36" paths, counter/seat heights, door swings) and skim ADA interior basics. Make a one-page cheat sheet you actually reference.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 2 — Train your eye
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Build a curated reference library: save 50 interiors you admire and label WHY each works (light, proportion, palette, material). Follow 5 working designers and read how they describe choices.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 3 — Mini project: redesign one real room
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Pick a real room. Produce a measured floor plan, a mood board, and a full FF&E schedule — every item with source, size, finish, and price — totaled to a fixed budget you set.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 4 — Render and present
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Create a simple rendered 'after' of your room in SketchUp + Enscape (or Photoshop), then assemble a clean 3-page presentation (before / plan + board / after) as the first piece of your portfolio.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 4 — Map the credential path
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Research CIDA-accredited programs near you and read the NCIDQ requirements and your state's licensing rules, so you know the real timeline from student to registered designer.

certificate.name: NCIDQ Certification (Council for Interior Design Qualification exam)

automates: Generating photoreal renderings and style variations from a rough sketch or plan
First-draft mood boards and color/material palettes
Quick space-planning and furniture-layout options
Drafting product spec descriptions and client-facing presentation copy
humanValue: Reading a client's real needs, taste, and budget — and earning their trust through a long, messy project
Verifying code, ADA, slip-resistance, fire-rating, and real-world performance of materials
Sourcing and negotiating with vendors and trades, and solving problems on a live job site
Owning accountability when something is wrong on site — AI can't stand in the room and fix it
aiImpact.riskNote: AI is rapidly automating the visual front-end — renderings, mood boards, and layout options — which compresses junior 'make it pretty' tasks and raises client expectations for speed. But the defensible core (measuring real spaces, code/accessibility compliance, FF&E procurement, vendor/contractor management, and on-site accountability) resists automation. Risk is moderate: the tools change the workflow more than they eliminate the role, but designers who only style and don't manage projects are exposed.

shift.intro: It's the boutique hotel lobby project, install is sixteen days out, and the principal designer just dropped the whole package on your desk with the words 'you've got this' before walking into a client lunch.
shift.closer: The shift was 10% beautiful stone and 90% chasing lead times, defending a number you didn't pick, and catching one spec line that would have quietly become a lawsuit.

beats.title: The Vague Wish
beats.situation: You're walking the empty lobby with the hotel owner, tape measure in hand. She gestures at the gutted vestibule and says, 'I want it to feel cozy but modern — boutique, not corporate. You know?' Her facilities manager stands behind her, arms crossed, muttering about 'whatever's easy to clean.'
beats.decision: How do you turn 'cozy but modern' into something you can actually draw and budget?

options.text: Pull out your phone, show her 3 reference images, and ask her to react — then nail down hard numbers: budget ceiling, opening date, daily guest count, and the cleaning crew's reality.
options.consequence: Three weeks later when she says 'this isn't what I pictured,' you open the signed program doc and the saved images — the scope creep conversation lasts four minutes instead of derailing the install.

options.text: Take careful measurements and write down her exact words to interpret later at your desk, where you can think without the client hovering.
options.consequence: Your measurements are perfect but 'cozy but modern' meant warm wood to you and white marble to her — you discover the gap two design rounds and one unbillable revision later.

options.text: Reassure her you've got the vision, snap a few wide phone photos, and promise a stunning concept board by Friday — keep the energy high and move fast.
options.consequence: Friday's board wows her aesthetically but ignores the facilities manager's cleaning concern; he kills your fabric choices in front of the owner and your credibility takes the hit.

beats.title: The Clearance Nobody Sees
beats.situation: Back in Revit, you're laying out the reception desk and a banquette seating cluster. The layout looks gorgeous and the owner will love how intimate it feels — but the path from the accessible entry to the front desk now squeezes to 34 inches past the banquette, and there's a 1.5-inch threshold at the vestibule.
beats.decision: The pretty layout pinches the accessible route. What do you do?

options.text: Re-anchor the banquette to hold a 36-inch minimum clear path and a 60-inch turning circle at the desk, and spec a beveled threshold under 1/2 inch — then re-render to prove it still feels intimate.
options.consequence: At the city inspection before opening, the accessibility path passes on the first walk-through; the GC, who expected a punch-list fight, starts actually trusting your drawings.

options.text: Keep the layout but add a note on the plan flagging the tight path for the contractor to 'resolve in the field' during install.
options.consequence: The contractor 'resolves it' by shoving the banquette 14 inches sideways on install day, breaking your symmetry and the power/data stub-up location you'd coordinated — it photographs crooked forever.

options.text: Leave it — 34 inches is basically 36, and a luxury boutique isn't a hospital. Prioritize the look and keep the intimate footprint.
options.consequence: Inspector red-tags the egress path two days before opening; you eat a rush re-order on a shorter banquette and a weekend of overtime, and the delay makes the soft-opening date slip.

beats.title: The Floor at the Door
beats.situation: Finishes are due to the client tonight. The owner is in love with a warm, honed French limestone for the lobby. The entry vestibule opens straight onto the street — guests will track in rain, snow, road salt, and grit every single day. You ask your AI design assistant to spec the entry flooring.
beats.decision: What flooring do you put down at the wet, street-facing entry?
beats.aiSuggestion: Use the honed French limestone across the entire lobby including the vestibule. It's a warm, high-end natural stone, it photographs beautifully, and it keeps you on budget.

options.text: Pull the limestone's tested DCOF value and porosity data first — it fails wet-slip (ANSI A326.3) and stains/etches under salt and water — so reserve it for a dry decorative zone and spec a wet-rated porcelain (DCOF ≥ 0.42) at the vestibule and walk-off threshold.
options.consequence: Two winters later the entry porcelain still looks new and nobody has slipped; the limestone lounge zone stays pristine because water never reaches it — the owner refers you to her next property.

options.text: Keep limestone for the visible lobby but ask the vendor to confirm it's 'okay for entries,' and add a sealer note to the spec to handle the moisture.
options.consequence: The sales rep says 'sure, people use it,' so you run it — within four months the vestibule stone is etched white from salt and dull from constant resealing the owner refuses to keep paying for; you're back specifying a replacement on your own dime of goodwill.

options.text: Take the AI's recommendation — run the honed limestone wall-to-wall through the vestibule. It's warm, on budget, and the renders look incredible.
options.consequence: Opening week a guest slips on the wet stone and the hotel's insurer pulls your spec sheet; the limestone gets ripped out and replaced under a liability claim, and your firm's name is on the document that approved it.

beats.title: Half the Order, Wrong Box
beats.situation: Eleven days to install. The freight delivery you've been chasing finally arrives: of 14 custom lounge chairs, only 9 came, two of those have gouged frames, and the upholstery on the good ones reads a half-shade off your approved sample. The vendor's lead time on a re-order is 6 weeks. Your install date is locked.
beats.decision: The order is short, damaged, and off-spec with no time to spare. What's your move?

options.text: Document everything with photos against the approved sample and PO, file the damage/shortage claim today, and source an in-stock acceptable substitute for the missing/damaged units so the room reads complete on opening day.
options.consequence: The claim is approved because your spec sheet and dated photos are airtight; the substitute chairs blend in, the room opens full, and the credit covers the swap — your margin survives.

options.text: Accept the 9 good-enough chairs, place the re-order for 5 more, and stage the lobby slightly under-furnished for opening, planning to complete it in 6 weeks.
options.consequence: Opening-day photos — the ones that sell the hotel for a year — show a sparse lobby; the owner is unhappy, and the half-shade color mismatch becomes obvious once all 14 finally sit together.

options.text: It's close enough — keep all 9 including the gouged ones facing the wall, skip the paperwork to save time, and just hope the rest show up before anyone notices.
options.consequence: The claim window lapses unfiled, so the vendor denies the damage credit; your firm eats the cost of 5 chairs plus the gouged two, turning a profitable project into a loss.

title: Journalist / Reporter
oneLineReality: You chase facts on deadline for modest pay in a shrinking industry, where the work is meaningful but the paychecks, job security, and sleep often are not.
typicalDay: Scan the morning budget, police scanner, X/social feeds, and press releases to pitch or get assigned a story
Work the phones and email to line up interviews; show up in person to a council meeting, courthouse, crime scene, or game
Interview sources, take notes and record audio, and file public-records (FOIA) requests for documents
Write and rewrite the piece against a hard deadline while an editor pushes back on holes and unclear lines
Fact-check names, titles, numbers, and quotes; add headline, photos, and post to the CMS
Monitor reaction, chase corrections, and start digging on tomorrow's story
workStyle: Deadline-driven and largely autonomous in the field, but tightly accountable to an editor and to the facts. A mix of solo reporting and tense back-and-forth on accuracy, framing, and fairness. Hours are irregular: nights, weekends, and whatever breaking news demands.
boringHardPart: The romantic image is breaking news; the real grind is sitting through four-hour public meetings, transcribing interviews, waiting weeks for records requests, and writing the same routine police-blotter and earnings briefs over and over while being paid little and watching colleagues get laid off.
keyTools: Otter.ai / Trint transcription and a digital recorder
Muck Rack and X (Twitter) for sourcing and distribution
Spreadsheets (Excel/Google Sheets) for data and budgets
crashCourse: Learn the inverted pyramid: lede first, then facts in order of importance
Master AP style and clean, libel-aware writing
Practice interviewing: open-ended questions, then nail down specifics and quotes
Learn to read a public budget, file a FOIA request, and verify a claim with primary documents
Build clips: pitch and publish for a student paper, local outlet, or your own newsletter

workSimulation.scenario: You cover city hall for a midsize daily. The council just voted 5-2 to raise the property tax rate. As the meeting breaks up, Councilmember Jane Ruiz tells you on the record: 'This is the first tax increase in a decade.' Your editor wants the story online in 30 minutes.
workSimulation.task: How do you handle Ruiz's 'first increase in a decade' claim before you publish?

options.text: Pull up the city's past budget ordinances or call the finance office to confirm the claim, and if you can't verify it in time, attribute it clearly to Ruiz rather than stating it as fact.
options.feedback: Correct. A source asserting something does not make it true. You verify with primary records when you can, and when the clock beats you, you attribute the claim so readers know it's the councilmember's assertion, not a confirmed fact. That's the core discipline of the job.

options.text: Publish it as a flat statement of fact in your own voice: 'The increase is the first in ten years.'
options.feedback: Dangerous. You'd be vouching for a politician's self-serving claim with the paper's credibility. If records show a 2019 increase you just printed a falsehood and handed Ruiz free spin. Never launder an unverified claim into your own voice.

options.text: Cut the claim entirely to play it safe and just report the vote.
options.feedback: Overcautious and lazy. The historical context is newsworthy and easy to handle correctly. Verification or attribution solves the problem; deletion just strips useful information readers want.

options.text: Call another councilmember for their opinion on whether it's really the first increase in a decade and print both views.
options.feedback: This is false balance. Whether the rate rose in the last ten years is a checkable fact in the budget records, not a matter of dueling opinions. Treating a factual question as he-said-she-said misleads readers.

workSimulation.aiSuggestion: The AI writing assistant drafts your lede: 'The City Council voted 5-2 Tuesday to raise the property tax rate, the first increase in a decade, a move that will cost the average homeowner about $400 more per year.'
workSimulation.aiMistake: The '$400 more per year' figure was never stated by any source or document. The AI generated a plausible-sounding dollar impact by inferring it, and it also folded Ruiz's unverified 'first in a decade' claim into the paper's own voice.
workSimulation.correctHumanJudgment: Strip the fabricated $400 number unless an official source or the budget document actually supports it, and attribute the 'first in a decade' line to Ruiz until verified. Ask the AI for its source for $400; it can't produce one, which exposes it as invented.

aiCatchOptions.text: The AI invented the '$400 more per year' homeowner cost figure that no source or document actually provided.
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Right. That specific dollar impact appears in no record and was stated by no one. The AI manufactured a confident, precise-sounding number, exactly the kind of hallucinated statistic that gets reporters and outlets burned.

aiCatchOptions.text: The AI used the wrong vote count; the council voted 7-0, not 5-2.
aiCatchOptions.feedback: No. The 5-2 count was given in the scenario and the AI reproduced it correctly. The flaw is the fabricated cost figure, not the vote tally.

aiCatchOptions.text: The AI wrote in passive voice, which violates AP style.
aiCatchOptions.feedback: No. 'The City Council voted' is active voice, and a style preference wouldn't be the serious problem here anyway. The real issue is a fabricated fact, not phrasing.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Learn the format
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Read 'The Elements of Journalism' and study AP style basics. Rewrite three real news events into tight inverted-pyramid stories and compare against how a pro outlet covered them.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Practice interviewing
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Interview two people in your community (a small-business owner, a local official). Record with permission, transcribe, and pull three clean, accurate quotes.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Learn public records
thirtyDayPlan.detail: File one real FOIA/public-records request with a local agency. Track it and learn what's public, what's redactable, and how long it takes.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Read a budget
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Download your city or school district's published budget and write a 400-word explainer of where the money goes, citing specific line items.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Mini project: publish a real story
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Report, write, and publish one ~600-word local news story to a student paper, community blog, or your own newsletter, with at least two on-the-record sources and verified facts. This becomes your first clip.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Build the portfolio and network
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Make a simple online clips page, set up a Muck Rack profile, and pitch two more stories or apply to one local-news internship or freelance outlet.

automates: Transcribing interviews and meeting audio
Drafting routine briefs: earnings, box scores, weather, police blotter, obituaries
Summarizing long documents, reports, and meeting agendas
Generating headlines and SEO/social copy variants
First-pass copyediting and AP-style fixes
humanValue: Showing up in person to witness events and read a room
Cultivating human sources who trust you with sensitive information
Verifying claims against primary documents and on-the-record people
Investigative digging that connects dots no dataset hands you
Ethical judgment on fairness, harm, anonymity, and what to publish
Accountability: a real byline that can be sued, corrected, and trusted
aiImpact.riskNote: AI already churns out commodity content (briefs, summaries, aggregation), which guts the entry-level rewrite jobs that used to train reporters and accelerates an industry already cutting staff. But original reporting, source relationships, physical presence, and legal accountability cannot be automated, so the work shifts toward verification and shoe-leather reporting rather than disappearing.

shift.intro: It's 6:40 a.m., your phone is buzzing with a police-scanner alert and a Slack from your editor, and you haven't even found pants that match yet.
shift.closer: You filed three stories, ate lunch at your keyboard, sat through a meeting longer than a feature film, and made $43 before taxes for the privilege of being right when it mattered.

beats.title: The Morning Budget
beats.situation: The scanner crackles about a warehouse fire across town. Meanwhile the city clerk just dropped a 90-page agenda packet for tonight's council meeting, and a tip email claims a local nonprofit is missing funds. Your editor is in the standup in 20 minutes and wants to know what you're chasing today.
beats.decision: What do you pitch as your day's lead?

options.text: Skim the council packet now, flag the tax-rate item as the likely lead, and pitch the fire as a quick web brief while you confirm the nonprofit tip on the side
options.consequence: Spotting the tax item early means you arrive at the meeting already knowing the numbers; your 5 p.m. story is sharper than the TV crews who walked in cold.

options.text: Chase the warehouse fire all morning because breaking news feels urgent and exciting
options.consequence: You get decent fire photos, but it was an empty building with no injuries; by noon it's a 200-word brief and you've burned the hours you needed to prep for the real story tonight.

options.text: Pitch the unverified nonprofit 'missing funds' tip as your splashy lead before making a single call
options.consequence: Your editor asks 'who's your source?' and you have nothing; she kills the pitch and now eyes your judgment for the rest of the week.

beats.title: Working the Phones
beats.situation: The nonprofit story has legs. The executive director won't call back. A board member hints by text that two grants were 'reallocated.' To prove anything you'd need the audited financials, which are public record but require a formal request that can take weeks.
beats.decision: How do you nail down the nonprofit money trail?

options.text: File the public-records request today in writing, AND pull the nonprofit's already-public IRS Form 990 online to source the numbers you can confirm right now
options.consequence: The 990 gives you two on-the-record figures to publish this week, and the records request you filed lands documents a month later that break the bigger story.

options.text: Run the board member's 'reallocated' text as the story, attributed to an anonymous source
options.consequence: It's technically sourced, but a single anonymous hint with no documents; legal flags it, the editor holds it, and a competitor publishes the documented version first.

options.text: Skip the paperwork and just publish that funds are 'missing,' figuring you'll correct it if you're wrong
options.consequence: The nonprofit's lawyer sends a demand letter; the paper runs a humiliating retraction and your byline is now a liability the editor mentions in your review.

beats.title: Four Hours In A Folding Chair
beats.situation: You've sat through 90 minutes of zoning variances and a 20-minute argument about a dog park before the council finally reaches the property tax item. Your laptop battery is at 8%, the public comment period is dragging, and you still need the actual rate change and budget figures, not just the vote.
beats.decision: The vote is coming; what do you lock down before you can leave?

options.text: Grab the finance director after the vote for the exact old and new millage rates and the official budget document showing the dollar impact
options.consequence: You walk out with the real numbers in writing; tomorrow when readers and rivals dispute the figures, you have the source document and you're untouchable.

options.text: Record the whole meeting and plan to transcribe the key vote details back at the office
options.consequence: You have audio but no documents; you spend an extra hour scrubbing the recording and still have to email staff after hours for the figures you could've grabbed in person.

options.text: Leave right after the hands go up for the vote since you've got the 5-2 count and can fill in the rest from memory
options.consequence: You misremember the rate, publish a wrong percentage, and run a correction that the council's communications office gleefully circulates to undercut your reporting.

beats.title: Thirty Minutes To Publish
beats.situation: The council voted 5-2 to raise the property tax rate. As the room empties, Councilmember Jane Ruiz tells you on the record: 'This is the first tax increase in a decade.' Your editor wants it online in 30 minutes. You paste your notes into the AI writing assistant to draft fast.
beats.decision: How do you handle Ruiz's 'first increase in a decade' claim and the AI's draft before you hit publish?
beats.aiSuggestion: The AI assistant drafts your lede: 'The City Council voted 5-2 Tuesday to raise the property tax rate, the first increase in a decade, a move that will cost the average homeowner about $400 more per year.'

options.text: Ask the AI for its source on the $400; when it can't produce one, cut the figure unless the budget doc supports it, and attribute 'first in a decade' to Ruiz until you verify it
options.consequence: You publish a clean, attributed story; days later a reader points out the last hike was actually six years ago, and because you wrote 'Ruiz said,' the error is hers, not the paper's.

options.text: Keep the '$400' number but soften it to 'roughly $400,' and run the decade claim as fact because a sitting councilmember said it
options.consequence: The hedge doesn't save you; the finance office says the real impact is $260 on an average home, and you eat a correction on the dollar figure even though the vote count was right.

options.text: Publish the AI's lede as written to beat the 30-minute deadline; it sounds authoritative and specific
options.consequence: The fabricated $400 and the unverified 'first in a decade' both run in the paper's own voice; the city disputes both, the story gets pulled for two corrections, and your editor bans AI-drafted ledes newsroom-wide.

title: Video Editor / Filmmaker
oneLineReality: You spend far more time alone in a dark room dragging clips and chasing client notes than you do on glamorous sets, and breaking in means building a reel before anyone pays you a living wage.
typicalDay: Ingest, transcode and organize the day's footage into bins and proxies so the project doesn't choke your machine
Build a rough assembly: lay down the best interview soundbites or the script's beats and find the story's spine
Cut to picture lock while fielding a stream of client/director notes ('can we try the other take?')
Add B-roll, lower thirds, captions and a temp music bed, then balance audio levels
Do basic color correction and a pass for sync, flash frames and audio pops
Export deliverables in three different specs (web, broadcast, vertical social) and chase the render that failed at 98%
workStyle: Mostly solo, seated, screen-focused work with headphones on, punctuated by collaborative review sessions; heavily project-based and deadline-driven, with a large share of editors freelancing or working contract-to-contract.
boringHardPart: The unglamorous grind of media management and revisions: syncing dual-system audio, relinking offline media, exporting to a dozen finicky delivery specs, and re-cutting the same 30 seconds for the eighth time because the client 'isn't feeling it' but can't say why.
crashCourse: Learn the language of the edit: cut, J-cut/L-cut, jump cut, match cut, and the 180-degree rule
Master one NLE (non-linear editor) end-to-end before chasing every shiny new app
Understand that 70% of a 'video' problem is actually an audio problem
Color and sound are not afterthoughts: a graded, leveled cut sells the work
Story first: a technically perfect cut with no emotional rhythm is a dead cut

workSimulation.scenario: You're editing a 2-minute corporate testimonial. The client handed you a 40-minute talking-head interview and an hour of B-roll. You've pulled the best soundbite, but to make one clean sentence you had to splice two takes together, which leaves an ugly jump cut where the speaker's head visibly snaps to a new position.
workSimulation.task: How do you handle the jump cut so the edit reads as seamless and professional?

options.text: Cover the splice with a relevant B-roll cutaway while the audio of the soundbite continues underneath
options.feedback: Correct. This is the bread-and-butter fix for interview editing: the audio carries the story while a cutaway hides the visual cut entirely. It also adds production value by showing what the speaker is describing.

options.text: Leave the jump cut as-is; modern audiences are used to jump cuts from YouTube
options.feedback: Wrong context. Stylized jump cuts work for fast vlogs, but in a polished corporate testimonial an unintentional head-snap reads as a mistake and undermines the client's credibility.

options.text: Put a 1-second cross-dissolve on every cut so nothing looks abrupt
options.feedback: Overused dissolves look dated and mushy, and dissolving a hard interview cut just turns a jump cut into a blurry smear. Dissolves imply a passage of time, which is the wrong message here.

options.text: Speed-ramp through the splice so the viewer flies past it
options.feedback: A speed ramp draws attention to itself and distorts the speaker's voice. It's a music-video flourish, not a fix for a testimonial that needs to feel sincere and steady.

workSimulation.aiSuggestion: The AI assistant says: 'Don't bother hunting for B-roll. Just select both interview clips at the splice and apply Premiere Pro's Morph Cut transition to every jump cut. It uses face tracking to automatically blend the frames, so all your interview cuts will look seamless with one click.'
workSimulation.aiMistake: Morph Cut only renders cleanly when the subject's head position, framing, lighting and background stay roughly consistent across the two clips. In this footage the speaker visibly shifts position between takes, so Morph Cut's frame interpolation will produce obvious facial warping and ghosting artifacts right on the most important soundbite.
workSimulation.correctHumanJudgment: A human editor doesn't trust the auto-render: after applying any Morph Cut you scrub or play the rendered transition frame-by-frame to inspect for warping. When the head moves too much (as it does here), you abandon Morph Cut and cover the splice with a B-roll cutaway instead, the reliable fix.

aiCatchOptions.text: Morph Cut warps and ghosts the speaker's face when their position and framing change between the two takes, so it can't reliably hide this particular jump cut
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Exactly right. Morph Cut is an interpolation trick that needs a stable subject; with the speaker shifting position, it will smear the face on the key soundbite. You'd catch this by reviewing the rendered transition before trusting it.

aiCatchOptions.text: Morph Cut permanently deletes the source clips, so you could never undo the edit if the client wants the original takes back
aiCatchOptions.feedback: False. Morph Cut is a non-destructive transition applied at the cut point; the source media is untouched and the edit is fully reversible. That's not the real flaw.

aiCatchOptions.text: Morph Cut only functions on footage shot at 60fps or higher, so it won't even apply to a standard 24fps interview
aiCatchOptions.feedback: False. Morph Cut works across standard frame rates including 24 and 30fps. The real problem isn't frame rate, it's the subject moving between takes.

typicalDegree: Bachelor's degree (film, video production, or communication); strong portfolio/reel often matters more than the diploma

certificate.name: Adobe Certified Professional: Premiere Pro (video editing)

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 1: Pick one NLE and learn its spine
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Install DaVinci Resolve (free) or Premiere Pro. Learn import, timeline, ripple/roll trims, J/L-cuts and export. Re-edit a scene from existing footage to internalize the interface.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 1-2: Study the grammar of editing
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Watch a few scenes with the sound off, then off-screen with only sound. Read or watch 'In the Blink of an Eye' (Walter Murch) and take notes on why cuts happen, not just how.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 2-3: Shoot and cut a 60-second story
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Mini project: film a simple real story (someone making coffee, a skater, a friend's hobby) with a beginning/middle/end. Capture clean audio and deliberate B-roll, then cut it to a music bed.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 3: Master audio and a basic color pass
thirtyDayPlan.detail: On that same project, level dialogue to about -12dB, clean noise, add room tone, then do a primary color correction so shots match. Notice how much more 'pro' it feels.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 4: Deliver, get feedback, and start a reel
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Export web, broadcast-spec and vertical versions. Post the cut to an editing community (r/editors, a Discord) for critique, apply one round of notes, and start a 30-second highlight reel of your best moments.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Ongoing: Recreate a cut you admire
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Frame-match a 30-second sequence from a film or ad you love, shot for shot, to reverse-engineer professional pacing and build muscle memory.

automates: Generating rough transcripts and text-based rough cuts from interview audio
Auto-syncing multi-camera and dual-system audio
Creating burned-in captions and subtitles
Basic shot logging, scene detection and culling of unusable takes
First-pass auto color matching and audio leveling
Reframing horizontal footage to vertical for social
humanValue: Story structure and emotional pacing: knowing which 8 seconds of a 40-minute interview actually land
Taste and rhythm in where to cut, hold, or breathe
Reading a client or director and translating vague notes ('make it pop') into concrete changes
Matching the edit to brand, tone and audience intent
On-set judgment, directing talent and capturing the footage in the first place
Catching the subtle continuity, sync and artifact errors that automated tools confidently miss
aiImpact.riskNote: Generative and assistive AI is rapidly automating the mechanical layers of editing (transcription, rough cuts, captions, reframing, first-pass color), which is eroding the low-end work where beginners traditionally earned their first checks. Narrative judgment, taste, client relationships and the actual filmmaking on set remain stubbornly human, so the path increasingly favors editors who direct the AI rather than compete with it.

shift.intro: It's 8:30 AM, the office is empty, your headphones are on, and a 64GB card from yesterday's shoot is staring at you with a 6 PM client deadline glued to it.
shift.closer: A real edit day is ten hours alone in a dark room solving boring problems perfectly, where the win is invisible and the only thing the client ever notices is the one frame you got wrong.

beats.title: The Card Dump
beats.situation: The shoot delivered 64GB of 4K clips plus a separate audio recorder file. Your timeline will be choppy and your machine will thrash if you cut straight off the native media, and the audio from the camera mic sounds thin.
beats.decision: How do you set up the project before you touch a single cut?

options.text: Copy everything to two drives, transcode to proxies, build dated bins, and sync the external audio recorder to the camera clips before cutting
options.consequence: Three weeks later the client requests a re-export; your media relinks instantly and the synced audio is already locked, saving you a full afternoon

options.text: Skip proxies but at least rename clips into bins so you can find the good takes fast
options.consequence: You cut smoothly until the 4K playback starts dropping frames during the client review, forcing an awkward 'it's just my machine' apology

options.text: Drag the raw card straight into a new timeline and start cutting to save time
options.consequence: At 5 PM a clip goes offline mid-export, and with no backup of the wiped card you spend the night begging the DP for the original files

beats.title: Finding the Spine
beats.situation: The brief wants a 2-minute story, but you have a rambling 40-minute interview. The subject says the same idea three different ways and buries the best line in the middle of a tangent.
beats.decision: How do you build the rough assembly?

options.text: Watch all 40 minutes once, paper-edit the soundbites into a spine on a string-out, then cut only the lines that carry the story
options.consequence: The director watches the rough and says 'that's basically the whole story already' — your notes round is short and you finish a day early

options.text: Pull the obvious good lines into a selects timeline and arrange them by gut feel
options.consequence: It plays fine but a key cause-and-effect beat is missing; the client asks 'why does he jump to that?' and you re-cut the middle

options.text: Cut chronologically from the start of the interview and trim later to fit time
options.consequence: You burn four hours building a 6-minute cut that has to be gutted, and the real story was in a tangent you never reached

beats.title: The Jump Cut
beats.situation: You found the perfect soundbite, but the one clean sentence only exists because you spliced two takes together. Right on the most important line, the speaker's head visibly snaps to a new position — an ugly jump cut on the hero moment.
beats.decision: How do you make the splice read as seamless?
beats.aiSuggestion: The AI assistant says: 'Don't bother hunting for B-roll. Just select both interview clips at the splice and apply Premiere Pro's Morph Cut transition to every jump cut. It uses face tracking to automatically blend the frames, so all your interview cuts will look seamless with one click.'

options.text: Lay a relevant B-roll cutaway over the splice so the cut is hidden while the audio runs clean underneath
options.consequence: The hero line plays invisibly seamless; at the review the client never even notices a cut was made and signs off on picture lock

options.text: Apply Morph Cut but scrub the rendered transition frame-by-frame; when you see the warping, rip it out and cover with B-roll
options.consequence: You catch the ghosting and fix it, but the inspect-and-redo costs you 40 minutes you needed for the audio pass

options.text: Drop Morph Cut on every interview cut, trust the auto-render, and move on as the AI suggested
options.consequence: On the big screen at the review the speaker's face visibly melts and ghosts on the key line; the client loses trust and demands you recut the whole section

beats.title: The 98% Render
beats.situation: Picture is locked and the client needs three deliverables tonight: a web H.264, a broadcast ProRes, and a vertical 9:16 social cut. With ten minutes to the deadline, the broadcast export crashes at 98%.
beats.decision: The deadline is now. What do you do?

options.text: Send the finished web file now to buy time, then find the corrupt frame, drop a render cache on it, and re-export the broadcast spec clean
options.consequence: The client has something to show their boss on time; the fixed broadcast master passes QC the next morning with zero kickbacks

options.text: Re-queue the exact same broadcast export and hope the crash was a fluke
options.consequence: It dies at 98% again on the same bad frame; you lose 25 minutes to two failed renders before you actually diagnose it

options.text: Screen-record the timeline playback and send that as the 'broadcast' file to beat the clock
options.consequence: The station rejects the off-spec, half-resolution file; you've burned your credibility and still have to deliver the real master by morning

title: Photographer
oneLineReality: You sell a feeling, not a photo: half your week is shooting, the other half is editing, emailing clients, and chasing invoices for a median ~$42k a year.
typicalDay: Scout and set up: arrive early, read the light, position subjects, and meter exposure before the client even notices you working
Shoot in bursts: 1-3 hours of actually pressing the shutter, constantly adjusting aperture, shutter, ISO, and posing on the fly
Cull and cull again: import 1,500 frames, reject 90% of them, and pick the keepers (the part nobody warns you about)
Edit in Lightroom/Capture One: color, exposure, retouch skin, match a consistent look across the whole gallery
Client and business admin: answer inquiry emails, send contracts and invoices, deliver galleries, post to Instagram to feed the next booking
Back up everything twice (card, drive, cloud) because a corrupted card on a wedding day is a career-ending lawsuit
workStyle: Mostly self-employed freelance or small-studio; project-based with irregular, often weekend and evening hours. A mix of intense on-location people-work and long solo stretches at a screen.
boringHardPart: Culling and editing. For every hour shooting you spend two to three hours at a desk sorting near-identical frames and color-correcting hundreds of images to a consistent look, often late at night to hit delivery deadlines.
keyTools: Full-frame mirrorless camera (Sony A7 IV, Canon R6, Nikon Z6)
Off-camera flash / strobes + light modifiers (softbox, reflector)
Color-calibrated monitor + fast SSD storage and backup drives
Instagram & a portfolio website (Squarespace/Pixieset) as the real sales engine
crashCourse: Master manual exposure: the aperture / shutter / ISO triangle until it is muscle memory, not a menu hunt
Learn light, not gear: how to see, shape, and modify natural and flash light (open shade, golden hour, fill flash)
Shoot RAW and learn a real edit workflow in Lightroom: import, cull, white balance, tone, export
Build a 20-image portfolio in ONE niche (weddings, portraits, food, or product) so clients know what they're buying
Learn the business: pricing, contracts, model releases, invoicing, and how to turn a shoot into the next referral

workSimulation.scenario: A client books outdoor headshots for their LinkedIn at the only time they're free: 12:30 pm on a cloudless day. The sun is directly overhead, carving harsh dark shadows into their eye sockets and a hot bright stripe across their forehead.
workSimulation.task: You have 30 minutes and need flattering, even light on the face. What do you do?

options.text: Move the subject into open shade (under a building overhang or tree) and bounce a reflector to add soft fill light on the face
options.feedback: Correct. Open shade gives soft, even light with no raccoon-eye shadows, and the reflector adds catchlights and lifts the face. This is the standard pro fix for harsh midday sun and costs nothing.

options.text: Keep them in direct sun and raise ISO to 800 so the image looks brighter overall
options.feedback: Wrong. ISO changes overall exposure, not the direction or hardness of the light. The ugly overhead shadows and squinting stay exactly the same, and you've added noise for nothing.

options.text: Position them facing directly into the sun so the front of the face is fully lit
options.feedback: Wrong. The subject will squint, tear up, and you'll get a tense, uncomfortable expression. Front-on midday sun is flat and unflattering even when they manage to keep their eyes open.

options.text: Fire the tiny pop-up flash at full power while they stand in direct sun
options.feedback: Wrong. A weak on-camera pop-up flash can't overpower midday sun and produces flat, harsh light with hard shadows. It fights the sun instead of solving the shadow problem.

workSimulation.aiSuggestion: An AI photo-assistant says: 'No need to move. Just shoot in the direct sun wide open at f/1.8, expose for the brightest part of the face, then in Lightroom lift Shadows to +100 to open up the eye sockets. The blur will hide the harsh background and editing will balance everything out.'
workSimulation.aiMistake: Exposing for the brightest part of the skin under harsh overhead sun clips the highlights on the forehead and nose to pure white. That data is gone, no slider recovers it. And pushing Shadows to +100 on hard noon light bakes in noise and ugly color casts under the eyes. The squinting expression also can't be edited away. Light has to be solved in-camera, not in post.
workSimulation.correctHumanJudgment: A human photographer knows you fix bad light before you press the shutter, not after. They'd reposition into open shade with fill so the exposure is even and recoverable, protecting the highlights and the subject's comfort.

aiCatchOptions.text: Blown-out highlights on the skin are clipped (pure white) data that no edit can restore, and lifting shadows +100 on hard light adds noise and color casts. The lighting must be fixed in-camera.
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Right. Once the forehead and nose clip to 255/255/255 there is no detail to recover, and aggressive shadow lifting on noisy midday files looks muddy. The AI tried to fix a lighting problem in software.

aiCatchOptions.text: The AI chose the wrong aperture: f/1.8 is too shallow and the face will be out of focus for a headshot.
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Plausible but not the real flaw. f/1.8 is shallow but usable for a headshot if you nail focus on the eyes; the actual failure is clipped highlights and unrecoverable harsh light, not the aperture itself.

aiCatchOptions.text: Lightroom can't adjust shadows independently, so the +100 Shadows step is impossible.
aiCatchOptions.feedback: False. Lightroom absolutely has an independent Shadows slider. The problem isn't that the edit is impossible, it's that lifting shadows can't rebuild clipped highlights or remove the noise it introduces.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 1: Get off Auto
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Learn the exposure triangle. Shoot 100 frames a day in full Manual mode, deliberately changing aperture, shutter, and ISO so you can predict the result before you shoot.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 1-2: See the light
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Photograph the same subject at noon, in open shade, and at golden hour. Compare the files to physically understand why light direction and quality beat any gear upgrade.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 2: Learn the edit workflow
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Shoot RAW and run one full Lightroom pipeline: import, cull to the best 20, set white balance and tone, retouch, and export web-ready JPEGs with a consistent look.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 3: Mini project - shoot a real person
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Do a free 1-hour portrait session for a friend. Deliver a polished gallery of 15 edited images. This forces posing, directing, lighting, and culling end-to-end.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 3-4: Pick a niche and build a portfolio
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Choose ONE lane (portraits, weddings, food, or product) and assemble a tight 20-image portfolio plus a simple Pixieset/Squarespace site so prospects see exactly what you sell.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 4: Learn the business side
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Write a basic client contract and model release, set three pricing packages, and post your project to Instagram. Reach out to 5 people to book your first paid mini-session.

First-pass color and exposure edits matched to your style via AI presets
Skin retouching, object removal, and sky/background replacement in Photoshop
Generative stock and simple product/catalog images that used to be paid shoots
Upscaling, denoise, and old-photo restoration

Directing and putting real people at ease so the expression is genuine, not generated
Reading actual light and space in the room and making split-second creative calls
The trust, contract, and accountability a client needs for a real event they can't reshoot
A distinctive personal style and relationships that drive referrals and repeat bookings
aiImpact.riskNote: Generative AI and stock libraries are gutting the low end (stock, simple product and catalog work) and AI now does much of the editing grunt work. But live, people-present photography (weddings, events, portraits, photojournalism) needs a human in the room with accountability, so the threat is real but uneven.

shift.intro: It's 7 AM, your trunk is a heap of cards and batteries, two clients on the calendar, and the only thing standing between you and a $42k year is whether you can solve light faster than it changes on you.
shift.closer: Photography looked like pressing a shutter; it was really three quiet hours of fixing light, sorting near-identical frames, and backing up files at 2 AM so one corrupt card can't end your career.

beats.title: The empty venue
beats.situation: You arrive 90 minutes early at a barn wedding. Ceremony is at 2 PM, and you can already see the midday sun will rake hard through the huge west windows right behind where the couple will stand.
beats.decision: Nobody's here yet. How do you use the hour before guests arrive?

options.text: Walk the room, meter the window light for 2 PM, mark a spot in open shade for portraits, and set a flash-fails backup plan.
options.consequence: At 2 PM your ceremony exposure is dead-on and the portraits glow; the wedding planner books you for her sister's wedding three weeks later.

options.text: Skip the walkthrough; you'll read the room live and fix any harsh light with on-the-fly flash.
options.consequence: Your flash recycles too slow during the vows and you miss the first kiss in clean light; you salvage it, but spend an extra hour that night rescuing the frame.

options.text: You've shot barns before. Grab coffee and chill until guests show.
options.consequence: The couple is rim-lit against blown-white windows; you burn four editing nights masking backgrounds and the gallery still looks flat.

beats.title: Noon sun, no shade
beats.situation: Between gigs, a LinkedIn-headshot client meets you outdoors at the only time they're free: 12:30 on a cloudless day. The sun is straight overhead, carving black shadows into their eye sockets and a hot white stripe across their forehead. You have 30 minutes.
beats.decision: You need flattering, even light on the face right now. What do you do?
beats.aiSuggestion: Your AI photo-assistant says: 'No need to move them. Shoot wide open at f/1.8 in the direct sun, expose for the brightest part of the face, then in Lightroom lift Shadows to +100 to open the eye sockets. The blur hides the harsh background and editing balances everything out.'

options.text: Move the client into open shade under the building's awning, add a touch of fill, and meter for even light on the face before shooting.
options.consequence: Highlights stay intact, eyes are open and relaxed; the client uses the shot the next morning and DMs you two referrals from their team that week.

options.text: Stay put but expose for the shadows to protect the eyes, planning to pull the bright forehead down later.
options.consequence: Eyes are saved but the forehead and nose still clip to paper-white; you spend an hour cloning texture back and the skin looks plasticky on close inspection.

options.text: Trust the AI: shoot at f/1.8 in direct sun, expose for the bright skin, fix it with Shadows +100 in post.
options.consequence: The clipped forehead is pure white with no data to recover, +100 shadows bake green-magenta noise under the eyes, and the squint can't be edited out; the client asks for a free reshoot and you eat the time.

beats.title: 1,500 frames, 60 finals
beats.situation: Cards imported. The headshot set plus a brand shoot leave you 1,500 frames staring back. The contract promises 60 delivered images, and your eyes are already burning.
beats.decision: How do you get from 1,500 to the keepers?

options.text: Do a fast first pass flagging only keepers, ruthlessly reject blinks and soft frames, then a second pass to refine down to the 60 strongest.
options.consequence: The final set is tight and every frame earns its place; the client posts six of them and tags you, and the post pulls in a new inquiry by Friday.

options.text: Keep 200 'just in case' and deliver the extras to look generous.
options.consequence: The client is overwhelmed, picks three soft near-duplicates as their favorites, and emails asking why some look blurry; the bloat makes your work read as unpolished.

options.text: Deliver every sharp frame and let the client choose their own; saves you the sorting.
options.consequence: You hand over 400 near-identical shots; the client feels they did your job, leaves a 3-star review citing 'no curation,' and doesn't rebook.

beats.title: Gallery due at 9
beats.situation: Sixty selects, gallery due 9 AM, you're color-matching skin tones shot under three different lights with your eyes half closed. The card is still the only copy of everything.
beats.decision: Last stretch before you can sleep. How do you close it out?

options.text: Build a base look, sync white balance across the set, spot-check skin tones on the calibrated screen, then back up to drive and cloud before bed.
options.consequence: The gallery lands at 8:40 with one consistent look; the cloud copy saves you a week later when the original drive dies mid-export.

options.text: Edit each image individually by feel to skip building a preset, then back up just to the drive.
options.consequence: You deliver on time but the skin tones drift warm-to-pink across the set; the client notices the inconsistency and you re-export 20 frames the next evening.

options.text: Batch one preset onto all 60, export, and crash without backing up; you'll copy it tomorrow.
options.consequence: The mixed-light frames look muddy and uneven, and at 6 AM the card throws a read error mid-copy; half the brand shoot is gone and there's no second copy to fall back on.

title: Lawyer (Attorney)
oneLineReality: You sell judgment and writing, not courtroom drama — most days are reading dense documents, drafting, and managing anxious clients, with pay that splits sharply between BigLaw riches and a long tail that barely clears the cost of the degree.
typicalDay: Read and mark up contracts, pleadings, or discovery documents for hours — the bulk of legal work is careful reading, not talking
Draft a brief, motion, demand letter, or memo and rewrite it three times until every sentence survives scrutiny
Take calls or emails from clients who want certainty you cannot honestly give, and translate law into plain decisions
Confer with opposing counsel to negotiate deadlines, settlement terms, or contract redlines
Log billable time in 6-minute increments and reconcile it against what you actually did
Research a narrow legal question across statutes, case law, and regulations to make sure your position holds up
workStyle: Mostly solo deep work at a desk punctuated by high-stakes interactions; deadline-driven and adversarial, with long hours common in litigation and corporate firms. Remote-friendly for transactional work, but court appearances, depositions, and closings are in person and unmovable.
boringHardPart: Document review and discovery: reading tens of thousands of emails and files to flag the few that matter, for days on end. The intellectual work is real, but the volume is grinding, the deadlines are immovable, and a single missed detail can blow up a case or a deal.
keyTools: Practice management and billing software (Clio, TimeSolv)
crashCourse: Read one real contract or court opinion and try to summarize the single most important clause in plain English
Learn IRAC (Issue, Rule, Application, Conclusion) — the structure every legal argument is built on
Take a free LSAT practice section to feel whether dense logical reading energizes or drains you
Shadow or interview a working attorney about hours and debt, not just the wins
Skim a state bar's rules of professional conduct to see the ethical lines you cannot cross

workSimulation.scenario: You are a first-year associate at a firm representing a 15-person software startup. The client is about to sign a Master Services Agreement (MSA) with an enterprise customer. The customer's draft includes a limitation-of-liability clause that caps your client's total liability but lists no exceptions.
workSimulation.task: The partner asks you to redline the limitation-of-liability clause to protect the client. Which change best balances closing the deal with protecting your client?

options.text: Make the cap mutual and add carve-outs so the cap does NOT apply to breaches of confidentiality, IP infringement indemnity, and gross negligence/willful misconduct.
options.feedback: Correct. A mutual cap is fair and likely to be accepted, while carve-outs preserve full recovery for the catastrophic risks (data breach, IP claims, bad-faith conduct) that a hard cap should never shield. This is the standard, deal-preserving market position.

options.text: Delete the limitation-of-liability clause entirely so your client can recover unlimited damages.
options.feedback: Wrong. Limitation clauses are mutual swords — deleting it exposes YOUR client to unlimited liability too, and the counterparty will never accept it. You would kill the deal and increase your client's risk.

options.text: Accept the customer's cap as drafted but lower the dollar figure by 20%.
options.feedback: Wrong. Haggling the number while leaving zero carve-outs means a data breach or IP suit is still capped at a token amount. You optimized the wrong variable and left the real exposures unprotected.

options.text: Demand unlimited liability for both sides with no cap at all.
options.feedback: Wrong. No sophisticated counterparty signs uncapped mutual liability, and it is not in your client's interest either. This is a non-starter that signals inexperience and stalls the negotiation.

workSimulation.aiSuggestion: The AI contract assistant drafts the carve-outs and proposes the liability cap as: 'each party's total liability shall not exceed the amounts paid by Customer to Provider in the twelve (12) months preceding the claim.' It says this is the standard market cap and recommends inserting it.
workSimulation.aiMistake: The cap is tied to amounts ALREADY PAID in the trailing 12 months. For a brand-new contract — or any low-spend early period — almost nothing has been paid yet, so the effective cap is near $0 in the months when disputes are most likely. It silently guts the client's own recovery.
workSimulation.correctHumanJudgment: A human catches that the cap should track contractual VALUE, not backward-looking payments. Fix it to 'the total fees payable under this Agreement in the 12 months following the Effective Date' or add a fixed dollar floor, so the cap is meaningful from day one regardless of how little has been invoiced.

aiCatchOptions.text: Pegging the cap to amounts already paid in the trailing 12 months makes the effective cap near $0 early in the term, when disputes are most likely — it should be based on contract value or carry a fixed floor.
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Right. The trailing-payments formula looks standard but quietly leaves the client with almost no recoverable amount during the risky opening months. Tie it to fees payable or add a floor.

aiCatchOptions.text: The AI forgot to make the limitation clause mutual, exposing only your client to the cap.
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Incorrect — the AI's language says 'each party's total liability,' so the cap is already mutual. The real flaw is the trailing-payments measurement, not mutuality.

aiCatchOptions.text: The AI applied the wrong governing law to the liability clause.
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Incorrect — governing law is a separate clause and the AI never touched it. This is a plausible-sounding distraction; the actual defect is that the cap measures paid amounts instead of contract value.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 1: Learn the core argument structure
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Master IRAC (Issue, Rule, Application, Conclusion) and write three short IRAC analyses on simple fact patterns from a free 1L resource.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 1-2: Test your reading stamina
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Take one timed LSAT Logical Reasoning and Reading Comprehension section. Note whether dense, adversarial reading energizes or exhausts you — this is the daily reality of the job.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 2: Read primary sources
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Read two real appellate opinions and one commercial contract end to end. For each, write the single most important holding or clause in two plain sentences.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 3: Talk to real attorneys
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Interview two working lawyers in different settings (e.g., a BigLaw associate and a public-defender or solo). Ask specifically about hours, debt load, and what they would do differently.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 4: Mini project — redline a contract
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Take a free sample NDA or MSA online and redline the limitation-of-liability and indemnification clauses, adding carve-outs. Write a one-page memo to a hypothetical client explaining your changes in plain English.

thirtyDayPlan.title: Week 4: Reality-check the finances
thirtyDayPlan.detail: Build a simple spreadsheet: 3 years of J.D. tuition at a target school plus living costs versus realistic entry salaries for that school's graduates. Decide if the math works for you.

Drafting routine clauses, NDAs, and standard contract first drafts
Legal research summaries and pulling relevant case citations
Deposition and transcript summarization
Due-diligence document tagging and data-room organization
humanValue: Strategic judgment on what risk a specific client should actually accept
Courtroom advocacy, oral argument, and live negotiation
Reading a client's real goals and managing them through fear and emotion
Bearing professional and ethical responsibility — a license and malpractice liability you cannot delegate to software
Catching the subtle, context-specific error an AI confidently produces (like a cap that reads to $0)
aiImpact.riskNote: AI is hollowing out the document-review and first-draft work that used to keep junior associates billable, which threatens the bottom of the profession. But the licensed, accountable core — judgment, advocacy, signing your name on advice a client bets their company on — is well protected. The risk is to entry-level leverage, not to senior attorneys.

shift.intro: 7:48 a.m., second coffee going cold, and the partner has already forwarded you a 60-page discovery dump and a contract that 'just needs a quick look' before the client signs Friday.
shift.closer: It looked like reading and typing all day, but every quiet hour was you alone deciding which buried sentence could sink a company — and owning it if you missed it.

beats.title: The Document Mountain
beats.situation: Discovery deadline is in 36 hours. You have 18,000 emails to review and flag anything responsive or privileged. A vendor offers predictive coding; the senior associate says 'just eyeball the ones with the keyword.' The volume is impossible to read fully by hand.
beats.decision: How do you run this document review under an immovable deadline?

options.text: Run a documented keyword + technology-assisted review, then manually sample and verify the cuts before producing
options.consequence: Two weeks later opposing counsel challenges your production; your logged methodology and sample QC hold up, and the judge accepts it as defensible.

options.text: Personally read every email start to finish, no tools, to be safe
options.consequence: You catch everything but blow the deadline by a day; the partner eats a sanctions-risk extension request and quietly notes you can't scale.

options.text: Just produce everything that hits the keyword and skip privilege screening to save time
options.consequence: Three privileged strategy emails go out the door; the inadvertent waiver fight costs the client weeks and nearly the case.

beats.title: The Client Who Wants Certainty
beats.situation: Your startup client calls, panicked: 'Are we going to win the dispute or not? Just tell me yes or no.' The honest answer is a range of probabilities, not a guarantee. They want comfort you can't legally or ethically promise.
beats.decision: How do you handle the client demanding a guarantee?

options.text: Translate the law into plain terms: lay out likely outcomes, risks, and a recommended path without promising a result
options.consequence: The CEO calms down, makes an informed call to negotiate, and later credits you for being the one advisor who shot straight.

options.text: Hedge with dense legalese and 'it depends' until they stop asking
options.consequence: You stay technically accurate but the client feels abandoned, second-guesses the firm, and shops the matter to another lawyer.

options.text: Tell them what they want to hear: 'Don't worry, we've got this, we'll win'
options.consequence: You lose a motion months later; the blindsided client threatens a malpractice complaint over your guarantee.

beats.title: The Liability Clause
beats.situation: First-year associate work: the 15-person software client signs a Master Services Agreement with an enterprise customer Friday. The customer's draft caps total liability but lists no exceptions. The partner says 'redline the limitation-of-liability clause to protect our client.' You open the firm's AI contract assistant for a first pass.
beats.decision: Which redline best balances closing the deal with protecting your client?
beats.aiSuggestion: The AI contract assistant drafts carve-outs and proposes the cap as: 'each party's total liability shall not exceed the amounts paid by Customer to Provider in the twelve (12) months preceding the claim.' It flags this as the standard market cap and recommends inserting it as-is.

options.text: Catch that a trailing-paid cap is near $0 early on; tie it to fees PAYABLE in the 12 months after the Effective Date and add a fixed dollar floor, plus carve-outs for IP, confidentiality, and indemnity
options.consequence: Six months in, a data incident hits during low-spend onboarding; the value-based cap with a floor gives your client real recovery instead of pocket change.

options.text: Keep the AI's trailing-payment cap but add the missing carve-outs for indemnity and confidentiality
options.consequence: The carve-outs help, but the general cap is still backward-looking; an early dispute leaves your client capped at the trickle they've invoiced so far.

options.text: Insert the AI's clause verbatim as the 'standard market cap' and send the redline to the partner
options.consequence: An early-stage breach surfaces; the cap computes to almost nothing paid yet, gutting your client's recovery, and the partner traces the gap straight to your redline.

beats.title: The Final Brief
beats.situation: Motion is due to the court at midnight. Your brief is solid but you found a controlling case that cuts against your argument. The partner left; nobody would notice if you quietly omitted it. The deadline is hard and you're exhausted.
beats.decision: What do you do with the adverse precedent the night the brief is due?

options.text: Cite the adverse case, then distinguish it on the facts and argue why it doesn't control here
options.consequence: The judge respects the candor; your distinction lands and the credibility carries weight in the ruling weeks later.

options.text: Mention it in a buried footnote without really engaging the holding
options.consequence: You technically disclosed it, but opposing counsel spotlights your weak treatment and the court leans their way on that point.

options.text: Omit the adverse case entirely and hope opposing counsel misses it
options.consequence: Opposing counsel cites it, the judge notes your duty of candor to the tribunal, and your firm's credibility takes a hit on every future filing in that courtroom.

title: Police Officer
oneLineReality: You spend most shifts on routine calls, paperwork, and waiting — punctuated by rare moments of real danger where your training and judgment are everything.
typicalDay: Attend roll call / briefing at shift start: review BOLOs (be-on-the-lookout alerts), overnight crime, and patrol assignments
Patrol an assigned beat in a marked unit, running plates and responding to dispatched calls (CAD) ranked by priority
Handle a mix of calls: traffic stops, welfare checks, noise complaints, thefts, minor crashes, and the occasional in-progress crime
Conduct field interviews, collect statements, photograph scenes, and secure evidence with a documented chain of custody
Spend a large chunk of the shift writing reports — incident reports, citations, use-of-force and arrest paperwork — in records management software
Testify in court or prep with prosecutors on days off or mid-shift when a case you worked goes to trial
workStyle: Shift-based and field-driven. You work rotating shifts including nights, weekends, and holidays, mostly outdoors and in your patrol car, alone or with a partner but always backed by dispatch and nearby units. Long stretches of low-key routine interrupted by unpredictable, high-adrenaline incidents. Heavy public contact, strict chain of command, body-worn camera always recording.
boringHardPart: Reports. A single arrest can mean an hour-plus of detailed, legally-precise writing, and sloppy paperwork gets cases thrown out or you sued. Add court appearances on your own time, mandatory overtime that wrecks plans, and the slow grind of repetitive calls (the same addresses, the same disputes) that rarely get truly 'solved'.
keyTools: CAD (Computer-Aided Dispatch) and the in-car MDT/laptop
Records Management System (RMS) for report writing
NCIC/state databases for warrant, plate, and license checks
Service weapon, TASER, OC (pepper) spray, baton, and handcuffs
Police radio, body armor, and a duty belt
crashCourse: Learn the constitutional basics that govern every stop: 4th Amendment (search/seizure), reasonable suspicion vs. probable cause, and Miranda
Ride along with a local department (most offer civilian ride-alongs) to see a real shift before committing
Get fit now — research your target academy's physical test (1.5-mile run, push-ups, sit-ups) and train to pass it cold
Understand the hiring funnel: written exam, physical, oral board, polygraph, psych eval, and a deep background investigation
Study use-of-force law and de-escalation frameworks (Graham v. Connor 'objective reasonableness') — the core of modern policing judgment

workSimulation.scenario: It's 11 PM. You stop a car for a broken taillight. The driver is sweating, hands trembling, and won't make eye contact. The neighborhood is known for drug activity. You suspect there may be contraband in the vehicle and you want to search it.
workSimulation.task: What is the legally sound next step that protects both the case and you from a lawsuit?

options.text: Order the driver out and search the whole vehicle now — nervousness in a high-crime area is enough to justify it.
options.feedback: No. Nervousness plus a high-crime area does not equal probable cause. A warrantless search on this basis is unconstitutional, the evidence gets suppressed, and you and the department are exposed to a civil rights lawsuit.

options.text: Run the license and registration, stay alert for articulable facts (plain-view contraband, odor, admissions), and only search if you develop probable cause or obtain voluntary consent.
options.feedback: Correct. You complete the stop's mission while building a lawful basis. Probable cause (e.g., plain-view contraband or odor) triggers the automobile exception — no warrant needed — and valid consent is always lawful. The case holds up.

options.text: Handcuff the driver and hold them at the roadside for 40 minutes until a K-9 unit can arrive to sniff the car.
options.feedback: Wrong. Under Rodriguez v. United States you cannot prolong a stop beyond the time needed for its original purpose to wait on a dog without independent reasonable suspicion. A 40-minute hold turns a lawful stop into an unlawful seizure.

options.text: Give a verbal warning and send the driver off without running their info — it's not worth the hassle.
options.feedback: Unsafe and negligent. You'd skip a basic officer-safety and warrant check, and ignore signs worth lawful follow-up. Doing nothing isn't the answer; doing it within the law is.

workSimulation.aiSuggestion: The department's CAD assistant flags the stop and advises: 'Subject shows multiple deception indicators and you're in a documented high-crime corridor. That gives you reasonable suspicion — you're clear to search the vehicle for officer safety. Proceed with the search.'
workSimulation.aiMistake: The AI treats 'reasonable suspicion' as if it authorizes a full vehicle search. It does not. Reasonable suspicion only supports a brief investigative detention (a Terry stop) and, for safety, a limited frisk of a person for weapons — not a search of the car for contraband. Searching a vehicle without a warrant requires the higher probable cause standard (or valid consent).
workSimulation.correctHumanJudgment: An experienced officer recognizes the two legal standards are not interchangeable: nervousness and the area might justify briefly detaining and investigating, but a contraband search of the car needs probable cause or consent. The officer keeps investigating to either develop PC or get consent, rather than searching on the AI's flawed green light and torpedoing the case.

aiCatchOptions.text: The AI confused 'reasonable suspicion' with the higher 'probable cause' standard that a warrantless vehicle search actually requires.
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Exactly right. Reasonable suspicion supports only a brief detention or a weapons frisk of a person — not a contraband search of the car. That needs probable cause or consent.

aiCatchOptions.text: The AI was wrong because any vehicle search first requires a warrant signed by a judge, no matter what.
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Incorrect. The 'automobile exception' lets officers search a vehicle without a warrant when they have probable cause. The AI's real error was the standard it applied, not skipping a warrant.

aiCatchOptions.text: The AI was wrong because courts never allow a high-crime area to be considered as a factor.
aiCatchOptions.feedback: Incorrect. Under Illinois v. Wardlow, presence in a high-crime area is a legitimate factor courts weigh. The flaw was using those factors to justify a search rather than just a detention.
